title: Parental and early child skills outweigh home numeracy environment in predicting maths development
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Studies on the home numeracy environment (HNE) show mixed evidence of its link with children's mathematical skills. A rarely considered aspect is parents' dual role as providers of the home environment and transmitters of genetic predispositions relevant for learning. Parents' maths abilities may serve as a proxy for the genetic transmission that confounds the home-child association, as proposed in the Familial Control Method. We examined whether numeracy activities at home predict children's maths development, while accounting for parents' maths ability and children's initial skill level.

METHODS: We analysed data from 244 Norwegian school children, 201 mothers and 146 fathers. Children's maths fluency was assessed in Grades 1, 3, 4, 5 and 6. Parents completed an HNE questionnaire and a maths assessment when children were in Grade 2. Relations among HNE, parental maths and children's maths development were tested using structural equation modelling.

RESULTS: Both formal and informal HNE predicted Grade 3 maths. After controlling for parental maths, only mothers' informal HNE remained associated with Grade 3 performance. When Grade 1 maths was included, only fathers' formal activities were related to Grade 3 skills, while both parents' maths still predicted Grade 3 performance. Only Grade 1 maths predicted Grade 3 as well as subsequent growth.

CONCLUSIONS: The finding that parental maths predicted children's maths beyond family activities underscores the importance of addressing familial confounding in research on the home environment. To better understand the role of the HNE in maths development, research should consider parents' skills, children's early skills and HNE as a dynamic process.

title: ADHD symptoms and learning difficulties: co-occurrence and directionality from Grades 1 to 9
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are at increased risk of learning difficulties. This association may reflect shared risk factors, ADHD symptoms hindering learning, or learning difficulties increasing ADHD symptoms. We aimed to map rates of co-occurrence among ADHD, dyslexia, dyscalculia, and reading comprehension difficulties and to investigate directional influences between ADHD symptoms and reading fluency, arithmetic, and reading comprehension.

METHODS: Reading fluency, arithmetic, and reading comprehension were assessed longitudinally in approximately 2,000 Finnish children across Grades 1-9 (ages 7-16). Attention/hyperactivity symptoms were measured with teacher ratings (Grades 1-4) and self-reports (Grades 6-9). ADHD, dyslexia, dyscalculia, and reading comprehension difficulties were based on a 10th percentile cut-off. Directionality between ADHD symptoms and academic skills was examined using random intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPMs) to separate stable traits from time-specific states.

RESULTS: Children with a learning difficulty were 1.14-1.76 times more likely to have ADHD, whereas children with one learning difficulty were 4.32-4.62 times more likely to have another. The RI-CLPMs showed consistent autoregressive effects across all domains, indicating stable within-person variation over time. At the between-person level (i.e. trait), academic skills were negatively related to ADHD symptoms, especially those reported by teachers. At the within-person level (i.e. state), ADHD symptoms were unrelated to reading fluency and arithmetic. However, at multiple time points, cross-lagged effects emerged from ADHD symptoms to subsequent reading comprehension, indicating that elevated ADHD symptoms predicted subsequent declines in reading comprehension.

CONCLUSIONS: Learning difficulties co-occurred more frequently with each other (homotypic) than with ADHD (heterotypic co-occurrence). Both ADHD symptoms and learning difficulties showed trait-like stability. After accounting for these, ADHD symptoms were no longer linked to reading fluency or arithmetic. However, more ADHD symptoms predicted later declines in reading comprehension, likely because comprehension requires sustained attention - often impaired in children with hyperactivity and inattention.

title: Impaired visual-motor integration function in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: potential neural correlates from resting-state fNIRS
abstract: Visual-motor integration (VMI) impairment is common in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), yet its underlying neurobiological basis remains unclear. This study aimed to explore the characteristics of VMI in children with ADHD and its statistical role in the association between functional connectivity (FC) and core symptoms. A total of 332 children with ADHD and 103 healthy controls (HC) completed the Beery-Buktenica Developmental Test of Visual-Motor Integration (Beery VMI). Group comparisons and dimensional correlation analyses were performed to explore the VMI characteristics of children with ADHD. Subsequently, 127 children with ADHD and 91 HC children underwent resting-state functional near-infrared spectroscopy. Mediation analyses were performed to investigate the role of VMI in the relationship between atypical FC and core symptoms of ADHD. Children with ADHD exhibited deficits in VMI performance, with 28.92% showing abnormal VMI. VMI was negatively correlated with core ADHD symptoms. At the network level, VMI showed significant statistical indirect associations in the relationship between FC of DMN-DMN, DMN-DAN, and DMN-VAN networks and inattention symptoms, and between FC of the DMN-DAN networks and hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms. At the channel level, VMI was also indirectly associated with FC of the left superior frontal gyrus (SFG)-right middle occipital gyrus (MOG) and ADHD core symptoms. Children with ADHD have deficits in VMI, and poorer VMI performance is associated with greater severity of core ADHD symptoms. Altered intra- and inter- network FC of the DMN may represent a potential neural correlate of VMI impairment in ADHD.

title: Psychiatric and substance use disorder polygenic scores are associated with the exposome in youth
abstract: Gene-environment correlations (rGE) present challenges for accurately estimating the individual and joint contributions of genetic and environmental influences on risk for psychiatric and substance use disorders. The present study examined rGE between polygenic risk scores (PGS) for psychiatric and substance use disorders and environmental exposures (i.e., exposome factors) using multi-level data spanning youth- and parent-reports, as well as objective measures of the built environment. Participants included 4,797 genetically similar to European reference populations, 1,585 genetically similar to African reference populations, and 2,012 genetically similar to Admixed American reference populations from the Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study. The ABCD study was conducted at 21 sites across the U.S and used a stratified probability sampling design to ensure the cohort recruited was demographically diverse. Based on factor-analytic work conducted by Moore et al. (2022) in the ABCD study, the exposome included 6 factors: household adversity, neighborhood adversity, positive day-to-day experiences, state conservatism/ruralness, family values, and pregnancy/birth complications. Disorder-specific PGS for psychiatric (e.g., major depressive disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) and substance use conditions (e.g., alcohol use disorders, cannabis use disorders), as well as PGS for common liability for externalizing and general substance use disorders, were used to examine genetic associations with the exposome factors. After adjusting for participant sex, age, log income-to-needs ratio, and genetic ancestry principal components, higher PGS for psychiatric (e.g., broad externalizing liability, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) and substance use disorders (e.g., general substance use disorders, cannabis use disorder) were positively associated with household adversity and negatively associated with positive day-to-day experiences. Our results indicate that polygenic risk for psychiatric and substance use disorders correlate with environmental factors in adolescence at multiple levels, most notably household adversity and positive day-to-day experiences. Findings underscore the importance of investigating rGE when examining these environmental exposures with genetic risk for psychiatric and substance use disorders.

title: From childhood to adulthood: an attempt to model long-term outcomes of ADHD using machine learning
authors: van der Plas N et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Childhood-onset attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) persists in 28% to 58% of individuals, and is associated with adverse long-term outcomes, like additional psychiatric diagnoses and lower educational attainment. Knowing early life predictors for adverse long-term outcomes might help develop preventive measures, but too few have been identified using conventional statistical models. The current study investigated the potential of machine learning in identifying predictors for ADHD persistence and long-term functioning of adults with childhood-onset ADHD.

METHOD: A total of 133 adults (M age  = 29.53, SD age  = 2.83, 75% males) from an 18-year prospective cohort study were assessed on ADHD persistence and long-term functioning. Machine learning models were developed using cross-validation, with and without additional resampling, and compared to a conventional logistic/linear regression model. With SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) we explored model behavior. Childhood predictors encompassed ADHD symptoms and treatment, other psychopathology, cognition, somatic characteristics, ADHD polygenic risk score, and parental demographics and psychopathology.

RESULTS: Performance of all models for ADHD persistence and functioning (quality of life) was low. Best performing models included the logistic regression model with resampling for ADHD persistence (AUC's all models  = .52-.58; AUC logistic regression, resampling  = .58), and the ridge regression model for long-term functioning (R 2 's all models  = -0.36-0.02; R 2 's ridge regression  = .02, RMSE's  all models  = 2.07-2.42; RMSE's ridge regression  = 2.07).

CONCLUSIONS: Findings highlight the complexity of predicting long-term outcomes of ADHD. Model improvement is crucial before models can inform clinical practice, e.g., by increasing sample size and investigating additional predictors.

title: Context-dependent gaze patterns in children with social anxiety disorder during repeated peer-evaluative stress: A naturalistic eye-tracking study
abstract: Childhood social anxiety disorder (SAD) has been linked to altered attention to socially relevant cues, but findings on gaze behavior in youth remain mixed, particularly in naturalistic social-evaluative contexts. We examined whether children with SAD differ from healthy controls (HC) in gaze to peer faces during repeated peer-evaluative speech tasks. Children aged 9-14 years with SAD (n = 37) and HC (n = 41) completed two peer-evaluative speech tasks while gaze behavior was recorded with mobile eye-tracking. Before the second speech, participants were randomly assigned either to parental support or self-instruction during the anticipation phase. Fixation probability and fixation duration on audience faces were analyzed across the first four minutes of each speech. During the first speech, no significant group differences were observed for fixation probability or fixation duration. During the second speech, children with SAD showed lower fixation probability than HC, whereas no group differences emerged for fixation duration. Exploratory analyses suggested that fixation probability during the second speech varied by support condition and age. These findings suggest that gaze differences in childhood SAD may be subtle and context-dependent rather than uniformly evident across social-evaluative situations. In this sample, reduced fixation probability was observed during the second speech task only. Further research with larger samples and designs that disentangle repeated exposure from task- or stimulus-specific factors is needed.

title: Adult Attention Deficit-Hyperactivity Disorder
abstract: Attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a medical condition that is present in approximately 2.5% of adults worldwide and manifests in a variety of different ways across the lifespan. Adults with ADHD often have coexisting psychiatric disorders such as anxiety, mood, sleep, substance use, and personality disorders and are at increased risk for coexisting somatic conditions such as obesity, cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease, type 1 and type 2 diabetes, and immune and inflammatory conditions. Hence, such adults may be seen by clinicians providing care for a wide range of psychiatric and somatic conditions. Nevertheless, ADHD remains unrecognized and undiagnosed in many persons. Assessment requires interviewing of the patient for core ADHD symptoms, coexisting conditions, and their functional effects, which can be facilitated by using standardized rating scales. Key components of treatment are psychoeducation and psychostimulant or nonstimulant medication, mostly in combination with psychosocial interventions and lifestyle guidance.

title: Change in HbA(1c) and weight after initiation of antipsychotic treatment in people with severe mental illness in England: an individual-level interrupted time-series analysis
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Second-generation antipsychotics contribute to excess cardiometabolic morbidity in people with severe mental illness, but the timing of early glycaemic change and whether it parallels weight gain remain unclear. We aimed to evaluate glycated haemoglobin A 1c  (HbA 1c ) and weight trajectories before and after initiation of antipsychotic treatment.

METHODS: We conducted an individual-level interrupted time-series analysis in England using electronic health records (EHR) from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink Aurum database between Jan 1, 2000, and June 7, 2023. Included participants were aged 18-59 years with severe mental illness (SMI) who had at least a second oral second-generation antipsychotic prescription issued within 90 days from their first antipsychotic prescription. Individuals were excluded if they had dementia, type 2 diabetes, or antipsychotic prescriptions before age 18 years. The exposure was the first recorded oral initiation of antipsychotic treatment. We used individual-level, interrupted time-series mixed models with linear splines to estimate rates of change in HbA 1c  and weight in people with SMI before treatment initiation, 0-90 days after initiation, and from 91 days to 2 years after initiation. An additional outcome was time to type 2 diabetes diagnosis or antidiabetic medication prescription. Analyses were stratified by sex, antipsychotic drug, and baseline glycaemic status. People with lived experience contributed to the research question, study approach, interpretation, and dissemination.

FINDINGS: Of the 96 849 eligible individuals, 53 558 (55·3%) were male and 43 291 (44·7%) were female. The mean age of participants was 37·2 years (SD 11·1; range 18-59); 62 683 (64·7%) reported their ethnicity as White, 5952 (6·1%) as south Asian, 6736 (7·0%) as Black, 3793 (3·9%) as other or mixed ethnicity, and 17 693 (18·3%) had missing ethnicity. 74 233 (76·6%) individuals had at least one recorded weight measurement and 24 084 (24·9%) had at least one HbA 1c  measurement. In the pre-treatment period, HbA 1c  increased at a rate of 0·01 mmol/mol per week (95% CI 0·00-0·01) and weight at a rate of 0·02 kg (0·02-0·02) per week. In the 0-90 days following antipsychotic treatment initiation, HbA 1c  increased at a rate of 0·12 mmol/mol per week (0·09-0·15) and weight at 0·21 kg (0·20-0·22) per week. From day 91 to 2 years, the rate of increase of HbA 1c  returned to pre-treatment levels (0·01 mmol/mol per week [0·00-0·01]) and weight increased at 0·03 kg (0·02-0·03) per week. Increases were largest for olanzapine (HbA 1c  0·18 mmol/mol per week [95% CI 0·12-0·25]; weight 0·28 kg [0·27-0·30]) and generally higher among women (HbA 1c  0·14 mmol/mol [0·09-0·18]; weight 0·22 kg [0·21-0·23]). Quetiapine was associated with weight gain (0·19 kg per week [95% CI 0·18 to 0·21]), but minimal HbA 1c  change (0·02 mmol/mol [-0·03 to 0·08]). Among 918 individuals with baseline prediabetes, 126 (13·7%)developed type 2 diabetes, corresponding to an estimated 2-year cumulative incidence of 19·0%, compared with 152 (1·7%) of 9171 individuals with normal baseline HbA 1c , corresponding to an estimated 2-year cumulative incidence of 3·0%.

INTERPRETATION: Antipsychotic treatment initiation was followed by rapid HbA 1c  and weight increases in the first 90 days followed by slower increases up to 2 years. Imperfect concordance between HbA 1c  and weight supports baseline and 12-week monitoring of both outcomes, followed by risk-stratified monitoring and intervention.

FUNDING: National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Three Research Schools Mental Health Programme, NIHR School for Primary Care Research, NIHR Applied Research Collaboration West Midlands, NIHR Dementia and Neurodegeneration Policy Research Unit, UK Research and Innovation, University College London Hospitals NIHR Biomedical Research Centre, and NIHR North Thames Applied Research Collaboration.

title: Long-term health, criminal justice, and socioeconomic outcomes among people subject to compulsory mental health care in Norway: a nationwide registry cohort study
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Compulsory mental health care aims to manage risk and treatment needs among people with severe mental illness, but evidence on long-term outcomes across health, justice, and socioeconomic domains is scarce. We aimed to compare long-term outcomes across adult groups defined by community treatment orders (CTOs), compulsory hospitalisation, compulsory observation, and voluntary mental health care, and the general population.

METHODS: In this nationwide registry cohort study, we identified all individuals aged 18-65 years with specialist mental health-care contact in Norway from Jan 1, 2015, to Dec 31, 2016 and general population comparators sampled via Statistics Norway based on age and sex. Follow-up was through 2021-23, depending on registry availability. Study groups were defined hierarchically: CTO, compulsory hospitalisation without CTO, compulsory observation without compulsory hospitalisation or CTO, voluntary mental health care, and no specialist mental health-care contact (ie, the general population). Outcomes included mortality and cause of death, self-harm treated in emergency departments or hospital, substance use disorder, victimisation, violent or sexual offence charges or imprisonment, subsequent compulsory care, acute admissions, and socioeconomic outcomes. Data for all groups were sourced from linked nationwide registries. Separate binomial regressions estimated sex-specific probabilities by group, adjusting for birth year. People with lived experience of mental health services advised study design and interpretation.

FINDINGS: The final study sample comprised 321 708 individuals (mean age 36·5 years, range 18-65) across five mutually exclusive groups: CTO (n=3331), compulsory hospitalisation (n=2907), compulsory observation (n=2554), voluntary care (n=177 396), and general population (n=135 520), 193 473 (60·1%) were female and 128 235 (39·9%) were male; ethnicity data were unavailable. Compulsory care groups were associated with substantially worse long-term outcomes across health, criminal justice, and socioeconomic domains than voluntary patients and the general population. Across compulsory care groups, female participants had higher adjusted probabilities of self-harm or suicide than male participants, whereas male participants had higher adjusted probabilities of substance use disorder and of being charged with or imprisoned for violent or sexual offences compared with female participants. The compulsory observation group had the highest adjusted probabilities of self-harm or suicide and substance use disorder across the five groups. Self-harm or suicide was recorded in 135 (12·1%) of 1115 female participants (adjusted probability 12% [95% CI 10-14]) and 75 (5·7%) of 1308 male participants (5·5% [4·4-6·9]). Substance use disorder was recorded in 407 (39·1%) of 1041 female participants (39% [36-42]) and 639 (53·2%) of 1202 male participants (53% [50-56]). Charges or imprisonment for violent or sexual offences were recorded in 146 (14·2%) of 1030 female participants (14% [12-16]) and 446 (37·4% [34-40]) of 1194 male participants. During 2015-21, including the inclusion period, suicide and other external causes accounted for 132 (55·7%) of 237 classified deaths in compulsory observation, compared with 1818 (38·2%) of 4754 in voluntary care and 174 (18·6%) of 938 in the general population. The CTO group had the highest adjusted probability of disability benefit receipt: 89% (95% CI 87-91) in female participants and 93% (92-94) in male participants; a substantial minority of disability-benefit recipients in the CTO group also had earned income.

INTERPRETATION: Compulsory care groups were associated with distinct long-term prognoses from the voluntary care and general population groups. These findings provide population-level benchmarks for service planning and policy evaluation and show that legally defined compulsory care groups should not be treated as a single prognostic population.

FUNDING: Research Council of Norway.

title: Estimates of Anxiety Symptoms Among US Adolescents
abstract:
Key Points Question What is the prevalence of anxiety symptoms among US adolescents, and how is anxiety symptom severity associated with mental health treatment? Findings In this nationally representative cross-sectional study of 15 730 US adolescents, 2851 (16.8%) reported moderate or severe anxiety symptoms. Greater symptom severity was associated with depression, suicidal thoughts, and substance use; however, nearly half of adolescents with moderate (793 [48.3%]) or severe (512 [41.2%]) symptoms received no past-year mental health treatment. Meaning Significant anxiety symptoms are common among US adolescents, yet many affected adolescents do not receive treatment, pointing to the need to improve early identification and access to evidence-based care.

Importance Anxiety symptoms are common among US adolescents and associated with substantial psychiatric burden, yet contemporary nationally representative estimates of anxiety symptom severity, associated clinical conditions, and treatment utilization are lacking. Objectives To estimate the prevalence of anxiety symptoms and symptom severity among US adolescents and examine associated co-occurring psychiatric conditions and treatment utilization. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional study used data from the 2024 National Survey on Drug Use and Health, a nationally representative survey of the US civilian, noninstitutionalized population. Participants included adolescents aged 12 to 20 years. Data were analyzed in June 2026. Exposure(s) Anxiety symptoms were assessed using the 7-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD-7) questionnaire, a brief self-report screener designed to identify probable generalized anxiety disorder and measure symptom severity. Main Outcomes and Measures National estimates of anxiety symptom severity were generated overall and by sociodemographic characteristics. Co-occurring psychiatric and substance use conditions and past-year mental health treatment utilization were examined across anxiety symptom severity categories. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with severe anxiety and receipt of mental health treatment. Results Among 15 730 adolescents (7725 [48.9%] female), 3642 (23.7%) reported mild anxiety symptoms, 1599 (9.6%) reported moderate symptoms, and 1252 (7.2%) reported severe symptoms. Female adolescents had substantially higher rates of moderate (13.4% vs 6.0%) and severe (10.8% vs 3.7%) anxiety symptoms than males. Among adolescents with severe anxiety symptoms, 802 (65.8%) met criteria for a past-year major depressive episode, 536 (48.2%) reported past-year suicidal thoughts, and 392 (31.0%) reported past-month substance use. Despite this high burden of co-occurring mental health conditions, 512 adolescents (41.2%) with severe anxiety symptoms and 793 (48.3%) of those with moderate anxiety symptoms received no mental health treatment during the preceding year. In multivariable analyses, mental health treatment was less likely among male adolescents, racial and ethnic minoritized adolescents, and uninsured adolescents. Conclusions and Relevance Per the results of this cross-sectional study, approximately 1 in 6 US adolescents reported moderate or severe anxiety symptoms in 2024, yet a substantial proportion received no mental health treatment. The high prevalence of anxiety symptoms, frequent co-occurrence with depression and suicidal thoughts, and large unmet need underscore the importance of improving early identification and access to evidence-based treatment for adolescents with anxiety symptoms.

This cross-sectional study estimates the prevalence of anxiety symptoms and symptom severity among US adolescents and examines associated co-occurring psychiatric conditions and treatment utilization.

title: Temporal, Geographic, and Polysubstance Patterns in Orphine Analogue Detections
abstract: INTRODUCTION Benzimidazol-2-ones, also known as “orphine analogs” or simply “orphines,” are synthetic opioids traced to pharmaceutical discovery programs in the 1960s, beginning with compounds such as bezitramide and R-6890 (spirochlorphine). 1 – 3 These drugs are μ-opioid receptor agonists, with some analogs estimated to be approximately 10 times more potent than fentanyl, and can produce classic opioid toxicity, including respiratory depression. 2 – 5 Orphine analogs first appeared in the US illicit drug supply in the third quarter of 2020 (2020 Q3) with brorphine. 2 As nitazene-class benzimidazole opioids have proliferated, 6 scheduling actions targeting these substances may have increased market pressure toward new synthetic opioids, including N -propionitrile chlorphine, colloquially known as “cyclorphine.” 2 , 7 Given limited data on this emerging drug class, we examined temporal, geographic, and polysubstance patterns in orphine analog detections. METHODS This cross-sectional study used data on orphine-positive biospecimens from the Center for Forensic Science Research and Education’s NPS Discovery program, a drug early warning system. 8 Data from 2020 Q3 through 2026 Q2 were analyzed. NPS Discovery tests biospecimens (e.g., blood, urine, serum, plasma) submitted by forensic laboratories, medical examiners, coroners, and clinical and public health agency partners. Drug identifications were made using liquid chromatography quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry (LC-QTOF-MS), with supplemental mass spectrometry platforms used as needed. This analysis focused on five orphine analogs: brorphine, chlorphine, spirochlorphine, N -propionitrile chlorphine, and SR-17018 (5,6-dichloro desmethylchlorphine). We described orphine-positive biospecimen counts by quarter and analog, US Census region, state, and co-detected psychoactive drug categories ( eMethods in Supplement 1 ). Co-positivity was defined as the presence of one or more additional psychoactive drug in an orphine-positive biospecimen. We also identified biospecimens in which naloxone was detected. This study was deemed exempt by the Virginia Commonwealth University Institutional Review Board under 45 CFR §46. The STROBE reporting guideline was followed. RESULTS From 2020 Q3 through 2026 Q2, we identified 142 orphine-positive biospecimens, representing 1.0% of total biospecimens (n=142/14,261), 0.6% of fentanyl-positive biospecimens (n=51/9,004), and 3.0% of nitazene-positive biospecimens tested during this period (n=13/430). The most commonly detected analog was N -propionitrile chlorphine (n=102; 71.8%), followed by brorphine (n=38; 26.8%), spirochlorphine (n=6; 4.2%), 5,6-dichloro desmethylchlorphine (n=3; 2.1%), and chlorphine (n=1; 0.7%) ( Figure 1A ). Quarterly counts showed two distinct waves: an early wave of 36 orphine-positive biospecimens in 2020 Q3, all involving brorphine, followed by a later wave from 2025 Q4 through 2026 Q2 dominated by N -propionitrile chlorphine, present in 100 of 102 biospecimens (98.0%) during this period. Orphine-positive biospecimens were concentrated in the South (n=75; 52.8%) and Midwest (n=53; 37.3%), with fewer in the Northeast (n=8; 5.6%) and West (n=6; 4.2%) ( Figure 1B ). Across 22 US states, detections were most common in Tennessee (n=50; 35.2%), Illinois (n=37; 26.1%), Texas (n=14; 9.9%), and Minnesota (n=10; 7.0%). Tennessee and Texas detections all involved N -propionitrile chlorphine, whereas Minnesota detections all involved brorphine. Illinois had a mixed pattern, with 24 brorphine-positive and 13 N -propionitrile chlorphine-positive biospecimens. Polysubstance involvement was common ( Figure 2 ). Orphine-positive biospecimens were most often co-detected with benzodiazepine-related compounds (n=53; 37.3%). Frequently co-detected synthetic opioids included fentanyl-related compounds (n=51; 35.9%) and nitazene-related compounds (n=13; 9.2%). Co-detection of stimulants was also common, including methamphetamine/other amphetamines (n=51; 35.9%) and cocaine-related compounds (n=29; 20.4%). Other co-detections included medetomidine-related compounds (n=16; 11.3%) and xylazine (n=11; 7.7%). Naloxone was detected in 33 orphine-positive biospecimens (23.2%). DISCUSSION This study documents the proliferation of orphine analogs across 22 US states, with a sharp rise since late 2025 driven by N -propionitrile chlorphine, frequently co-detected with fentanyl-related compounds. Naloxone appeared in nearly one-fourth of orphine-positive biospecimens, consistent with attempted reversal of opioid-induced respiratory depression. 4 These findings provide timely evidence of orphine analogs as an emerging drug threat in the US illicit drug supply. One possible explanation for this shift is China’s generic scheduling of nitazene analogs in July 2025, which may have created an opening for the introduction of alternative synthetic opioid classes, including orphine analogs. 2 , 6 , 7 Our study showed that N -propionitrile chlorphine-positive biospecimens rose rapidly immediately following this regulatory intervention, while only a minority of orphine-positive biospecimens also contained nitazene-related compounds, consistent with this market substitution hypothesis. This study has limitations. NPS Discovery data are based on both random and for-cause testing of submitted biospecimens. 8 Although biospecimens can be received from across all 50 states, submissions are not systematically received from all jurisdictions; thus, findings may not be nationally representative. 8 These findings have important implications for clinicians, public health agencies, and policymakers. Orphine analogs are not routinely included in forensic or clinical toxicology testing, fentanyl and nitazene test strips do not reliably detect orphine analogs, and no orphine-specific test strips are available. 2 , 7 Clinical guidance for managing orphine-involved overdoses, development of orphine-specific test strips, broader access to confirmatory testing, and naloxone distribution remain key priorities. As several internationally reported analogs were not observed in this dataset, including fluorphine and iodorphine, 7 proactive surveillance is critical to monitor their potential entry into the US illicit drug supply. title: Sociodemographic, Criminological and Clinical Determinants in Suicide After Release From Prison: A 23-Year National Cohort Study
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Suicide risk is elevated after prison release, but population-level evidence on temporal risk patterns and associated factors remains limited. We aimed to describe characteristics of individuals who die by suicide after release from Norwegian prisons, compare their suicide mortality with the general population, and examine risk factors over time.

MATERIAL AND METHODS: Data from the Norwegian Prison Release Study (nPRIS), including all people in prison in Norway (2000-2022), were linked to the Norwegian Cause of Death Registry, the Norwegian Prison Registry, the Norwegian Patient Registry, and Statistics Norway. We calculated crude mortality rates (CMR) per 100,000 person-years, standardized mortality ratios (SMR), annual age-standardized years of life lost rate (ASYR), and Cox proportional hazards models.

RESULTS: From 2000 to 2022, 1183 suicides (9.1% of all deaths; CMR 81; 95% CI 76-85) occurred after release (90% male). The SMR was higher in women (SMR 8.64; 95% CI 7.17-10.34) than men (SMR 3.98; 95% CI 3.76-4.22). In multivariable models (2009-2022; n = 57,034; 516 suicides), strong independent associations with suicide 6 months post-release included self-harm (adjusted HR [aHR] 4.76; 95% CI 2.60-8.72), severe mental illness (aHR 1.95; 95% CI 1.16-3.27), release from high-security prisons (aHR 1.93; 95% CI 1.12-3.33), and pretrial detention (aHR 1.82; 95% CI 1.06-3.13).

CONCLUSIONS: Suicide risk is substantially and persistently elevated relative to the general population, peaks immediately after release, and is concentrated among people with prior self-harm, severe mental illness, and those released from high-security settings.

title: Universal suicide risk assessment for veterans and soldiers in all healthcare settings: A nursing imperative
abstract:
PURPOSE: Suicide remains a major public health concern among U.S. veterans and active-duty military personnel. This narrative review examines evidence supporting routine suicide risk screening and considers its implementation as a clinically appropriate, trauma-informed process rather than an inflexible requirement at every encounter.

METHODS: A structured narrative review used targeted searches of PubMed, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and Scopus, supplemented by federal surveillance reports, clinical guidance, and policy documents. Evidence was synthesized across five domains: suicide prevalence and trends; clinical, cultural, and system-level risk factors; recognition gaps in general healthcare; routine screening and early intervention; and nursing leadership in implementation.

RESULTS: Veterans and active-duty personnel experience multifactorial suicide risk associated with post-traumatic stress disorder, depression, moral injury, substance use, chronic pain, traumatic brain injury, transition-related stressors, stigma, and access to lethal means. Missed opportunities for recognition also occur in nonpsychiatric settings. Validated screening can facilitate early identification but requires pathways for secondary assessment, safety planning, referral, and emergency response.

CONCLUSIONS: Routine suicide risk screening should be integrated into healthcare encounters when screening can be completed safely, privately, and with an established response pathway. Nurses are well positioned to lead standardized workflows, culturally responsive communication, staff education, and quality improvement. Broader implementation requires organizational policy, workforce preparation, and further evaluation across military and civilian healthcare systems.

title: Suicide in People With Co-occurring Substance Use and Mental Health Conditions: An Integrative Literature Review to Inform Risk Formulation in Mental Health Nursing
abstract:
ABSTRACT People with co‐occurring substance use and mental health conditions experience disproportionately high levels of suicidal ideation, attempts and deaths compared with those with either condition alone, yet guidance for suicide risk formulation in this group is limited. This integrative literature review synthesised evidence on suicidality in adults with co‐occurring conditions, identified risk and protective factors, and refined risk formulation approaches for mental health nursing. Using Whittemore and Knafl's methodology and Toronto and Remmington's stepwise guidance, CINAHL, Embase, Medline and PsycInfo were searched without date limits. Empirical studies of adults with co‐occurring substance use and mental health conditions were included, alongside relevant grey literature; specialist populations (e.g., prison, veteran, neurological/developmental) were excluded. Thirty‐three quantitative studies and six grey literature sources (total n = 39; 35 883 participants across 19 countries) were appraised using Critical Appraisal Skills Programme tools and the AACODS checklist. Co‐occurring conditions were consistently associated with elevated suicidality, especially mood disorders, notably depression, combined with alcohol use disorder. Risk factors were mapped onto an extended 5Ps model: presenting, predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protective domains, with an additional Patient Experience domain to capture barriers to care, service dissatisfaction and stigma. Protective factors were comparatively scarce. Applying the Integrated Motivational–Volitional model highlighted psychological processes, including mental pain, perceived burdensomeness, impulsivity and access to means, that may contribute to suicidal behaviour. For mental health nurses and other mental health professionals, incorporating patient experience and IMV‐informed processes into an extended 5Ps framework may support more thorough suicide risk formulation and the development of safety and treatment plans that promote safer, more equitable and integrated care for people with co‐occurring conditions.

1 Introduction Co‐occurring substance use and mental health conditions (previously termed ‘dual diagnosis’) are common in mental health services and are associated with elevated suicide risk. In England, nearly half of those who die by suicide have a history of problematic alcohol use and over one‐third have a history of problematic drug use (an unreported proportion will have been using both alcohol and drugs and will be accounted for in both percentages), with even higher proportions among mental health patients (National Confidential Inquiry into Suicide and Safety in Mental Health [NCISH] 2025 ). Despite this, service responses remain fragmented, and specific guidance for suicide risk assessment in this population is limited. Co‐occurring conditions encompass a wide spectrum of mental health diagnoses and symptoms, combined with diverse patterns of alcohol and drug use, different levels of dependence and states of intoxication (Public Health England 2017 ). Studies examining the prevalence of co‐occurring conditions suggest that 30%–50% of people with serious mental illness also have a co‐occurring drug or alcohol problem (Regier et al. 1990 ; Weaver et al. 2001 ). The Comorbidity of Substance Misuse and Mental Illness Collaborative study found that 44% of mental health service users reported hazardous or harmful alcohol or drug use within the previous year (Weaver et al. 2003 ). Recent articles cite these studies when providing prevalence estimates, further demonstrating the lack of current research on co‐occurring conditions. Globally, suicide is a leading cause of death, with an estimated 727 000 deaths in 2021 (World Health Organisation [WHO] 2025 ). In the United Kingdom, 26% of suicides between 2012 and 2022 occurred among people who had been in contact with mental health services in the preceding year (NCISH 2025 ). Alcohol and drug use are highly prevalent in this group, and the national suicide prevention strategy for England (Department of Health and Social Care [DHSC] 2023 ) identifies people in contact with mental health and substance use services as a key priority group. Historically, people with co‐occurring conditions have often been required to address their substance use before being accepted for mental health treatment (Care Quality Commission 2015 ; Making Every Adult Matter 2022 ), despite evidence that substances often function as coping mechanisms in the context of unaddressed mental distress (National Institute for Health and Care Excellence [NICE] 2016 ). NCISH ( 2024 ) reported that 70% of people who died by suicide whilst under the care of alcohol and drug services had not been in contact with mental health services in the preceding year, prompting recommendations for joint working between drug and alcohol and mental health services and routine assessment of substance use within mental health settings. Various models of risk assessment are used by organisations providing mental health care, and the forms used vary between services. NCISH ( 2018 ) examined the use of risk assessment tools across UK mental health services. All 85 providers of mental health care were asked to describe the tools they used, and clinicians, patients and carers were invited to complete an online survey. The study found little consistency in the length, content or use of risk tools. Most were checklists intended to predict future behaviour, with scores used to inform management decisions. However, risk scales have limited value in guiding risk management (Large et al. 2017 ; Oates 2018 ) and poor predictive validity (Chan et al. 2016 ; Quinlivan et al. 2014 , 2016 ; Steeg et al. 2018 ). NCISH ( 2018 ) therefore recommended an approach that incorporates a formulation of risk based on the person's current situation, history and social circumstances. It also recommended training staff to undertake formulation collaboratively, personally and individually with the person and, where appropriate, their family or carer. The 5Ps model of risk formulation is widely used in UK mental health services. Weerasekera ( 1993 ) initially proposed the model following a literature review that identified the need for a comprehensive and memorable approach to formulation. Macneil et al. ( 2012 ) subsequently developed the model, which considers presenting problems, predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protective factors (Table 1 ). In practice, substance use is frequently recorded in a single section, usually as a perpetuating factor that interferes with treatment. Given the heightened suicide risk in people with co‐occurring conditions, this conceptualisation and approach is likely to be overly simplistic and may lead to unsafe decisions regarding mental health care. 2 Research Question The research question was developed to further understanding of the reasons for the elevated suicide risk in this patient group and to explore how risk can be better recognised, identified and responded to within mental health settings. What risk factors for suicidality are associated with co‐occurring substance use and mental health conditions, and how can these inform clinical risk formulation in mental health services? 3 Aims This review aimed to: Synthesise evidence on factors associated with suicidality in adults with co‐occurring substance use and mental health conditions. Apply these findings to a formulation framework widely used in mental health services (the 5Ps) and critically appraise its adequacy in this context. Propose an enhanced risk formulation model that accounts for the complex historic and current factors related to increased suicide risk in this patient group across all risk domains, with a sixth domain (Patient Experience), informed by the Integrated Motivational–Volitional (IMV) Model of Suicidal Behaviour. Identify gaps in the literature and highlight implications for mental health nursing practice and future research. 4 Methods 4.1 Design An Integrative Literature Review (ILR) was chosen because both suicidality and co‐occurring conditions are conceptually broad and studied using heterogeneous designs. A conventional narrow systematic review (e.g., focusing on one diagnosis–substance pairing) would have overlooked the complexity encountered in clinical practice. The ILR approach, as outlined by Whittemore and Knafl ( 2005 ) and elaborated by Toronto and Remington ( 2020 ), allows inclusion of diverse methodologies and grey literature, supporting practice‐oriented synthesis. The clinical problem was identified through practice experience in UK mental health services and repeated NCISH reports highlighting the high proportion of suicide deaths among those with problematic use of substances combined with a lack of specific guidance on suicide risk assessment for this group. 4.2 Search Strategy Searches were conducted in Medline, CINAHL, PsycInfo and Embase using controlled vocabulary and keywords relating to dual diagnosis/co‐occurring conditions and suicide/suicidality. The primary MeSH term was ‘dual diagnosis (psychiatry)’ combined with terms such as ‘suicide’, ‘suicidal ideation’, ‘suicide attempts’ and ‘suicidology’. Alternative co‐occurring condition terms were piloted but yielded large numbers of irrelevant results; therefore, ‘dual diagnosis’ was retained as the most specific indexing term. Search terms for each database are presented in Table 2 . No date limits were applied because no prior review was identified that specifically addressed suicidality in the context of co‐occurring conditions. A search of the Cochrane Library confirmed the absence of relevant systematic reviews. Grey literature was not subject to the database search and was identified through discussion with Progress (Co‐Occurring Mental Health, Alcohol & Drugs), a UK‐based national consortium of senior clinicians in co‐occurring conditions, and through targeted searches of key organisations (NCISH, NICE, Royal College of Psychiatrists, DHSC, Public Health England). 4.3 Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria Table 3 summarises the criteria used. Studies were included if they: Focused on adults with co‐occurring substance use and mental health conditions (diagnosed by ICD/DSM or equivalent), and Reported suicidality, defined as suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, or suicide deaths. Exclusions: Studies including participants aged under 18 years were excluded. Studies of prison populations were also excluded because this review examines co‐occurring conditions and suicide in mental health care rather than custodial settings. Incarceration is associated with an increased suicide rate (Zhong et al. 2021 ), and prisons in the UK operate within a distinct care system tailored to the custodial environment. Studies that solely focus on participants with acquired or traumatic brain injury were excluded because brain injury introduces distinct neurocognitive, behavioural, and physiological changes that substantially alter the mechanisms underlying suicidality. Individuals with brain injury have been shown to have a 2.23 times higher rate of suicide attempts (Lu et al. 2020 ). Studies focusing solely on veterans were excluded because there are variable rates of suicide in this group dependent on nationality. For example, the suicide rate among US veterans is 1.5 times higher than the general population (Ruiz et al. 2022 ), whereas in the UK the rate is similar to those who have never served in the armed forces (Rodway et al. 2023 ). The studies found in the search related largely to US veterans. Many included studies may nevertheless have contained individual participants with a history of incarceration, diagnosed or undiagnosed brain injury, developmental conditions or veteran status, unless the study explicitly excluded these groups. The exclusion criteria applied only to studies focused solely on those specialist populations. Studies where tobacco was the sole substance of use, where substances were prescribed as part of the study, or where results were not specific to people with co‐occurring conditions. Articles not reporting suicidality and those available only as abstracts or machine‐translated texts. 4.4 Screening and Selection The database search yielded 448 records, of which 47 were duplicates. The titles and abstracts of the remaining 401 records were screened against the inclusion and exclusion criteria, yielding 85 potentially eligible studies. Full texts were retrieved for 82 studies. To validate the primary reviewer's decisions in accordance with Covidence ( 2025 ) guidance for systematic reviews, a second reviewer (C.J.N., M.Z. or A.G.) independently screened a 20% sample of the full‐text articles. Thirty‐three empirical studies met the inclusion criteria, including one identified through reference searching. Six grey‐literature sources were also included, resulting in a total of 39 publications. The selection process was documented in a PRISMA‐style flow diagram (Page et al. 2021 ; Haddaway et al. 2022 ; Figure 1 ). 4.5 Quality Appraisal All empirical studies used quantitative observational designs: 14 case–control, 14 cross‐sectional and five cohort studies. Appropriate CASP checklists were used for appraisal (Critical Appraisal Skills Programme 2023 ). The review forms part of a doctoral project and was led by the primary reviewer. Although duplicate appraisal of every study is considered best practice, the project's infrastructure and timescale did not permit this. Instead, 20% of included articles were independently double‐appraised by A.G., producing good inter‐rater reliability. This partial double‐appraisal strategy was specified in the review protocol registered with PROSPERO. Each study was rated across domains of validity, results and relevance to the local population and was then assigned an overall quality rating of low, medium or high. Section ratings were determined as follows. A section was rated high quality when all answers to its checklist questions were ‘yes’. It was rated medium quality when half of the answers were ‘no’ or ‘can't tell’, and low quality when more than half were ‘no’ or ‘can't tell’. When most categories were rated at the same level, the overall study rating reflected that level. When categories were divided equally between two levels, the lower rating was assigned. title: GLP-1 receptor agonist initiation and risk of psychiatric hospitalisation and emergency department presentation in adults with schizophrenia and type 2 diabetes in the USA: an observational cohort study using electronic health records data
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Many individuals with schizophrenia have persistent psychotic symptoms despite antipsychotic treatment, and the disorder is associated with a disproportionately high burden of metabolic dysregulation. Whether GLP-1 receptor agonists are associated with psychiatric benefit alongside their metabolic effects remains unknown. We aimed to examine associations between GLP-1 receptor agonist initiation and psychiatric hospitalisation and emergency department presentation in adults with schizophrenia and type 2 diabetes, compared with DPP-4 inhibitor initiation, SGLT2 inhibitor initiation, and non-initiation.

METHODS: In this observational cohort study, we used electronic health record (EHR) data from the US NeuroBlu Data repository to construct a cohort of adults (≥18 years) with documented diagnosis of schizophrenia and comorbid type 2 diabetes. The exposure was the initiation of GLP-1 receptor agonists, compared with non-initiation or initiation of DPP-4 inhibitors or SGLT2 inhibitors. The index date, from Jan 1, 2018, was defined as the date of the first recorded psychiatric visit at which both a diagnosis of schizophrenia and comorbid type 2 diabetes were present in the participant's record. Time zero (T 0 ) was the date of the first prescription of any of these agents between Jan 1, 2018, and Oct 1, 2025; for non-initiators, T 0  was the index date. Participants contributed person-time from T 0  until 2 years of follow-up, the last recorded clinical observation in the NeuroBlu Data repository, or the end of the observation period (March 24, 2026), whichever happened earliest. The main outcomes of interest included risk of psychiatric hospitalisation and psychiatric emergency department presentation. Inverse probability weighting was applied to balance demographic, clinical, and pharmacological covariates, and weighted regression models were used. Analyses were conducted using an intention-to-treat framework, whereby exposure status was defined according to the medication initiated at T 0 .

FINDINGS: A total of 70 257 individuals met the inclusion criteria; mean age was 53·1 years [SD 12·32] and 33 882 [48·2%] were women. Among the 70 257 eligible individuals, 9093 (12·9%) initiated GLP-1 receptor agonists, 4968 (7·1%) initiated DPP-4 inhibitors, 5328 (7·6%) initiated SGLT2 inhibitors, and 50 868 (72·4%) were non-initiators. In weighted regression analyses, GLP-1 receptor agonist initiation was associated with a lower risk of psychiatric hospitalisation compared with non-initiation (weighted hazard ratio [HR] 0·76 [95% CI 0·71-0·82]), DPP-4 inhibitor initiation (0·82 [0·75-0·90]), and SGLT2 inhibitor initiation (0·83 [0·78-0·88]). GLP-1 receptor agonist initiation was also associated with a lower risk of emergency department presentation than non-initiation (0·71 [0·65-0·77]), DPP-4 inhibitor initiation (0·87 [0·80-0·95]), and SGLT2 inhibitor initiation (0·80 [0·73-0·88]).

INTERPRETATION: GLP-1-based therapy initiation was associated with lower psychiatric acute-care use than non-initiation and initiation of DPP-4 or SGLT2 inhibitors in adults with schizophrenia and type 2 diabetes. Potential residual confounding and selection bias restrict generalisability of the results. The findings suggest that lower psychiatric acute-care use could be a favourable secondary benefit when GLP-1-based therapies are clinically indicated for metabolic management, although their use as primary psychiatric treatments require investigation in randomised and mechanistic studies.

FUNDING: Synergy for the Development of Innovative Clinical Treatments in Schizophrenia (SYNDICAT) project (GNT2035912).

title: Online Sports Betting Legalization and Behavioral Health Care Use
abstract:
This cohort study investigates the association between online sports betting legalization and behavioral health care use.

Key Points Question What is the association between online sports betting legalization and behavioral health care use? Findings In this quasi-experimental difference-in-differences study including almost 62 million enrollee-years, online sports betting legalization was associated with an increase in the probability of people with employer-sponsored health insurance having a prescription fill or outpatient visit related to depression or anxiety. Associations were more precise and robust for men than women, and legalization was not associated with changes in prescriptions or outpatient visits for a substance use disorder. Meaning Results suggest that state legalization of online sports betting was associated with measurable increases in mental health care use and may increase strain on the behavioral health system.

Importance The number of states with legal online sports betting has grown from 1 to 31 since 2018, expanding access to gambling. Despite the known behavioral health burdens associated with gambling, little is understood about legalization’s impact on mental health and substance use treatment use. Objective To evaluate the association between online sports betting legalization and treatment use for mental health conditions and substance use disorders (SUD). Design, Setting, and Participants This was a quasi-experimental staggered difference-in-differences study using claims data from January 2016 to December 2023. The setting was a large, national convenience sample of people with employer-sponsored health insurance. Included in the analysis were men and women aged 18 to 64 years living in states that legalized online sports betting during 2018-2022 or had not by the end of the study period. Exposure State legalization of online sports betting. Main Outcomes and Measures Outcomes were measured at the state-year level, weighted by number of enrollees as follows: proportions of enrollees with 1 or more prescription fills for antidepressant, antianxiety, or SUD medications and proportions of enrollees with 1 or more outpatient, emergency department, or inpatient visits with a diagnosis for depression, anxiety, or SUD. Results Among 61 951 305 enrollee-years, 31 914 852 (52%) were women, and the mean (SD) age was 41.9 (13.5) years. Online sports betting legalization was associated with increases in the probability of antidepressant use (men: 0.57 percentage points; 95% CI, 0.26-0.89 percentage points; women: 1.08 percentage points; 95% CI, 0.23-1.94 percentage points) and antianxiety use (men: 0.32 percentage points; 95% CI, 0.14-0.50 percentage points; women: 0.64 percentage points; 95% CI, 0.16-1.12 percentage points), but there was no detectable change in SUD medication use. Legalization was also associated with increases in the probability of an outpatient diagnosis for depression (men: 0.34 percentage points; 95% CI, 0.20-0.49 percentage points; women: 0.57 percentage points; 95% CI, 0.25-0.89 percentage points) and anxiety (men: 0.67 percentage points; 95% CI, 0.32-1.01 percentage points; women: 1.15 percentage points; 95% CI, 0.50-1.81 percentage points) but not SUD. Legalization was not associated with behavioral health diagnoses in the emergency department and inpatient settings. Conclusions and Relevance Results of this quasi-experimental difference-in-differences study suggest that online sports betting legalization was associated with an increase in outpatient and prescription mental health care use among people with employer-sponsored health insurance. These findings underscore the importance of prevention and treatment of potential adverse health consequences of legalized online sports betting.

title: Evaluating the Effect of Positive Childhood Experiences on the Risk of Psychiatric Disorders in Early Adulthood
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: While the negative impacts of traumatic childhood experiences are well established, less is known about whether positive childhood experiences (PCEs) contribute to long-term mental health. The aim of this study was to estimate the effect of PCEs on the risk of psychiatric disorders in early adulthood.

METHODS: Participants included 3,499 children from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children. Eligible participants were nonrandomly exposed to PCEs (e.g., "school enjoyment" or "feeling safe in neighborhood") between ages 0 and 17, measured as a score ranging from 0 to 10. Inverse probability weighting (IPW) was used to account for the likelihood of PCE exposure conditional on confounders. The effect of PCE score on risk of psychiatric disorders at age 24, using IPW- and confounder-adjusted estimates, is reported. Subgroup analysis of individual disorders was subsequently conducted.

RESULTS: In unweighted analyses, each one-unit increase in the PCE score was associated with a 12% decrease in the odds of psychiatric disorder (odds ratio=0.88, 95% CI=0.82, 0.95). In the IPW- and confounder-adjusted model, this effect was retained (odds ratio=0.89, 95% CI=0.82, 0.95). Robust associations between PCEs and lower odds of depressive disorder (odds ratio=0.84, 95% CI=0.76, 0.93) and generalized anxiety disorder (odds ratio=0.91, 95% CI=0.84, 0.99) were found. The findings for PCE score and psychotic disorder were inconclusive.

CONCLUSIONS: The findings indicate that PCEs are associated with reduced odds of meeting criteria for psychiatric disorders in early adulthood, particularly depression. Further research should explore PCEs as a potential preventive strategy that might reduce the burden of psychiatric disorders in early adulthood.

title: The effect of tele-nursing counseling on functioning and medication adherence in individuals with bipolar disorder: A randomized controlled trial
abstract:
AIM: This study was conducted to determine the effect of tele-nursing counseling on functioning and medication adherence among individuals with bipolar disorder.

METHOD: The research was directed utilizing a randomized controlled experimental design with pretest and posttest control groups. The study included 70 individuals (experimental = 35, control = 35) who were followed at a Community Mental Health Center (CMHC). The experimental group received structured tele-nursing counseling consisting of weekly telephone interviews and supportive text messages for eight weeks. The control group continued to receive standard clinical care. Data were gathered utilizing the Introductory Information Form, the Functioning Assessment Short Test (FAST), and the Morisky Medication Adherence Scale (MMAS).

RESULTS: At the end of the eight-week intervention, there was a statistically significant difference between the experimental and control groups in terms of functional levels (adjusted between-group difference [experimental minus control] = -6.8, 95% CI: -9.8 to -3.7; p < 0.001) and medication adherence (adjusted between-group difference = -2.11, 95% CI: -2.4 to -1.8; p < 0.001), adjusting for baseline scores.

CONCLUSION: The findings suggest that tele-nursing counseling may be an influential supportive intervention for cultivating functioning and medication adherence among individuals with bipolar disorder.

title: Feasibility, Acceptability, and Preliminary Outcomes of a Group-Based Brief Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy Protocol for Suicide Prevention in a Brazilian Public Mental Health Service: A Mixed-Methods Pilot Study
abstract:
ABSTRACT Introduction We evaluated the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary outcomes of group‐adapted brief cognitive‐behavioral therapy for suicide prevention (BCBT) in a Brazilian public psychiatric outpatient service. Methods This single‐arm, nonrandomized, mixed‐methods pilot enrolled 27 adults across two cohorts receiving 16 weekly group sessions. Feasibility and acceptability were assessed, and suicidal ideation was monitored weekly using the Beck Scale for Suicide Ideation (BSI). Results Enrollment targets were met; 70.4% had ≥ 4 recorded sessions, and no intervention‐related adverse events were recorded. All six questionnaire respondents rated recommendation at 8–10. Four provided qualitative responses, highlighting shared suffering recognition and an interpretive theme of hope instillation. The linear BSI slope was nonsignificant ( B = −0.29, p = 0.129); multiple imputation yielded B = −0.36 ( p = 0.018). An exploratory quadratic model indicated greater decline later in treatment ( p = 0.008). Among 18 participants with ≥ 4 recorded sessions and baseline BSI, scores decreased by 8.2 points from baseline to the last observation ( d = −0.67; p = 0.011). Conclusions Group‐adapted BCBT showed preliminary feasibility and acceptability, with uncontrolled signals of reduced suicidal ideation. Controlled evaluation is needed to establish efficacy.

1 Introduction Suicide constitutes a major public health burden, with an estimated 727,000 deaths worldwide in 2021 (World Health Organization 2025 ). In Brazil, the suicide mortality rate increased by 57% between 2000 and 2019 (Damiano et al. 2024 ). These trends highlight the need to expand access to evidence‐based, suicide‐specific psychotherapeutic interventions within the Brazilian public mental health system. However, a qualitative study of a Brazilian psychosocial care network identified barriers to psychotherapy access and reported that some group activities functioned primarily as opportunities for prescription renewal (Sampaio and Bispo Júnior 2021 ). Brief cognitive‐behavioral therapy for suicide prevention (BCBT), described in foundational work by Rudd ( 2012 ) and subsequently manualized by Bryan and Rudd ( 2018 ), has accumulated robust evidence of efficacy. In a landmark randomized clinical trial with military personnel, BCBT reduced suicide attempts by 60% over a two‐year follow‐up (Rudd et al. 2015 ). More recently, a telehealth‐delivered trial demonstrated a 41% reduced risk of attempts compared to present‐centered therapy (Baker et al. 2024 ), and a subsequent military trial confirmed that BCBT participants were less likely to attempt suicide during follow‐up (Bryan et al. 2025 ). BCBT has also shown promise in inpatient settings, reducing post‐discharge attempts by 60% (Diefenbach et al. 2024 ). However, these trials have been conducted almost exclusively in high‐income countries and in an individual‐therapy format. Critical gaps persist. First, evidence for group‐based delivery of BCBT remains limited. In an early randomized trial of a group‐based problem‐solving intervention among suicidal young adults in a military outpatient setting, both intervention and usual‐care participants improved, while the intervention retained high‐risk participants more effectively (Rudd et al. 1996 ). More recent work includes a randomized trial protocol comparing group BCBT with dialectical behavior therapy skills groups among military service members (Baker et al. 2023 ). Second, evidence on psychosocial interventions for self‐harm in LMICs remains limited, particularly regarding culturally adapted interventions and delivery models (Aggarwal et al. 2021 ). Resource constraints make scalable approaches essential (Patel et al. 2018 ). Third, routine session‐by‐session monitoring during naturalistic delivery warrants further investigation. Group delivery may extend access where specialist capacity is limited and provide opportunities for shared learning and peer support (Baker et al. 2023 ; Yalom and Leszcz 2020 ). These considerations motivate feasibility testing but do not establish equivalence with individual BCBT. The present pilot evaluated the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary clinical outcomes of group‐adapted BCBT in a Brazilian public psychiatric outpatient service using mixed methods. It was intended to inform the BCBT‐BR randomized controlled trial, which compares BCBT with supportive psychotherapy at the same site ( NCT07574658 ; Beiram et al. 2027 ). 2 Methods 2.1 Study Design and Setting This single‐arm, nonrandomized, mixed‐methods feasibility pilot, which included exploratory clinical outcomes, evaluated a group BCBT intervention delivered as part of routine clinical care at a university‐affiliated psychiatric outpatient program established in 2024 to integrate specialized care, training, and research on high‐complexity psychiatric conditions, including treatment‐resistant depression, self‐harm, and suicidality. The study involved adults aged 18–65. Group sessions were co‐facilitated by two psychologists trained in cognitive‐behavioral therapy who had completed a BCBT workshop led by a psychologist with expertise in the approach. The therapists participated in weekly supervision with psychiatrists and psychologists. Trainee observers were present during some sessions. After both treatment cohorts had completed the intervention and approval had been obtained from the local ethics committee, outpatient clinic staff who were not involved in data collection explained the study to participants and obtained written informed consent from all participants for the use of their data in this study. 2.2 Intervention The intervention was adapted from the BCBT manual by Bryan and Rudd ( 2018 ). The manual and accompanying worksheets and intervention materials were translated into Brazilian Portuguese by one of the authors (LB), without back‐translation. Although individual BCBT and the published group protocol use approximately 12 treatment sessions (Baker et al. 2023 ; Bryan and Rudd 2018 ), the local adaptation was planned as a 16‐session group program to allow additional discussion, sharing of individual examples, in‐session practice, review, and consolidation of core BCBT components. Before the group intervention, each participant completed a separate 90‐min individual session focused on a narrative assessment of their most recent suicidal crisis. This was followed by 16 weekly group sessions lasting approximately 2 h each, including a 10‐min break. The intervention preserved the progression from crisis management and emotion regulation to work on suicide‐related beliefs and relapse prevention. Additional time was devoted to developing reasons for living and the survival kit, practicing cognitive strategies, and reviewing and integrating previously learned skills. Adaptations included a family session addressing psychoeducation, lethal‐means safety, and crisis support; a structured review session using a quiz; and a midpoint feedback session reviewing individual symptom trajectories. The final sessions emphasized skills integration and relapse prevention, culminating in rehearsal of coping responses to a previous suicidal crisis and a hypothetical future crisis. 2.3 Participants and Cohorts Two consecutive cohorts were enrolled. Cohort 1 ( n = 14) received 16 weekly group sessions from March to July 2024; Cohort 2 ( n = 13) from September to December 2024. Participants were eligible if they were aged 18–65, were treatment‐seeking outpatients or recently discharged (within 30 days), and reported current suicidal ideation or a history of suicide attempt. Exclusion criteria included acute psychosis or mania, substance intoxication or withdrawal requiring stabilization, severe cognitive impairment, or moderate‐to‐severe intellectual disability. Two participants from Cohort 2 were excluded due to absent BSI data, yielding an analytic sample of N = 25. Patients were identified through referrals from services within the hospital complex and from the public healthcare network of the city of São Paulo. A designated outpatient program staff member assessed eligibility for the clinical group using the criteria above. 2.4 Feasibility, Acceptability, and Exploratory Clinical Outcomes Consistent with the conceptual framework for pilot and feasibility studies (Eldridge et al. 2016 ), the study focused on feasibility and acceptability. Feasibility indicators were recruitment (≥ 10 participants per cohort), retention (≥ 60% completing ≥ 4 of 16 sessions), attendance patterns, and safety (absence of intervention‐related adverse events). A BSI record for a scheduled session was used as a proxy for attendance; missing BSI was treated as absence for these analyses. Retention used all 27 enrolled participants as the denominator, including the two without BSI data. Acceptability was assessed in Cohort 1 through a post‐intervention questionnaire containing nine five‐point rating items and one recommendation item with response options from 1 to 10 and three open‐ended questions: (1) “How has group therapy impacted your life?”; (2) “Which aspects of the therapy and/or the therapists do you think could be improved?”; and (3) “Is there any other message, suggestion, criticism, or comment you would like to record?” Inter‐member trust, therapists' skills in creating a safe and supportive environment, and overall satisfaction were assessed using separate five‐point items. Recommendation was a separate item; its wording referred to a 0–10 scale, although the available options were 1–10. Other items assessed comfort sharing experiences, cohesion, encouragement of participation, perceived changes in ideation and planning, and usefulness of discussions and activities. Item wording and response anchors are provided in Table S1 . Suicidal ideation was monitored weekly using the Beck Scale for Suicide Ideation (BSI; Beck et al. 1988 ), completed electronically. The self‐report BSI total comprises items 1–19 (range 0–38); items 20 and 21 concerning past suicide attempts were excluded. BSI trajectories were treated as exploratory signal‐detection outcomes to inform the design of a future definitive trial, not as evidence of treatment efficacy. 2.5 Data Analysis Likert‐type items were treated as strictly ordinal (Boone and Boone 2012 ) and summarized as counts and proportions for the reported response categories. Open‐ended responses were analyzed using content analysis (Bardin 2011 ) by a single author, Mariana Filippini Cacciacarro (MFC). No second coder was involved; therefore, intercoder agreement was not assessed. For the revised reporting, frequencies were tabulated at the participant level among the four participants who provided open‐ended responses, with each participant counted once per category and categories allowed to overlap. Hope instillation was retained as an interpretive theme from the original content analysis and was not assigned a separate participant frequency. Quantitative and qualitative data were integrated to contextualize findings. Longitudinal BSI data were analyzed using linear mixed‐effects models with random intercepts and slopes. Session was centered at Session 1. Model 1 estimated linear change; Model 2 added cohort and its interaction with session; Model 3 adjusted linear change for age and sex. Additional exploratory models included quadratic time (Model 4), log (session) with a corresponding random slope (Model 5), and centered baseline BSI and its interaction with session (Model 6). Model 6 included baseline among the repeated outcomes and is descriptive, not an independent test of baseline severity as a predictor. Models 1–5 used 248 observations from 25 participants; Model 6 used 239 observations from 22 participants with baseline BSI. Estimates used restricted maximum likelihood and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom; likelihood ratio tests and AIC/BIC comparisons used maximum likelihood. Given 38.0% missing BSI values (52.0% at Session 16), sensitivity analysis used multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE; van Buuren and Groothuis‐Oudshoorn 2011 ): 10 imputations, predictive mean matching, and 20 iterations. Model 7 repeated the linear model in each completed dataset (25 participants, 400 observations) and pooled estimates using Rubin's rules (Rubin 1987 ). Available‐data models and imputation rely on missing‐at‐random assumptions (Fitzmaurice et al. 2011 ; Sterne et al. 2009 ). Baseline‐to‐last‐observation comparisons used paired t ‐tests and Wilcoxon signed‐rank tests among participants with ≥ 4 recorded sessions and baseline BSI ( n = 18). Paired Cohen's d was the mean change divided by its standard deviation.
