title: A psychiatric nurse-led awareness and peer support intervention for suicide prevention among university students
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate a suicide prevention program combining awareness training and peer support among university students.

METHODS: A quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control group design with an embedded qualitative component was conducted with 63 university students. The intervention was structured within a psychiatric nursing framework informed by Peplau's Interpersonal Relations Theory. The seven-week program comprised a baseline assessment in week 1, five weekly group-based peer support sessions (weeks 2-6), and suicide prevention awareness training followed by post-intervention assessment in week 7. Quantitative data were collected using standardized measures of hopelessness, depression, suicide probability, peer support, and suicide-related knowledge. Qualitative data were analyzed using thematic analysis.

RESULTS: Compared with the control group, students in the intervention group demonstrated significant reductions in hopelessness, depression, and suicide probability scores, and significant increases in peer support and suicide-related knowledge (p < .05). Significant time×group interactions indicated that these changes were attributable to the intervention. Qualitative findings revealed enhanced awareness, empathy, supportive attitudes, and strengthened beliefs in the preventability of suicide.

CONCLUSION: Structured interventions integrating awareness training and peer support may effectively reduce suicide-related psychological risk factors and strengthen protective social mechanisms among university students. These findings support the implementation of nurse-led, peer-based preventive strategies within psychiatric nursing and campus mental health services.

title: Caring Letters and Suicide Mortality Among US Veterans Who Contacted the Veterans Crisis Line: A Prespecified Secondary Analysis
abstract:
Key Points Question Is the US Department of Veterans Affairs Veterans Crisis Line (VCL) caring letters (CL) intervention associated with reduced suicide mortality, and are there differences in patient outcomes by signatory? Findings In this prespecified secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial of 227 502 veterans who contacted the VCL, 87 926 received CL from a clinician or a peer veteran signatory, and 139 576 did not. CL receipt was not associated with suicide mortality, and no differences in outcomes were identified by signatory. Meaning These findings suggest that the CL intervention may not reduce suicide mortality among veterans at high suicide risk who contact the VCL.

This secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial examines the association between caring letters receipt and suicide mortality among veterans who contacted the US Department of Veterans Affairs Veterans Crisis Line and whether outcomes differ by clinician or peer veteran signatory.

Importance Caring letters (CL) is one of the only suicide prevention interventions to ever reduce suicide mortality in a randomized clinical trial, but the results have not been replicated. The US Department of Veterans Affairs Veterans Crisis Line (VCL) CL intervention was previously evaluated, but suicide mortality data were not available at that time. Objectives To examine the association of the VCL CL intervention with suicide mortality among US veterans, and to determine whether there are differences in outcomes by signatory. Design, Setting, and Participants This prespecified secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial includes a randomized parallel trial of US veterans, combined with an observational comparison of no CL receipt with any CL receipt. Veterans Health Administration (VHA) patients (aged ≥18 years) who contacted the VCL between June 11, 2020, and June 10, 2021, were randomized to receive CL from either a VA clinician or a peer veteran signatory. Veterans who contacted the VCL between June 11, 2018, and June 10, 2021, and did not receive the intervention were included as an observational historical control group. Suicide mortality analyses were completed between March and September 2025. Intervention Veterans received 9 CL messages over a period of 1 year from either a clinician or peer veteran signatory. The signatory was randomly assigned. Main Outcomes and Measures The main outcome for these analyses was suicide mortality among veterans in the 12 months following the index VCL contact. Suicide mortality was compared using χ 2 tests and time-to-event models. Results This study included 227 502 VHA patients (mean [SD] age, 53.6 [16.9] years; 84.4% men) who contacted the VCL. A total of 87 926 veterans received the CL intervention; the remaining 139 576 comprised the historical control group. A total of 625 suicides (0.27%) occurred during the study period. The suicide mortality rate was similar between the CL and historical control groups (0.29% and 0.27%, respectively; P = .31). Within the CL group, outcomes did not differ between peer letter and clinician letter recipients (0.21% and 0.22%; P = .95). Conclusions and Relevance In this analysis, among VHA patients who contacted the VCL, CL receipt was not associated with suicide mortality, and no differences in outcomes were identified by signatory. Future research should explore the potential benefits of increased health care utilization, a finding reported in the parent trial. Trial Registration isrctn.org Identifier: ISRCTN27551361

title: Effectiveness of rTMS vs. Pharmacotherapy in Late-Life Treatment-Resistant Depression: An Observational Study of Individual Participant Data From Two Randomized Clinical Trials
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: The authors compared the effectiveness and tolerability of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) versus pharmacotherapy augmentation and switching strategies in older adults with late-life treatment-resistant depression (LL-TRD).

METHODS: This observational study used individual participant data from 758 participants age 60 or older with LL-TRD from two randomized controlled trials: an rTMS trial of once-daily bilateral treatment for 4-6 weeks, and a pharmacotherapy trial comparing aripiprazole augmentation, bupropion augmentation, and switch to bupropion. Restriction, propensity score weighting, and regression adjustment were used to account for differences in trial design and eligibility criteria. The primary outcome was the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) 10 weeks after treatment initiation.

RESULTS: After accounting for differences in participant characteristics, rTMS was associated with lower MADRS scores than aripiprazole augmentation (difference: 4.16 points, 95% CI=2.32, 6.00), bupropion augmentation (difference: 6.08 points, 95% CI=4.06, 8.09), and switch to bupropion (difference: 6.36 points, 95% CI=4.55, 8.17). rTMS was also associated with a higher response rate (defined as reduction ≥50% in MADRS score from baseline to week 10) than aripiprazole augmentation (adjusted odds ratio [AOR]=3.83, 95% CI=1.08, 13.56), bupropion augmentation (AOR=4.87, 95% CI=1.15, 20.68), and switch to bupropion (AOR=4.02, 95% CI=1.12, 14.47). Participants who received rTMS were significantly more likely to experience headache than those who received pharmacotherapy.

CONCLUSIONS: This analysis suggests that rTMS for LL-TRD may be superior to pharmacotherapy and supports the use of rTMS earlier in the treatment algorithms for LL-TRD.

title: The effect of psychoeducation-based motivational interviewing on schizophrenia-related knowledge and hope among individuals with schizophrenia: A single-blind randomized controlled trial
abstract:
BACKGROUND: A lack of schizophrenia-related knowledge and low levels of hope among individuals with schizophrenia can negatively affect treatment adherence, personal recovery, and long-term clinical outcomes. Although psychoeducation and motivational interviewing have demonstrated positive effects in these areas, randomized controlled trials evaluating their combined effects on schizophrenia-related knowledge and hope remain limited.

OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to examine the effects of psychoeducation-based motivational interviewing on schizophrenia-related knowledge and hope in individuals with schizophrenia.

METHODS: This single-blind randomized controlled trial included 44 individuals with schizophrenia receiving care at a Community Mental Health Center in Turkey. Participants were randomly assigned to the intervention group (n = 21) and the control group (n = 23). The intervention group received a psychoeducation-based motivational interviewing program consisting of one preparatory session and five main sessions, whereas the control group received routine care. Data were collected through face-to-face interviews using the Demographic Information Form, Schizophrenia Knowledge Scale, and Schizophrenia Hope Scale at three time points: baseline, post-intervention, and one-month follow-up. Data were analyzed using repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA).

RESULTS: At baseline, no significant differences were observed between the groups in schizophrenia-related knowledge or hope (p > .05). Following the intervention, the experimental group demonstrated significant improvements in schizophrenia-related knowledge (F = 176.060, p < .001, η 2  = 0.898) and hope (F = 99.782, p < .001, η 2  = 0.833), and these improvements were maintained at the one-month follow-up.

CONCLUSION: Psychoeducation-based motivational interviewing is an effective psychiatric nursing intervention for improving schizophrenia-related knowledge and hope among individuals with schizophrenia. Integrating this person-centered, recovery-oriented approach into routine mental health services may enhance active participation in treatment and support personal recovery.

title: Key Decision Points for Personalization and Customization in Self-Guided Digital Suicide Prevention: Qualitative Interview Study
abstract:
Abstract Background Young adults in the United States experience high rates of suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STB) but low engagement with traditional care, highlighting the need for accessible and scalable digital interventions. Self-guided digital safety planning interventions (SPIs) can expand access to support but introduce important decisions about what content to deliver, when systems should intervene, and how users retain control over system actions. Personalization, defined as system-initiated adaptation, and customization, defined as user-initiated control, may offer complementary approaches to these decisions. However, how they should be coordinated to preserve autonomy and reduce burden during periods of distress remains unclear. Objective This study aims to identify key decision points in self-guided digital SPIs and characterize what, when, how, and by whom (system or user) safety planning functions should be controlled. We further examined how personalization and customization can jointly support autonomy, reduce burden, and promote safety. Methods Nine young adults (ages 18‐24) with lived experience of suicidal thoughts and behaviors were recruited from an asynchronous remote community comprising individuals who had engaged with the Mental Health America (MHA) website. Participants completed semistructured individual interviews via Zoom. Three coders analyzed interview transcripts using codebook thematic analysis. One coder open-coded all transcripts to develop a preliminary codebook. Two additional coders then applied the codebook to overlapping transcripts, after which all coders revised the codebook and resolved discrepancies by consensus before coding the remaining transcripts. Themes were interpreted using the 5W1H (Who, What, Where, When, Why, and How) framework as an organizing lens for identifying and structuring decision points. Results Participants identified 3 classes of decision points for self-guided digital SPIs: (1) system-level decisions about what content and actions are automatically provided; (2) user-level decisions about when and at what pace safety planning unfolds; and (3) shared decisions requiring coordination between users and the system. Participants favored system personalization of decision aids, coping suggestions, brainstorming prompts, example messages for contacting trusted others, affirmations, and relevant resources. In contrast, participants wanted control over the timing and pacing of safety planning and the representation and organization of their safety plans. Participants also emphasized that systems should obtain explicit permission before taking safety-relevant actions, such as contacting trusted others or connecting users with crisis counselors in response to increases in detected risk. Conclusions Personalization and customization can function as complementary mechanisms for allocating decision authority within self-guided digital SPIs. The findings support a model of permissioned automation in which systems reduce cognitive and emotional burden through adaptive support while users retain control over safety-relevant actions. This decision-point framework provides a foundation for designing and evaluating self-guided suicide prevention technologies that balance adaptation, autonomy, and safety.

Introduction A widening discrepancy between the elevated suicide risk among young adults and the low use of mental health services indicates a critical need for research and interventions. Suicide is one of the leading causes of death in the United States. In 2024, 14.3 million (5.5%) of adults (aged 18 or older) had serious thoughts of suicide within the past year, and 2.2 million attempted suicide [ 1 ]. Suicide prevention interventions are often delivered through formal mental health care settings; however, over 41% of adults who endorse a need for mental health treatment do not receive treatment [ 1 ]. These data suggest that traditional service delivery models are not sufficiently reaching this population. The safety planning intervention (SPI) is considered a best practice [ 2 , 3 ] in behavioral health settings when working with individuals who have elevated suicide-related thoughts or behaviors. The SPI was developed as a brief and collaborative clinician-delivered intervention [ 4 ] that aims to support patients in coping with suicidal thoughts and resisting suicidal behaviors by creating a highly personalized list of internal and external coping resources [ 5 ]. The SPI often comprises 7 steps: (1) identifying warning signs, (2) coping strategies, (3) people who can provide distraction, (4) trusted contacts to help in a crisis, (5) professional resources, (6) lethal means safety, and (7) reasons for living. It also includes follow-up contact from providers to support connections to care and support using one’s safety plan [ 4 ]. However, young adults face structural and attitudinal barriers, such as cost, stigma, and limited access to providers, that prevent them from engaging in formal mental health treatment [ 6 , 7 ]. Moreover, this clinician-delivered intervention may face demand barriers, such as young adults’ strong preferences for self-reliance and autonomy [ 8 , 9 ]. Digital SPIs offer a potential pathway to circumvent these barriers by offering low-burden, accessible, and scalable interventions via mobile platforms [ 10 , 11 ]. As digital versions of SPIs have expanded, it is important to distinguish between collaborative SPIs completed jointly with clinicians through telehealth platforms and self-guided SPIs completed independently with structured system directions and guidance [ 12 ]. Emerging randomized controlled trials comparing in-person and digital SPIs suggest that some self-guided and interactive digital SPIs are acceptable, feasible, and yield effective safety plans that rival clinician-delivered safety plans [ 12 , 13 ]. Digital SPIs have been developed across various platforms and populations, with many offering self-guided formats designed to help individuals manage suicidal crises [ 14 - 18 ]. These self-guided safety plans demonstrate acceptability and show promise for increasing the accessibility of SPIs. Within self-guided digital SPIs, there are decision points that must be considered as part of their design, specifically how users are expected to engage with safety planning tools and the level of decisional authority they can retain throughout the planning process. We organize these decision points using the 5W1H (Who, What, Where, When, Why, and How) framework, a structure used in human-centered design work to identify and organize decision points in complex behavioral interventions [ 19 ]. In this study, what , when , and how organize the primary decision-point domains, while who , where , and why function as contextual conditions that cut across those domains, grounding the needs-assessment logic that shapes how each decision point should be operationalized. The current study adopts a clear conceptual distinction between personalization and customization as 2 mechanisms through which control over functionality and decision support can be implemented in a self-guided digital SPI. Personalization typically involves the system automatically tailoring content to users based on user data, while customization involves users actively choosing and modifying the interface or content [ 20 , 21 ]. In this study, personalization refers to system-initiated adaptation, in which the intervention automatically tailors features of, or content within, a system, while customization refers to user-initiated control that defines when, what, and how users can actively make choices about their experience using a system, increasing user autonomy and engagement [ 20 , 22 ]. Prior research identifies both personalization [ 23 ] and customization [ 24 ] as facilitators of engagement with digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) among young people. To understand how both personalization and customization can be applied in self-guided digital SPIs, we conducted one-on-one interviews with young adults with lived experience of suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STB). We aimed to answer the following research questions: (1) what are the key decision points in digital SPIs? (2) How do personalization and customization function as mechanisms for allocating autonomy and decision authority across safety planning decision points? Methods Participants Nine young adults who participated in a larger asynchronous remote community (ARC) study about the design of text-based, self-guided digital safety plans [ 25 ] provided affirmative informed consent to participate in individual interviews to understand their needs and preferences regarding digital safety planning ( Table 1 ). Participants were recruited by email if they had participated in the parent study [ 25 ]. Eligibility criteria for the parent study required participants to reside in the United States, be between 18 and 24 years old, own a smartphone, possess proficiency in English, and report suicidal ideation within the 2 weeks prior to recruitment. Suicidal ideation was assessed using a modified item from the DSM-5 -CCSI ( Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders [Fifth Edition] Cross-Cutting Symptom Inventory [ 26 ]), the DSI-SS (Depression Severity Index–Suicidality Subscale [ 27 ]), and an item (#9) from the BDI-II (Beck Depression Inventory–Second Edition [ 28 ]). Exclusion criteria included manic or psychotic symptoms endorsed within the 2 weeks prior to recruitment or the presence of strong suicidal desire, operationalized as a score of 2 or greater on BDI-II item 9. Procedures The parent project examined (1) the overall needs and preferences of young adults with STB for suicide prevention and (2) the needs and preferences young adults had for a SPI delivered via interactive text messaging [ 25 ]. Participants were recruited for the parent project through an advertisement embedded on Mental Health America’s (MHA) screening website, where they host free, validated screening tools [ 29 ]. Individuals early in their mental health journeys go to learn more about their mental health symptoms and plan next steps [ 30 ]. The advertisement was shown to individuals who accessed a resource page about STB and reported recent suicidal or self-harm ideation on one of MHA’s online mental health screening tools. Interested individuals who clicked on the advertisement were directed to a Northwestern University–hosted study information page. Those wishing to participate could complete eligibility screening surveys via Northwestern’s REDCap (Vanderbilt University) [ 31 , 32 ]. Eligible individuals reviewed informed consent documentation and provided affirmative informed consent prior to any study procedures. Participants (N=9) in this interview study were recruited from a pool of individuals who participated in one of 2 ARC groups [ 25 ] that explored the needs and preferences of young adults who have experienced STB as part of the parent research project. The parent ARC study included 30 participants, with 15 participants in each of the 2 groups. Interview invitations were sent to 26 of the 30 ARC participants, prioritizing those who had made at least one ARC post. The 26 invitees included 2 participants who had not engaged in ARC activities, whom we invited to capture potential perspectives from individuals who may have disengaged from the ARC forum; neither responded. Four ARC participants were not invited because they had no engagement with ARC activities; one of these participants had previously withdrawn from the study. Of the 26 participants invited, 9 scheduled and completed an interview, 1 declined, and 2 reported scheduling conflicts that could not be resolved and did not respond to additional scheduling options. The remaining 14 participants did not respond to multiple outreach attempts. These 9 individual interviews were conducted by the principal investigator, a doctoral-level clinical psychologist, or a full-time research assistant with a bachelor’s degree. The interview guide was drafted by the study principal investigator, JM, drawing on interview guides used in the team’s prior research, the aims of the current study, and his experience in suicide prevention, digital mental health, and qualitative research. MHA collaborators (TN and KR) also reviewed the guide to ensure that it was appropriate for young adults seeking mental health information through the MHA platform. The guide also aimed to elicit additional details and clarifications beyond what participants shared in their ARC elicitation groups. Data for the present study comprise transcripts from 9 individual interviews. Interviews were conducted via Zoom, with camera use optional. Interviews were conducted by JM and SAP. SAP had communicated with participants about study logistics. Neither of the 2 interviewers had a preexisting personal or clinical relationship with participants. Both interviewers were familiar with techniques for eliciting detailed responses while remaining neutral and maintaining fidelity to the semistructured interview guide. Interviews lasted approximately 20 to 40 minutes, and participants received US $8 for completing the interview. This sample size of 9 reflects the number of ARC participants who completed the follow-up interview. Reflexivity Statement The research team included 9 authors with diverse backgrounds and levels of experience, including practicing clinicians, behavioral health researchers, mental health professionals, and social science students. The team represented a range of educational and professional backgrounds, including psychology, social work, digital mental health, communications, human-computer interaction, and computer science, as well as career stages ranging from early-, middle-, and advanced-career researchers and staff to doctoral-level faculty members and trainees, including master’s degree students. Collectively, the team has a strong interest in the development and evaluation of digital mental health tools and interventions and in increasing access to suicide prevention care. The team is aware of its predisposition toward the potential of accessible digital suicide prevention tools to increase access to mental health care. At the time of the study, JM was a clinical psychologist and faculty member with clinical and research experience in suicide prevention. SAP was a research assistant who helped administer the ARC activities and communicated with participants about study logistics. title: Stimulant Persistence in Adult ADHD: A Retrospective Analysis of a Large Clinical Cohort
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Network meta-analyses suggest dexamphetamines (dAMP) may yield more favourable short-term outcomes than methylphenidate (MPH) in adults with ADHD, yet evidence on long-term comparative persistence remains scarce. This study compared 12-month treatment persistence between MPH and dAMP in a large multicentre cohort and explored associations with ADHD clinical presentations and objectively measured core symptoms.

METHODS: Stimulant persistence was defined by the primary outcome, 'time-to-transition', the interval from initiation to switching stimulant classes, transitioning to non-stimulants or complete discontinuation. Patients were censored at 12 months or at last clinical contact. A multivariable mixed-effects Cox proportional hazard model with a random intercept for clinicians was used to estimate hazard ratios (HR) and assess the relative impact of stimulant class on persistence, including its interactions with DSM-based clinical presentations and objective indices.

RESULTS: Among 12,995 participants (49% female), 62% initiated dAMP and 38% MPH. Median time-to-transition was 33.1 weeks for dAMP versus 15.0 weeks for MPH. MPH was associated with a 45% increased hazard for non-persistence compared to dAMP (HR = 1.45, 95% CI [1.36-1.55]). Regarding clinical and objective factors, hyperactive/impulsive presentation (HR = 1.14, p = 0.025) and objective impulsivity (HR = 1.05, p = 0.002) were independently associated with non-persistence. A significant interaction was observed between stimulant class and objective hyperactivity (p = 0.003), indicating that dAMP's persistence advantage became more pronounced with increasing motor activity (HR = 1.09). Nevertheless, these associations were secondary to the overarching effect of the stimulant class itself.

CONCLUSION: Treatment with dAMP demonstrates significantly superior 12-month persistence compared to MPH in adults with ADHD. While clinical and objective measures of impulsivity and hyperactivity identify patients at higher risk for treatment non-persistence, dAMP's advantage remains consistent across all presentations. These findings suggest that prioritizing dAMP may enhance long-term treatment persistence in adult ADHD clinical practice.

title: Artificial Intelligence in suicide prevention: promise, peril, and clinical implications for clinical practice
abstract:
Abstract The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into psychiatry is progressing rapidly, with promising yet underexplored applications in suicide prevention. While most existing studies have focused on suicide risk prediction, AI could be applied more broadly across the suicide prevention continuum. This review explores AI’s potential in improving the detection of suicidal ideation (SI), enhancing clinician training, and expanding patient access to psychotherapeutic support. Studies suggest that AI models may identify SI more sensitively than clinicians by detecting subtle linguistic or semantic cues. Furthermore, AI-based virtual patients have been shown to improve clinicians’ confidence and accuracy in suicide risk assessments, particularly when used alongside traditional training methods. On the patient side, CBT-inspired AI tools offer scalable, on-demand support, but most remain unregulated and clinically unvalidated. Despite their perceived empathy and availability, such tools pose ethical and clinical risks. Many patients use AI tools without professional guidance, a trend clinicians often underestimate. This disconnect calls for urgent regulatory oversight and professional engagement. Without clear clinical validation, AI-based tools may evolve outside medical frameworks, exposing vulnerable individuals to preventable harm. Psychiatry must not only adapt but also lead, ensuring that innovation is harnessed responsibly to serve patients with empathy, safety, and scientific rigor.

Introduction The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is spreading rapidly across developed countries, including among patients with mental disorders. In clinical neuroscience, AI can be viewed as a set of computational tools that mimic certain aspects of human cognition—such as information processing, language comprehension, and risk evaluation. When applied to psychiatry, AI models can process and interpret complex data to identify mental health risks, assist in clinical diagnosis, or personalise interventions. Importantly, AI does not replicate human understanding or empathy, but it can detect subtle markers in data that may escape human attention, such as linguistic patterns associated with suicidal ideation. In a recent U.S. survey among adults with a mental disorder who had used an AI large language model (LLM), such as ChatGPT, within the past year, nearly half reported using it as a form of psychological support (Rubin 2026 ). Even more strikingly, two-thirds of these individuals stated that interacting with AI improved their mental health condition. In younger populations, AI use for mental health purposes is also substantial. A recent survey of adolescents and young adults (ages 12–21) found that approximately 13% used AI for mental health advice, with this percentage increasing significantly among those over 18. Among AI users, over 65% used it monthly for mental health-related advice, and more than 90% found it very helpful (McBain et al. 2025 ). These numbers highlight that a significant proportion of individuals with mental health conditions are using AI tools without any clinical supervision. Alarmingly, most psychiatrists are unaware of this widespread usage—or outright deny it—despite its potential impact on both patients and clinical practice (Frances, 2026 ). When used correctly, AI could offer substantial benefits in mental health care. However, unsupervised, or inappropriate use may lead to serious and even life-threatening consequences. This issue is particularly critical in the field of suicidal behaviours (i.e., suicide and suicide attempts). A recent tragic case involved a suicidal adolescent who disclosed his suicidal thoughts to an AI-based LLM and eventually died by hanging, reportedly after the AI explained to him how to tie the knot (Nagata et al. 2026 ). Despite such catastrophic events, AI may still hold promise in improving care for suicidal individuals (Lee et al. 2021 ). Numerous studies have shown promising results in predicting suicide risk using LLMs and machine learning (ML) algorithms, based on electronic health records or social media data (Arowosegbe and Oyelade 2023 ; Levkovich and Omar 2024 ; Badian et al. 2023 ; Mansoor and Ansari 2024 ; Du et al. 2018 ; Wu et al. 2023 ; Sherekar and Mehta 2025 ). While improving the prediction of suicidal behaviour is undeniably important, many other potential applications of AI in suicide prevention remain underexplored. Indeed, the implementation of predictive models in real-life clinical practice is still far from reality. In contrast, some AI-based tools could be applied more immediately to support suicide prevention, such as: (i) detecting suicidal ideation in clinical settings through analysis of clinical interviews; (ii) improving clinician training; and (iii) supporting patients in coping with suicidal thoughts. While these applications may offer real benefits, it is essential to consider the potential risks of relying too heavily on AI, especially in the context of vulnerable individuals. Accordingly, the aim of this review is to examine these three domains of direct AI application in suicide prevention, while critically discussing their potential benefits and associated risks and to address the broader challenges of integrating AI safely into suicide prevention practices. Clinical judgment and Artificial Intelligence: Complementarity, not substitution Suicidal behaviours can be conceptualised as existing along a continuum, ranging from passive suicidal ideation (SI) to active ideation, suicide attempts, and ultimately death by suicide. Identifying patients experiencing SI is thus the crucial first step in this chain, offering an opportunity to intervene early and prevent progression to more severe outcomes (Nobile et al. 2022 ; Courtet and Baca-García 2024 ). This is not only essential from a suicide prevention standpoint, but also because SI is itself associated with worse psychiatric prognosis, including treatment resistance and recurrence in mood disorders (Nobile et al. 2024 ; Bergfeld et al. 2018 ). Yet, detecting SI remains a substantial clinical challenge. Studies have revealed a concerning level of discordance—up to 75%—between clinicians’ evaluations and patients’ self-reports regarding suicidal thoughts (Nobile et al. 2023 ; Nobile et al. 2024 ; Gao et al. 2015 ). In most cases, patients reported SI that clinicians failed to detect. However, this discrepancy cannot be attributed solely to limitations in clinical judgement. A significant body of evidence suggests that some patients, particularly adolescents and individuals from diverse or vulnerable backgrounds, may not disclose suicidal thoughts during clinical encounters due to stigma, fear of hospitalisation, uncertainty, or a weak therapeutic alliance (Uhl et al. 2023 ). This is far from a trivial oversight: approximately 56% of individuals who die by suicide have consulted a healthcare professional within the four weeks preceding their death (O’Rourke et al. 2023 ). Moreover, patients who only endorse SI via self-report questionnaires, but not during clinical interviews, appear to carry a suicide attempt risk equivalent to those whose SI is confirmed by clinicians (Nobile et al. 2024 ; Uhl et al. 2023 ). These findings highlight both the limitations of clinical judgement alone and the challenges related to patient disclosure underscoring the need for enhanced tools to detect SI more reliably. AI, and in particular large LLMs, could be instrumental in this regard. Some studies have begun to explore the capacity of AI to assess presence of SI based on patient narratives or structured data, offering an alternative and potentially more sensitive detection method. For instance, a recent study compared SI assessments made by ChatGPT-4 and ChatGPT-3.5 against those of 379 mental health professionals on patient’s vignettes (Levkovich and Elyoseph 2023 ). Their findings suggest that ChatGPT-4 matched clinicians’ accuracy in predicting suicide attempts and even showed greater sensitivity in detecting SI and psychological pain. In contrast, ChatGPT-3.5 significantly underestimated suicide risk across all conditions tested, particularly in the most severe cases. These results highlight two key points. First, AI systems, particularly more recent versions, may be capable of identifying SI with a level of precision comparable to human clinicians. Second, different AI models vary widely in their performance, and under certain conditions, older versions may dangerously underestimate risk. This calls for caution: while AI may enhance SI detection, it also introduces the possibility of error, particularly when used uncritically or without awareness of model limitations (Arowosegbe and Oyelade 2023 ; Levkovich and Omar 2024 ; Bernert et al. 2020 ). Importantly, AI could also serve as a valuable complement in clinical settings, by offering a form of ‘second reading’ of clinical interviews. One could imagine a system that transcribes patient–clinician dialogues in real-time and analyzes subtle linguistic markers suggestive of SI ( e.g., increased use of intensifiers or personal pronouns, or tone shifts associated with hopelessness). Such markers may escape clinician attention, especially in time-constrained or emotionally charged consultations. Moreover, such approaches may be particularly valuable in identifying patients who do not explicitly disclose suicidal thoughts, by detecting indirect or implicit linguistic signals associated with distress or suicidality. In this regard, a very recent study demonstrated that AI models trained on naturalistic patient–provider interviews were able to detect SI using both acoustic and semantic features, providing additional cues that may not be consciously perceived by clinicians (Lho et al. 2025 ). Nevertheless, these tools should be used with great caution. Over-reliance on AI could lead to automation bias, where clinicians overly trust algorithmic outputs even when these conflict with their own judgement or the clinical context (Perlis 2026 ). In practice, these kinds of misjudgments could either inflate perceived risk, leading to unnecessary interventions, or deflate it, missing patients in need of urgent care. Clinicians must therefore remain the primary decision-makers. To avoid inappropriate use and maximise AI’s potential, clinical training must integrate AI literacy, especially in suicide prevention (Elyoseph et al. 2024 ). Moreover, beyond immediate decision-making risks, an additional concern relates to the long-term impact of AI integration on the development of clinical expertise. As AI tools become increasingly embedded in training and practice environments, future clinicians may rely on them from the earliest stages of their education. This raises the possibility of cognitive offloading, where critical aspects of clinical reasoning are delegated to AI systems, potentially limiting the development of independent judgement and expertise. Indeed, emerging evidence suggests that increased reliance on AI tools may be associated with reduced critical thinking abilities, with cognitive offloading acting as a mediating factor (Gerlich 2025 ). Over time, such reliance could lead to a form of ‘AI learning dependency’, in which clinicians may struggle to critically evaluate or challenge algorithmic outputs, particularly in complex or ambiguous clinical situations such as suicidality. From an educational perspective, this also raises the question of when AI should be introduced during clinical training. Premature exposure to AI tools may hinder the development of independent clinical reasoning, as trainees may rely on algorithmic support before acquiring core assessment skills. A staged approach could therefore be considered, in which AI is introduced later in training once foundational competencies in clinical judgement have been established. Such an approach may help ensure that AI enhances, rather than supplants, the development of critical thinking and decision-making skills in future clinicians. In sum, while AI may improve the detection of SI, particularly in cases where clinicians might miss subtle cues, it should not be viewed as a substitute for clinical expertise. Used in a complementary manner, AI has the potential to bridge current gaps in SI detection and contribute meaningfully to prevention strategies. Training the human copilot: AI as a tool for clinician education in suicidal behaviors Given the high rates of under-detection of SI by clinicians and the potential support AI can offer in refining risk assessments, it is crucial to integrate AI technologies not only into clinical tools but also into the training of healthcare professionals. Importantly, this applies not only to psychiatrists but also to general practitioners (GPs), who are frequently the first medical professionals to encounter patients with suicidal thoughts (Stene-Larsen and Reneflot 2019 ; Feldman et al. 2007 ). Even though mood disorders are a primary risk factor for suicidal behaviour, fewer than 40% of GPs report routinely evaluating SI in patients with mood disorders (Feldman et al. 2007 ). Thus, strengthening the ability of psychiatrists but also GPs and other non-specialist clinicians to detect SI is a pressing public health objective. In this context, the integration of AI-based tools into clinician training offers a promising path forward. These tools can serve dual purposes: first, by educating practitioners on how AI systems work, what their limitations are, and how to interpret their outputs cautiously; and second, by actively assisting in the acquisition of clinical interviewing and risk assessment skills. One of the most innovative uses of AI in this domain is the deployment of virtual patient simulators, chatbots powered by natural language processing, which allow clinicians to practice suicide risk assessments in a controlled environment. For example, a virtual agent named ‘Alex’ was developed and designed to train mental health clinicians in assessing suicide risk (Foster et al. 2015 ). This virtual interaction provided a safe and repeatable learning experience. Clinicians trained with Alex were found to be more confident and effective in eliciting information related to suicidal thoughts compared to those trained using traditional methods. Similarly, another study evaluated the impact of a conversational agent designed to simulate patients presenting with SI (Martínez-Miranda 2017 ). The study demonstrated that clinicians trained with this AI-powered agent showed better recognition of verbal and non-verbal cues associated with suicide risk, and greater ease in navigating difficult conversations than clinicians trained with traditional methods. These findings support the use of AI-based simulations as a scalable and engaging complement to classical educational formats such as workshops or lectures. title: Low-threshold secondary and tertiary suicide prevention measures for individuals with suicid-related thoughts and behaviors: a scoping review
abstract:
Introduction Suicide rates remain persistently high in many regions worldwide, including Germany. The 2024 German National Suicide Prevention Strategy emphasizes the strengthening of evidence-based approaches. In this context, a comprehensive synthesis of low-threshold secondary and tertiary suicide prevention measures for adults is required. Methods This scoping review set out to address this need and followed established methodological guidance and the PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines. PubMed and Web of Science were searched on September 1, 2025, for studies published from January 1, 2005, onwards. To be eligible for inclusion, studies needed to examine low-threshold secondary or tertiary suicide prevention measures targeting adults with suicide-related thoughts and behaviors (STBs). Interventions focusing on primary medical care, psychotherapy, pharmacotherapy, gatekeepers and means restriction were excluded. Results Out of 1,897 records, 24 studies met the inclusion criteria. Most studies investigated voice-based ( n = 9; 37.5%) and text-based ( n = 7; 29.2%) crisis interventions within suicide prevention lifelines. These interventions consistently demonstrated reductions in suicidal ideation and psychological distress, with one exception: a moderated peer-to-peer forum. Outreach messages ( n = 3; 12.5%) and web-based educational (and counseling) measures ( n = 5; 20.8%) showed promising but more heterogeneous findings. Outcomes indicated potential benefits, though the evidence was less consistent. Discussion The findings suggest that voice- and text-based crisis interventions are supported by a growing evidence base, primarily demonstrating short-term effects. Web-based educational (and counseling) measures and outreach messages, while heterogeneous, show potential for individuals with STBs through the use of emerging technologies. Future research should examine mechanisms of action, long-term outcomes, and employ randomized controlled trial designs (where feasible) to strengthen the evidence base. Systematic review registration https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/K2B83 .

Introduction Suicid-related thoughts and behaviors (STBs) constitute a major global public health concern ( 1 ). Over the past decades, various suicide prevention initiatives, improved access to care, and societal developments have contributed to a notable decline in suicide rates in many countries ( 1 , 2 ). Nevertheless, this decline has not progressed in recent years to the extent anticipated under the WHO Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) ( 3 ). In Germany, following a marked reduction between 1980 and 2000, suicide rates have remained largely stable over the past 25 years, ranging between 9,000 and 10,000 cases annually ( 2 ). In 2024, the German Federal Ministry of Health published a National Suicide Prevention Strategy, with the aim of strengthening evidence-based suicide prevention in Germany ( 4 ). As part of this initiative, recommendations are needed that specifiy which secondary and tertiary preventive measures are most suitable to support the strategy. Against this backdrop, the present scoping review was conducted to synthesize the available evidence on low-threshold secondary and tertiary suicide prevention measures, to identify effective measures, and to provide evidence for the German National Suicide Prevention Strategy. In the final report of the German National Suicide Prevention Programme, Fiedler et al. ( 5 ) define low-threshold suicide prevention as encompassing “professional, semi-professional, and lay-supported services” that provide “barrier-free access for help-seeking individuals across the full spectrum of suicidal ideation and behaviour” and aim to reduce suicidality while providing psychosocial support. According to the authors, such services should be easily accessible, confidential, ideally free of charge, and available without waiting periods. Secondary and tertiary suicide prevention measures differ from primary prevention in that they target individuals who already experience or have experienced STBs. Primary prevention, in contrast, focuses on the general population or at-risk groups without manifest symptoms, aiming to prevent the emergence of STBs. Secondary measures relate to the early management of suicidal ideation, for example through crisis intervention, whereas tertiary measures focus on relapse prevention, such as the prevention of repeating suicide attempts ( 6 ). In practice and research, secondary and tertiary measures are often difficult to distinguish and are therefore considered jointly in this review ( 7 ). Table 1 provides an overview of (low-threshold) measures for primary, secondary, and tertiary suicide prevention. In practice, a wide range of suicide prevention measures are implemented, and a variety of secondary and tertiary suicide prevention strategies have been analyzed in the research literature. Over the past 10–15 years, research on these measures has increased markedly. Several scoping and systematic reviews have attempted to provide an overview of the various areas of suicide prevention and the available evidence. Some reviews have focused on measures for specific populations [e.g., men ( 8 , 9 ), students ( 10 ), older adults ( 11 )], or geographic regions [e.g., rural areas ( 12 )], while others have examined specific intervention types, such as web-based suicide prevention ( 13 – 15 ). Miller et al. ( 16 ) primarily examined the mechanisms underlying the effectiveness of Lifelines in the United States. The focus of Miller et al. ( 16 ) is not primarily on the effects of the intervention on STBs, and their analysis is limited to a single region. A recent review published in 2025 assessed the effectiveness of gatekeeper programs ( 17 ). Among other outcomes, changes in the behavior of trained individuals were observed (e.g., whether they intervened more frequently or in different ways). In summary, existing reviews have largely focused on specific interventions, target populations, or geographic regions, or have addressed aspects other than the effectiveness of interventions in relation to STBs or psychological distress. To date, no comprehensive overview exists regarding the effects of low-threshold secondary and tertiary suicide prevention measures on STBs in adults. This gap is addressed by the present review. Where previous research intersects with our research question, it has been taken into account. For this reason, gatekeeper programs will not be addressed in our review. Excluded from the present review are also suicide prevention measures with a main focus on medical care (e.g., outpatient and inpatient care), pharmacotherapy, and psychotherapeutic treatment, as strong evidence already exists in these domains. Some reviews covering multiple suicide prevention strategies have demonstrated effectiveness primarily for these measures. Mann et al. ( 18 ) showed that primary care training, psychiatric treatment and follow-up, as well as pharmacotherapy, are effective in reducing STBs. Additional studies provide comprehensive evidence for psychotherapeutic interventions ( 19 – 22 ). These measures are also reflected in clinical recommendations, including those of the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence ( 23 ). A particularly suicide-focused psychotherapy appears to be a potentially effective approach ( 24 ). Zalsmann et al. ( 25 ) reviewed evidence for seven types of suicide prevention measures (public and physician education, media strategies, screening, restriction of access to means, treatment, and internet or hotline support) and also found support for pharmacological and psychotherapeutic interventions, school-based awareness programs, and means restriction. For the remaining types of measures, the need for future research was emphasized due to the lack of randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Means restriction is not considered in the present review, as robust evidence already exists and it is classified as structural prevention because it modifies environmental conditions rather than individual behavior [e.g., ( 26 , 27 )]. The aim of this scoping review is to systematically identify and map the existing evidence on low-threshold secondary and tertiary suicide prevention measures for adults. After excluding primary medical, psychotherapeutic, pharmacological interventions, and gatekeeper programs, examples of measures relevant for our aims and based on Mann et al. ( 18 , 25 ) and Zalsmann et al. ( 25 )-include Lifelines (voice- or text-based crisis support), on site counseling, information and training programs, risk detection (screening) and outreach, as well as self-help and peer-to-peer support. The broad research question (Which low-threshold prevention measures targeting adults can be considered effective based on current available evidence?), heterogeneous measures, and assumed methodological diversity of the studies in the field (ranging supposedly from RCTs, quasi-experimental to qualitative studies) suggest that a scoping review is the most appropriate approach ( 28 ). Methods This scoping review followed the approach outlined by Arksey et al. ( 28 ), more recent adaptations ( 29 – 32 ) and the PRISMA-ScR guidelines ( 33 ). The following steps were carried out: (1) Development of a research question, (2) Identification of relevant studies, (3) Selection of studies, (4) Structured data extraction from the included studies, (5) Synthesis and reporting of results. The study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework ( 34 ). Search strategy To identify relevant studies, searches were conducted in two databases: PubMed and Web of Science. The search strategy was developed through an iterative process. Three content domains were defined (suicide prevention; secondary/tertiary suicide prevention measures; access/low threshold), each represented by various search terms linked with the Boolean operator AND. Within the three content domains, different search terms were linked with the Boolean operator OR. A requirement was that suicid * and prevention * appear together in the title and abstract; the remaining search terms could appear in either the title or the abstract. Appropriate MeSH terms were used in the PubMed search. The full search strategies and database-specific adaptations are available on OSF ( https://osf.io/kjt39 ) and in the Supplementary material . An example of an abbreviated PubMed search query is (suicid * [ti] AND prevention * [ti]) AND (suicid * [tiab] AND prevention * [tiab]) AND (“Suicide Prevention”[Mesh] OR “Crisis Intervention”[Mesh] OR helpline * [tiab] OR “Counseling”[Mesh] AND “Health Services Accessibility”[Mesh] OR barriers[tiab] OR “health care barrier * ”[tiab] OR “low-threshold”[tiab]). In addition to database searches, the reference lists of included articles were manually screened. The search was restricted to articles published between January 1, 2005, and September 1, 2025 (the date of the search). This time period was applied because it encompasses the emergence and major developments of suicide prevention interventions and related research. Only articles published in English or German were considered. Inclusion and exclusion criteria The inclusion and exclusion criteria were developed through an iterative process. Studies were included if they assessed low-threshold secondary or tertiary suicide prevention measures. Secondary and tertiary suicide prevention encompasses measures for individuals with current or past suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STBs). To clearly classify an intervention as secondary or tertiary suicide prevention, individuals with STBs were required to participate in the intervention and to be involved in its evaluation. In addition, studies had to assess at least one outcome related to STBs or psychological distress. An additional inclusion criterion was low-threshold access. Accordingly, only studies on interventions that were accessible without major formal barriers (e.g., without referral requirements, long waiting times, or financial barriers, or with anonymous access) were included. Furthermore, only studies involving individuals aged 18 years and older were considered. Only peer-reviewed articles were included, encompassing all study designs, such as randomized controlled trials (RCTs), observational studies, and quantitative and qualitative research. As described in the Introduction, studies on suicide prevention measures primarily focused on medical care (e.g., outpatient and inpatient care and related aftercare interventions), pharmacotherapy, psychotherapeutic treatment, or means restriction were excluded from the present review. During the review process, the eligibility criteria were further refined to exclude gatekeeper programs, as a dedicated review on this topic had recently been published ( 17 ). No search of gray literature was conducted. Since critical appraisal of methodological quality is not a required component of scoping reviews ( 28 ), no formal quality assessment was conducted or used to inform decisions regarding study inclusion or exclusion. Methodological limitations of the included studies are presented in the Supplementary material accompanying the extracted data ( 34 ). Study selection All records retrieved from the databases were imported into the web-based tool Rayyan ( www.rayyan.ai ), where duplicates were removed by CS2. The initial title and abstract screening, as well as the management of included and excluded articles, was also conducted using Rayyan. The entire study selection process was carried out independently by CS1 and CS2. In cases of disagreement, HG, LS and DH were consulted, and a consensus was reached through discussion. First, titles and abstracts of all articles were screened, and a preliminary selection was made based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Of the pre-selected studies, all full texts were reviewed to determine the extent to which the inclusion and exclusion criteria were met. Disagreements were discussed jointly by CS1, CS2, HG, LS and DH to decide for or against inclusion. For example, it was discussed whether services for individuals bereaved by suicide without STBs should be considered tertiary prevention, and to what extent identification based on suicide-related Google searches adequately captures individuals experiencing STBs. In both cases, the studies were not included because individuals with STBs were not clearly involved. Figure 1 shows the detailed study selection process. title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: transition to psychotic disorders
abstract: It is well recognized that Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is associated with heightened risk for common psychiatric disorders; early identification and treatment of ADHD may help reduce some of this risk. However, the substantially increased risk of bipolar disorder, psychosis, and schizophrenia (hereafter psychotic disorders) is often overlooked (odds ratios 4.7-8.9). Given how common ADHD is, there is growing pressure for greater involvement of primary care services, especially for less complex forms of ADHD. However, those at highest risk for transition to a psychotic disorder need to be prioritised for secondary care follow up. Currently it is unknown how to stratify ADHD according to risk or indeed why only some develop a psychotic disorder. This perspective examines key hypotheses that may explain why transition occurs only in a subset of individuals. One hypothesis is that features suggestive of ADHD may represent early manifestations of psychotic disorders, although direct support for this is limited. The potential role of ADHD treatment is also considered; current data indicate that therapeutic use of methylphenidate is not associated with increased risk of psychotic disorders, while uncertainty remains for amphetamines. The possible mediating roles of ADHD-evoked environmental exposures are discussed, but evidence for mediation is lacking. We also consider the evidence that ADHD and psychotic disorders result from shared underlying neurodevelopmental processes. We highlight key clinical implications for screening and monitoring individuals with ADHD for psychotic disorders and consider what factors may help in weighting risk. Finally, we identify important evidence gaps for future research.

title: The role of white matter microstructure in the association between childhood maltreatment and adult post-traumatic symptoms
abstract: Childhood maltreatment (CM) is a risk factor for adult post-traumatic symptoms and white matter (WM) alterations. It remains unknown how WM microstructure is affected alongside two common military conditions, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). Data from 299 participants (53% male, 35.69 ± 12.23 years of age) of the Injury and Traumatic Stress (INTRuST) clinical consortium was analyzed. The study included 56 individuals with PTSD (41 with comorbid mTBI), 107 with mTBI, and 136 controls (no PTSD and/or mTBI). Diffusion parameters (mean, axial, and radial diffusivity, MD, AD, RD; fractional anisotropy, FA) in major WM tracts were extracted from diffusion MRI. CM was assessed using the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ). Multiple regression models examined associations between CM severity and WM diffusion. Moderation analyses assessed the effect of PTSD and/or mTBI on these associations. Mediation analyses examined how WM diffusion affects the associations between CM and both PTSD and post-concussive symptom severity. Greater CM severity was associated with lower MD and AD, independent of PTSD and/or mTBI. WM diffusion, particularly in the corpus callosum and the superior longitudinal fasciculus, mediated the associations between CM severity and both PTSD (MD b ab  = 0.022, AD b ab  = 0.019-0.034) and post-concussive symptoms (MD b ab  = 0.028-0.040, AD b ab  = 0.032-0.047). Findings suggest that WM alterations are more strongly associated with CM itself than with either PTSD and/or mTBI. Mediating effects in regions critical for sensory integration highlight the role of WM microstructure as a neurobiological pathway through which CM might predispose to post-traumatic symptoms.

title: Excitation-Inhibition Balance and Fronto-Limbic Connectivity Distinguish TMS Treatment Outcomes in Refractory Depression
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) targeting the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) is effective for treatment-resistant depression, but outcomes remain variable. The neurophysiological mechanisms underlying response remain poorly understood, limiting precision neuromodulation.

METHODS: We combined transcranial magnetic stimulation with electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) and connectome-based Jansen-Rit neural mass modeling to investigate the mechanistic basis of treatment efficacy in 90 patients with treatment-resistant depression. Individualized whole-brain models were fitted to pre- and post-iTBS TMS-evoked potentials, yielding subject-specific estimates of synaptic connectivity, excitation-inhibition (E/I) balance, and cortical dynamics. Brain states were defined by singular value decomposition of the model's population activity, and partial least squares analysis with nested cross-validation identified the brain-state pattern distinguishing responders from non-responders.

RESULTS: We identified two neurophysiological signatures associated with treatment response. First, responders showed greater post-treatment reductions in 3-10 Hz oscillatory power, driven by shifts in E/I balance toward greater inhibitory control through reduced excitatory drive and increased inhibitory-to-pyramidal connectivity. Second, a pre-treatment brain state characterized by opposite-polarity dynamics between subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) and left DLPFC distinguished responders from non-responders, consistent with prior fMRI findings on frontolimbic anticorrelation. Neural trajectory analysis further revealed greater dynamical reorganization and increased attractor stability in responders following treatment.

CONCLUSIONS: These findings provide a neurophysiologically-informed framework linking iTBS treatment efficacy to specific changes in cortical E/I balance and frontolimbic circuit dynamics, pointing toward candidate markers that, with subject-specific structural connectivity and independent validation, may inform personalized neuromodulation approaches in treatment-resistant depression.

title: Genetic architecture and risk of suicide attempt across neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Suicide attempt (SA) is prevalent among individuals with neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions, yet similarities and differences in the genetic architecture of SA across these conditions remain unclear.

METHODS: In the iPSYCH cohort (N=98,069), SA was identified using ICD-10 codes among individuals diagnosed with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) (N=22,962), autism (N=17,670), schizophrenia (N=5,974), bipolar disorder (N=3,028), depression (N=28,844), and controls (N=34,049). We evaluated 21 polygenic scores (PGSs) in individuals with and without SA within each diagnosis, stratified individuals into PGS quantiles, estimated absolute SA risk, and conducted sex-stratified analyses.

RESULTS: SA was 1% among controls but ranged from 5% in autism to 31% in schizophrenia. Several PGSs were increased in individuals with SA across diagnoses, including PGS for ADHD, depression, and substance use disorders (SUD). SA-PGS stratification showed marked SA absolute risk differences, e.g., 40% in the top PGS tertile vs 29% in the lowest tertile in schizophrenia. PGS-loads did not differ between females and males with SA across diagnoses. However, absolute SA risk differed substantially. In the highest SA-PGS tertile in ADHD, the absolute SA risk reached 36% for females and 22% for males and was further increased to 48% in those with comorbid SUD.

CONCLUSIONS: SA genetic architecture is similar across neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions and individuals can be stratified into SA risk groups based on PGSs, and co-occuring SUD. Being a female or having comorbid SUD are strong risk factors for SA, however SA common variants, still affect SA risk in the presence of those factors.

title: Sex differences in circulating endocannabinoid concentrations during adolescence: Associations with pubertal development
abstract: Endocannabinoids contribute to sex-related processes, including puberty. In 1,159 adolescents, females showed significantly lower concentrations than males across five endocannabinoids (AEA, 2-AG, PEA, OEA, and 2-OG). Sex-by-puberty interactions were significant for AEA, PEA, and OEA. Exploratory analyses revealed sex-specific associations between endocannabinoids and self-reported pain, stress, internalizing, and attentional problems.

title: Testing neurobiological models of reward/incentive sensitization in the continuation of alcohol use disorder (AUD) symptoms in young adults with AUD: A four-year longitudinal study
abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) remains an urgent public health problem. Alcohol response phenotype may be an important factor underlying vulnerability to and progression of AUD. This study examined the prospective association between acute alcohol responses and continued or remitted AUD over time in young adults with AUD. This sample was N = 101 AUD participants (M age =27.1 ± 4.0 SD yrs) comprising the third cohort of the Chicago Social Drinking Project. They completed two beverage challenge  laboratory sessions (0.8 g/kg fixed-dose alcohol vs. placebo) and four years of follow-up to ascertain future AUD symptoms, drinking behaviors, and consequences. Retention was high with an overall 99.2% follow-up rate. Analyses identified three AUD trajectory subgroups over follow-up including a high AUD trajectory subgroup (n = 37), a medium AUD trajectory subgroup (n = 48), and a low AUD trajectory subgroup (n = 16). Generalized estimating equations showed that greater sensitivity to alcohol's pleasurable effects, including stimulation and hedonic and motivational reward (liking and wanting, respectively) predicted more AUD symptoms over follow-up (ps<0.001) and were positively associated with AUD trajectory subgroups. However,  sedation, heart rate, and cortisol response to alcohol were not  significantly associated with AUD trajectory subgroups. In sum, greater alcohol stimulation, liking, and wanting prospectively predicted the continuation and increasing severity of AUD over a four-year period. The findings challenge theoretical models emphasizing reward deficit and global tolerance in addiction and support the role of positive reinforcement, indexed by sensitivity to alcohol's pleasurable effects, as an important factor in AUD  persistence. CLINICAL TRIAL: Name: Chicago Social Drinking Project Registration #: NCT00961792 URL: http://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT00961792.

title: Zebrafish behavioral phenomics reveals functional subtypes of autism risk genes
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a highly heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition caused by many genetic mutations, each conferring modest individual risk. Despite its genetic complexity and clinical burden, no effective treatments targeting core symptoms are available. Although ASD is diagnosed as a single disorder, accumulating evidence suggests that it comprises biologically distinct subtypes, yet how genetic risk maps onto phenotypic substructure remains poorly defined. Here, we apply zebrafish behavioral phenomics to systematically link ASD risk genes to functional behavioral subtypes in vivo. Using an unsupervised deep learning-based behavioral profiling platform, ZeChat, we characterized the behavioral repertoires of zebrafish mutants for 11 high-confidence ASD risk genes. ZeChat analysis revealed distinct behavioral phenotypes for each mutant that was classified into three behavioral subtypes (Clusters 1-3) via hierarchical clustering of their behavioral fingerprints. By integrating mutant phenotypes with a large neuroactive drug phenomics database, we identified subtype-specific correlations with serotonergic, dopaminergic, and opioid receptor-modulating compounds. Using an orthogonal social preference assay, Fishbook, we further demonstrate subtype-specific pharmacological rescue of social deficits, including selective rescue of the Cluster 3 mutants arid1b, adnp, grin2b, pten, and the Cluster 2 mutants pogz and shank3, by μ-opioid receptor antagonists. Together, these results demonstrate a scalable in vivo framework for behavioral phenomics-driven classification of ASD risk genes into functional subtypes and discovery of targeted rescue strategies.

title: Neural Circuits of Social Behavior in Autism Spectrum Disorder: From Mechanism to Intervention
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Difficulties in social communication and interaction are core diagnostic features of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), yet interventions targeting these difficulties have modest and variable effects. Understanding mechanistically distinct contributions to social behaviors may identify new therapeutic opportunities.

METHODS: This narrative review integrates human neuroimaging studies, supporting rodent circuit neuroscience, clinical intervention research, and developmental studies. We organize the findings into four overlapping functional-computational domains and relate these domains to the Research Domain Criteria Social Processes framework.

RESULTS: The four domains are: (1) Social Reward and Social Interest, encompassing the incentive and hedonic value of social contact and motivation to engage; (2) Social Memory and Social-Affective Value, encompassing recognition of familiar individuals and learned affective or motivational associations; (3) Social Cue Perception, Action Representation, and Social Prediction/Timing, encompassing the processing and forecasting of dynamic social information; and (4) Higher-Order Social Cognition and Model Updating, encompassing mental-state inference and the updating of person-specific social models. Because these domains are not independent, interactions among reward, memory, cue processing, prediction, and higher-order inference create multiple possible developmental entry points, such that early differences in one process may alter experience-dependent learning in others. Evidence for specific causal cascades remains preliminary and requires longitudinal testing.

CONCLUSIONS: A circuit-and-development framework may improve hypothesis generation, domain-specific phenotyping, target-engagement assessment, and mechanism-aligned outcomes. Clinical translation, however, requires caution. Biomarkers should be validated as predictors of treatment response, cascade models should be tested longitudinally, and interventions should combine mechanism-informed targets with behavioral support that promotes generalization to daily life.

title: Development of a messenger RNA therapy for schizophrenia
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Few gene-disease associations identified by human genetic studies lead to new drugs that advance to first-in-human trials. Schizophrenia exemplifies this translational gap: thousands of gene-disease associations have been reported, but antipsychotics act via mechanisms introduced in the 1950s. To close the gap, clinical research strategies are needed that generalize across genes and diseases.

METHODS: Candidate drug targets were defined as genes linked to schizophrenia by population-based studies. Clinical validation of candidate targets was performed through family-based studies. The molecular effects of clinically validated targets were confirmed by correcting mutations in the neurons from affected family members. For one validated target, a messenger RNA (mRNA) drug was developed, and pre-clinical studies of the drug were performed.

RESULTS: Carriers of rare protein-truncating variants (PTVs) in schizophrenia risk genes were identified in 30,813 patients of a US healthcare system. These included two female relatives with a rare PTV in GRIA3, which encodes the GluA3 subunit of the AMPA-type glutamate receptor. Further investigation of the family found an X-linked pattern of inheritance between the PTV and severe mental illness. Correction of the PTV in neurons of affected male family members restored GRIA3 expression. A GRIA3 mRNA drug was developed and in mice was well tolerated, resulted in broad brain expression of GluA3, and rescued behavioral abnormalities in a pharmacologically induced psychosis model (MK-801).

CONCLUSIONS: Further development toward clinical evaluation of a novel GRIA3 mRNA drug to treat schizophrenia is warranted.

title: A living systematic review, meta-analysis, and open data resource of trials of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD
abstract: 3,4-Methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) has emerged as a potential treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). However, rapidly changing evidence in a fast-moving field can be challenging to integrate. Here, we present a living systematic review and open-data meta-analytic resource on MDMA treatment for PTSD. In this initial release, 6 randomized controlled trials comprising 286 participants are included in the database. All six studies included in the review to date are sponsored by the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies (MAPS). Our primary model uses inverse-variance random-effects meta-analysis of standardized mean differences on primary outcomes of PTSD. Compared to control conditions, MDMA-assisted therapy (MDMA-AT) showed a greater reduction in PTSD symptoms (Hedges' g = -0.71). Meta-regressions on dosing variables were explored. Treatment with MDMA-AT as compared to placebo also resulted in higher response (risk ratio [RR] = 1.35) and remission (RR = 2.25) rates. Most studies included in the database had a low risk of bias according to Cochrane guidelines, though these fail to capture pertinent challenges in the field such as expectancy, functional unblinding, potential issues with study conduct, and safety. The current findings were assigned an overall low certainty rating using the GRADE approach. Together, this systematic review and meta-analysis suggests that MDMA-AT results in short-term decreases in PTSD symptoms across studies to date. This living systematic review, meta-analysis, database, and online dashboard ( sypres.io ) will continue to be updated as evidence emerges, providing a valuable, open, and transparent resource for researchers in a rapidly evolving field.

title: Enhancing cGMP signaling with psilocybin reduces head twitch and restructures the synaptic proteome while maintaining antidepressant response
abstract: Psilocybin produces antidepressant effects, but perceptual effects limit tolerability. We hypothesized that enhancing cGMP signaling with a phosphodiesterase-9 inhibitor (PDE9i) would diminish a rodent behavioral readout of 5-HT₂AR activation, while preserving antidepressant-like effects. PDE9i attenuated psilocybin-induced head-twitch while maintaining the antidepressant-like response. PDE9i-psilocybin reduced 5-HT₂AR-related pathways while enhancing synaptogenesis signaling.

title: A machine learning approach to predicting high-risk irritability trajectories across the transition to adolescence
abstract: Youth irritability, characterized as proneness to anger/frustration, is associated with negative mental health outcomes. This study identified irritability trajectories across the transition to early adolescence and applied machine learning to identify preadolescent predictors of irritability trajectories. Data are from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, a large longitudinal study that tracks youth development from preadolescence ( n  = 11,862, ages 8.92-11.08 years,  M  = 9.91,  SD  = 0.62). The baseline sample was 47.83% female ( n  = 5,680), 63.35% White, 15.74% Black, 12.07% Biracial or Multiracial, 2.32% Asian, and 20.30% Hispanic. Using parent-report youth irritability scores across four years, latent class growth analysis (LCGA) identified four distinct irritability trajectories: low stable ( n  = 8,692, 73.28%), high decreasing ( n  = 1,083, 9.13%), low increasing ( n  = 1,449, 12.22%), and high chronic ( n  = 638, 5.38%). Machine learning approaches generated predictive models for irritability trajectories, including baseline youth psychopathology, physical health, neurocognitive abilities, psychosocial environment, demographics, parent psychopathology, and brain structure metrics. The models demonstrated strong performance in detecting probability of being in the high chronic and low stable trajectories but poorer performance in classifying the irritability trajectories characterized by change. The most prominent predictors included youth externalizing and internalizing problems, parent psychopathology, and sleep problems. Findings provide insight into preadolescent predictors of irritability across a critical developmental period.

title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of fear conditioning in children who have experienced childhood trauma or maltreatment
abstract: Childhood trauma has been identified as a major risk factor for the development of fear-related disorders in adulthood. Exposure to trauma might impact fear learning and extinction processes, which in turn may increase risk for these disorders. A PubMed, PsycInfo, and Web of Science search was conducted through May 6, 2025. Studies that used classical fear conditioning paradigms, measured indicators of fear response, examined childhood trauma or maltreatment in populations aged 18 or younger were included. Effect sizes were calculated for response to threat cues, response to safety cues, and differential fear response during acquisition and extinction, if included. Ultimately, 14 studies met the criteria for the qualitative review and 12 were quantitatively meta-analyzed (aggregate n = 1094). Results showed that trauma exposure was significantly associated with blunted responses to the threat cue during early acquisition when compared to children with little or no trauma exposure (g = -0.40; p < 0.01; k = 4). When assessing trauma exposure continuously, greater trauma exposure was significantly associated with lower responding to the safety signal (r = -0.10; p < 0.05; k = 8) and more pronounced discrimination (r = 0.15; p < 0.001; k = 8) in early acquisition. No significant effects were observed for extinction albeit studies were limited (k = 4). Findings suggest that trauma-exposed children exhibit altered fear learning patterns during acquisition. Future research should examine the impact of early life trauma on the development of fear learning and potential for acquiring fear-related disorders into adulthood.

title: Headache disorders among Indigenous communities: A scoping review undertaken with knowledge keeper guidance
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: We performed a scoping review of literature on headache etiology, classification, prevalence, and treatment in Indigenous communities in Canada, the United States, Australia, and New Zealand.

BACKGROUND: In the United States, analysis of national prevalence indicates that Indigenous Americans lead all other racial/ethnic groups in headache prevalence.
