Risk factors associated with headache burden, including diabetes, head injury, psychological trauma, environmental exposures, and lack of access to appropriate diagnosis and treatment, have been documented in Indigenous communities across the geographies studied.

METHODS: A systematic search of literature in PubMed, Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature, Scopus, and Informit Indigenous Collection was conducted through January 2026 using descriptors of headache, migraine, and Indigenous populations across Canada, the United States, Australia, and New Zealand. Of the 616 citations identified, 30 publications from 1981 to 2024 were included in the present review and analyzed under the following areas of inquiry: (1) headache classification, (2) headache etiology, (3) headache prevalence, (4) headache treatment, and (5) barriers to headache care.

RESULTS: Analysis of national data in the United States indicates a higher prevalence of headache in Indigenous communities in comparison to all other communities. In Canada, evidence from smaller studies suggests a similar pattern. Prevalence data for Indigenous communities in Australia and New Zealand remains limited. Ethnographic data and expert informant data from Indigenous communities demonstrate conceptualization and treatment of headaches within biopsychosocial models that relate individuals to the life of their community and land. There were no data from medical headache treatment trials or intervention studies specific to or inclusive of Indigenous patients with headache. Barriers to headache care for Indigenous peoples were identified prior to diagnosis, at the point of assessment, and in treatment. Addressing these barriers demands system level changes as well as development of individual relations of respect and care for Indigenous patients.

CONCLUSIONS: Included studies from Canada, the United States, Australia, and New Zealand reported a high prevalence of headache in some Indigenous communities and suggest that this burden may result from or be associated with a combination of intergenerational trauma, adverse childhood experiences, lower socioeconomic status, head injury, environmental contaminants, and systemic racism resulting in barriers to diagnosis and care. Despite this apparent burden, the literature reveals a paucity of quality, headache-specific research conducted with Indigenous peoples across all four regions of study. To close gaps in headache diagnosis, treatment, and prevention, research and program development must be led by, or conducted in meaningful collaboration with, Indigenous communities in a manner that recognizes and uplifts Indigenous knowledge systems, healing, and conceptualizations of headache.

Headache burden is disproportionately high in Indigenous communities in Canada, the United States, Australia, and New Zealand, yet headache‐specific research conducted with Indigenous peoples remains limited. Our review found that Indigenous understandings and treatments of headache are often connected to land and community; however, systemic racism, barriers to care, gaps in communication, and lack of Indigenous‐led research limit effective diagnosis and treatment. To close these gaps, future work must be carried out by, or in meaningful collaboration with, Indigenous communities in a manner that uplifts diverse Indigenous knowledge and healing systems.

title: Food insecurity, adverse childhood experiences, and eating disordered behavior in college students
abstract: Objective:  Food insecurity (FIS) is a substantial concern for many college students. Evidence suggests that FIS and adverse childhood events (ACEs) are separately linked to higher rates of eating disordered behavior.  Method:  The present study examines food insecurity and ACEs together as predictors of eating disordered behavior in a sample of students ( n  = 346) from an Appalachian university.  Results : indicate that rates of food insecurity were fairly high in this sample, with approximately 70% of the sample experiencing childhood and current food insecurity. Current food insecurity and ACEs were each associated with eating disordered behavior, with a model including both variables accounting for more of the variance in eating disordered behavior.  Conclusions:  Implications for these findings within a college campus are discussed, including consideration of trauma-informed approaches to better understand and address the combination of food insecurity, ACEs, and eating disordered behavior.

title: Trajectories of suicidal ideation and attempts across the academic year: longitudinal study of UK university students
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Suicide is a leading cause of death among young adults, yet few studies have examined longitudinal trajectories of suicidal ideation and attempts across the academic year in UK university students.

AIMS: The study aimed to identify demographic and psychosocial factors associated with lifetime suicide risk, examine factors associated with changes in risk trajectories, and evaluate the relationship between suicidal ideation and attempts over an academic year.

METHOD: Participants comprised 3295 students from 5 UK universities who completed longitudinal surveys in autumn and spring terms 2021-2024 in the Nurture-U study. Suicidal ideation and attempts were assessed with Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale items. Demographic, psychosocial and mental health measures were examined as potential risk and protective factors. Regression models with multiple imputation were used, with case-control analyses for smaller subgroups.

RESULTS: Approximately 45.5% of students reported baseline lifetime suicidal ideation and 9.5% reported a past attempt. Factors associated with lifetime suicidal ideation included minoritised sexual orientation or ethnic background, male or gender-diverse identity, previous mental health treatment and adverse childhood experiences. Among students with lifetime ideation at baseline, 61.1% did not report ideation in the spring term, whereas new-onset ideation occurred in 3.5% of participants. Among students with prior ideation only, 1.3% made a suicide attempt during the academic year, whereas 10.5% with prior attempt history made a suicide attempt. Increases in depressive symptoms and rumination were associated with new attempts at follow-up.

CONCLUSIONS: Most students experiencing suicidal ideation during university have risk factors before university entry. Suicidal ideation alone showed limited specificity for identifying those most at risk of future attempts, highlighting the importance of targeted support for high-risk groups and ongoing monitoring of symptoms throughout the academic year.

title: The secondary school transition as a turning point for internalizing symptoms: Trajectories, correlates, and early adulthood outcomes
abstract: Internalizing disorders are the most common adolescent mental disorders. Using complementary variable-centered and person-centered approaches, we examined whether internalizing symptoms across eight years of adolescence (Grades 5-12) followed a continuous developmental trend or were disrupted by the transition to secondary school, and if different subgroups followed different pathways. Participants were 701 Canadian youth (52.9% girls; 75.9% white). Annual self-reported internalizing symptoms (ages 11-18) were examined using piecewise latent growth curve analysis (LGCM), revealing significant curve and level discontinuity at the transition, with distinct developmental phases in elementary and secondary school. Girls, youth with lower household income, and those with higher bullying victimization and lower social support showed elevated symptoms and/or steeper growth. An LGCM yielded four classes: Low (51.8%), Moderate (32.5%), Increasing (10.6%), and Declining (5.1%). The Declining and Moderate classes had comparable risk for early adulthood outcomes, demonstrating equifinality. Although beginning with similar levels, the Increasing class was at elevated risk compared to the Moderate class, demonstrating multifinality. Findings underscore that the secondary school transition can be viewed as a transition-linked turning point for a subset of adolescents, with implications for targeted screening and intervention beginning in elementary school.

title: Adverse Childhood Experiences and Unintended Pregnancy: Evidence From North Dakota PRAMS, 2017-2020
abstract:
HIGHLIGHTS • Study used 4 years of Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System data from North Dakota (2017–2020). • Higher cumulative adverse childhood experience (ACE) exposure showed a dose–response relationship with unintended pregnancy. • Women with ≥4 ACEs had ∼2 times higher odds of unintended pregnancy. • Cumulative ACE score outperformed factor-based and individual-item ACE models. • Two specific ACEs (household substance use and parental separation/divorce) showed independent associations.

Introduction Unintended pregnancy remains a significant public health issue with lasting consequences. Adverse childhood experiences are linked to risky behaviors and poor reproductive outcomes; however, limited research has examined optimal approaches to measuring adverse childhood experience exposure in rural populations. This study examines the relationship between adverse childhood experiences and pregnancy intendedness in North Dakota from 2017 to 2020. Methods This cross-sectional study used North Dakota Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System data (N=2,973). A cumulative adverse childhood experience score was calculated. Exploratory factor analysis identified 2 adverse childhood experience groupings (abuse/neglect and household dynamics). Pregnancy intendedness was dichotomized as intended or unintended; a sensitivity analysis supported this categorization. Multivariable logistic regression assessed the associations between adverse childhood experiences and unintended pregnancy, controlling for sociodemographic and behavioral factors. The models compared the cumulative adverse childhood experience score, factor-based groupings, and individual adverse childhood experience items. Results Unintended pregnancy was more common among women with ≥4 adverse childhood experiences (51%) than among women with no adverse childhood experiences (32%). A dose–response relationship was observed, with increasing adverse childhood experience exposure associated with increased odds of unintended pregnancy. In adjusted models, younger age, being unmarried, higher parity, marijuana use before pregnancy, and higher adverse childhood experience exposure were independently associated with unintended pregnancy, whereas no significant differences were observed by residence or maternal race. The cumulative adverse childhood experience score showed greater predictive value than factor-based or item-only models. Sensitivity analyses revealed consistent adverse childhood experience gradients across subcategories of unintended pregnancy. Conclusions Higher cumulative adverse childhood experience exposure is associated with a greater risk of unintended pregnancy. Findings support the use of cumulative adverse childhood experience measures in reproductive health research and highlight the importance of trauma-informed care and upstream strategies that address childhood adversity.

INTRODUCTION Unintended pregnancy, defined by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) as a pregnancy that is mistimed or unwanted, has declined nationally from 43.3% in 2010 to 41.6% in 2019. 1 , 2 Rates have dropped most among women aged 15–19 and 20–24 years. 2 Despite the reduction in the prevalence rates of unintended pregnancies, the issue remains a public health concern owing to its impact on maternal outcomes, including psychosocial well-being, and its behavioral and economic implications. 3 Disparities in pregnancy intendedness exist. Women aged 15–44 years living below the federal poverty level experience 60 unintended pregnancies per 1,000 women, compared with 30 per 1,000 women at twice the federal poverty level. 3 In addition, rates are higher among unmarried and young adult women. 3 Additional risk factors include cohabiting, being non-Hispanic Black or African American, having less than a high-school education, having limited knowledge and use of contraception, and partner intentions. 1 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 Behaviors such as smoking, substance abuse, and having multiple sexual partners also increase the risk. 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 For example, women who consumed alcohol had 3.4 times higher odds of unintended pregnancy, and combined tobacco and alcohol use increased the odds to 5.1. 11 Risky sexual behavior (e.g., unprotected sex, having multiple sexual partners, early sexual initiation), which is more common among those with adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), also increases the risk of unintended pregnancy. 1 , 5 , 10 , 12 , 13 , 14 ACEs are traumatic events during childhood that impact physical, mental, and emotional well-being across the lifespan. 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 In the U.S., 64% of adults report at least 1 ACE, and 17% (nearly 1 in 6) report ≥4 ACEs. 15 Examples include abuse, neglect, witnessing violence in the home, household substance abuse, parental separation or divorce, or incarceration of a household member. 15 ACEs are associated with an increased risk of physical and mental health challenges and chronic conditions, including cancer, diabetes, heart disease, and suicide. 16 , 18 , 21 , 22 , 23 Prior research has shown that higher ACE scores are associated with an increased risk of unintended pregnancy. 5 , 14 , 24 A dose–response relationship has been observed between ACEs and unintended pregnancy. 5 , 6 , 25 , 26 A study carried out by Dietz et al. 24 (1999) found that women who experienced ≥4 ACEs were 1.5 times more likely to have an unintended first pregnancy during adulthood than women with 0 ACEs. Another study observed that there was a higher proportion of early sexual initiation by age 15 years among women who had any ACEs than among women with no ACEs. 14 Limited research has explored ACEs and unintended pregnancy in rural states such as North Dakota (ND). This analysis aggregated 4 years of ND Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System (PRAMS) data to examine this relationship more robustly. In addition to evaluating the association between ACEs and pregnancy intendedness, factor analysis was used to compare the predictive value of alternative approaches to measuring ACE exposure, including cumulative ACE scores, factor-based groupings (abuse/neglect, household dynamics), and individual ACE items. These analyses help to inform best practices for modeling childhood adversity in reproductive health research, especially in rural populations. The findings can inform evidence-based public health strategies. METHODS Study Sample The ND PRAMS is a collaborative surveillance project of the CDC and the ND HHS. PRAMS provides data not available from other sources, which can be used to identify groups of women and infants at high risk for health problems, monitor changes in health status, and measure progress toward the goals of improving the health of women and infants. The PRAMS protocol was approved by the CDC’s IRB. 27 This study was reviewed by the ND HHS IRB Chair and was determined not to need ND HHS IRB review. The ND PRAMS aggregated data set obtained from ND HHS contained no identifying information, and access to the data was limited to coauthors with a signed data-sharing agreement with ND HHS. This study included data from 3,016 women who completed the ND PRAMS survey from 2017 to 2020; 1.4% of respondents who did not answer the question about pregnancy intendedness were excluded, resulting in a final N of 2,973. ND PRAMS response rates exceeded the CDC’s required threshold annually (i.e., 50%) for creating a weighted statewide sample for each of the 4 years (70.2% in 2017, 59.9% in 2018, 59.1% in 2019, and 60.5% in 2020). The majority of respondents completed their survey questionnaire by mail (79.0%), whereas 21.0% completed it after being moved to the phone phase of data collection. Measures Predictor variables were drawn from questions measuring ACEs. The ACEs module included 10 binary (yes/no) questions answered retrospectively about experiences before age 18 years, including abuse/neglect and household dynamics. A cumulative ACE score (0–10) was calculated on the basis of the number of yes responses. Respondents missing responses to any ACE question (4.9%) were not assigned a cumulative ACE score but were included in item-specific ACE analyses. Cronbach’s alpha showed good reliability of the cumulative score (alpha=0.83). ACE scores were categorized as 0, 1, 2–3, and ≥4. The cumulative category of ≥4 is consistent with other ACEs research examining dose–response relationships. 17 , 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 In addition, we combined responses of 2 and 3 ACEs experienced to retain a large enough number for analysis purposes. Factor analysis of the 10 ACE items identified two factors. Cronbach’s alpha was calculated to test each factor’s reliability; both factors demonstrated adequate reliability. Factor 1 (alpha=0.78) included abuse/neglect items (i.e., physical abuse, emotional abuse, sexual abuse, physical neglect, and emotional neglect). Factor 2 (alpha=0.70) included items related to household dynamics (i.e., domestic violence, mental illness, separation/divorce, incarcerated household members, and substance abuse). The outcome variable was pregnancy intendedness, which was assessed by asking how women felt just before becoming pregnant. Responses were dichotomized into intended and unintended per CDC PRAMS questions, aligning with prior research. 31 , 33 , 34 , 35 Unintended pregnancies comprised responses of I wanted to be pregnant later, I didn’t want to be pregnant then or at any time in the future , and I wasn’t sure what I wanted , and intended pregnancies comprised responses of I wanted to be pregnant sooner and I wanted to be pregnant then . Secondary sensitivity analyses were conducted by disaggregating the unintended category into 2 subcategories (later/never, not sure), with intended pregnancy serving as the reference group. Results from the disaggregated sensitivity analyses are presented in Table A.1 (available online). For categorical predictor variables with more than 2 levels, p -values represent the overall survey-adjusted associations across categories. Posthoc pairwise comparisons were not conducted because these analyses were intended to describe population-level distributions rather than testing all possible subgroup contrasts. To reduce the risk of Type 1 error from multiple comparisons, statistical interpretation focused on overall associations in descriptive tables and on adjusted comparisons from the multivariable regression models using the reference groups. Several demographic variables collected on the survey were used as covariates. The variables used were age (≤24, 25–29, 30–34, and ≥35 years), race (White; Black; American Indian; and other races, including multiple races); ethnicity (Hispanic/not Hispanic), educational level (high-school diploma/GED or less, some college/Associate’s degree, college graduate), and geographic residence (urban county/rural county). Marital status was defined as married at the time of birth or other. Prior live births were categorized as 0, 1, 2, and ≥3. ACE items included exposure before the age of 18 years to emotional abuse, physical abuse, sexual abuse, physical neglect, and emotional neglect as well as witnessing domestic abuse, mental illness in the home, separation/divorce in the home, a household member incarcerated, and substance abuse in the home. Statistical Analysis Analyses were conducted using SPSS (version 29) Complex Samples module and R (Version 2026.01.0+392). CDC’s complex weighting design ensured a representative statewide sample. 27 Chi-square tests assessed the associations between pregnancy intentions and predictor variables. A backward stepwise logistic regression removed variables with p >0.1 to generate the best-fitting model of variables associated with pregnancy intendedness. Weighted proportions and CIs were calculated using survey-adjusted methods. Associations between categorical variables were evaluated using the Rao-Scott adjusted chi-square test with statistical significance set at p <0.05. Multiple modeling approaches were explored, including individual ACE items alone, ACE factor groupings, and cumulative ACE score. Because the ACE factor groupings were derived from the same underlying ACE items as the cumulative score, these measures were evaluated in separate exploratory models to avoid multicollinearity. The final model prioritized the cumulative ACE score because it reflects the dose–response relationship between childhood adversity and pregnancy intendedness, and it demonstrated a stronger and more consistent association than the factor-based or individual item models. Exploratory models comparing ACE operationalization strategies are presented in Table A.4 (available online). RESULTS The sample analyzed in this study (weighted n =39,825; raw n =2,973) was 74.9% White, 6.5% Black, and 8.3% American Indian; 94.4% were not Hispanic ( Table 1 ). The age distribution was 21.7% for ages ≤24 years, 34.7% for ages 25–29 years, 30.3% for ages 30–34 years, and 13.3% for ages ≥35 years. Two thirds of the women were married at the time of birth (66.8%). Education was nearly evenly split among women having a high-school diploma/GED or less (29.7%), some college/Associate’s degree (32.6%), and a college degree (37.7%). In the PRAMS questionnaire, women were asked how they felt about becoming pregnant. The 15.8% who said they wanted to be pregnant sooner and the 44.4% who said then comprised intended pregnancies (60.2%). The 16.9% who said that they wanted to be pregnant later, the 5.2% who said never, and the 17.8% who said not sure comprised unintended pregnancies (39.9%). Univariable associations with pregnancy intendedness by select characteristics are shown in Table 1 . Women aged ≤24 years (60.0%) were significantly more likely than women in other age groups to report an unintended pregnancy. Women with a high-school diploma/GED or less (55.5%) were significantly more likely to report that their pregnancy was unintended than women with some college or an Associate’s degree (43.3%) and college graduates (24.5%). Women with ≥3 prior live births were more likely to have unintended pregnancies (55.3%) than women with fewer prior births. Women who reported using marijuana (71.4%), who used Adderall/stimulants (61.1%), and/or who used amphetamines/meth (77.5%) in the 12 months before pregnancy were more likely to indicate that their pregnancy was unintended than women who did not use these drugs. Table A.2 (available online) further describes the distribution of ACE score categories across sociodemographic and behavioral characteristics. Univariable associations with pregnancy intendedness by individual ACEs, ACE score, and ACE factors are shown in Table 2 . The rate of unintended pregnancy was highest among women with ≥4 ACEs (51.3%) and lowest among women with 0 ACEs (32.4%). Analysis of ACEs related to abuse and neglect revealed the highest rate of unintended pregnancy among women who reported emotional neglect

title: Childhood trauma and cognitive decline in women: an empirical analysis of cognitive vulnerability in later life
abstract:
Childhood trauma has lasted consequences for women’s cognitive health and this may contribute to memory decline and increased vulnerability to cognitive impairment in later life. A cross sectional study was carried out to assess the correlation between childhood trauma and cognitive status among 55 women aged 58–79 years were selected from Departments of Psychiatry and General Medicine, Tanta University Hospital, Egypt. The Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) was used to evaluate cognitive performance, the Global Deterioration Scale (GDS) for global clinical staging, and the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ) for childhood adversity. Overall, emotional abuse was exposed the most with a high mean score on the CTQ subscale. Pearson correlations and multiple linear regression models (controlling for age) showed that emotional neglect and physical neglect were the strongest predictors across both outcomes. For MoCA performance, emotional neglect (β = −0.0877, r = −0.85, p < 0.01) and physical neglect (β = −0.0100, r = −0.80, p < 0.01) showed the largest effects. GDS coefficients had an absolute value that was proportionately smaller (emotional neglect: β = 0.0112; physical neglect: β = 0.0013) and, consistent with the higher-is-worse nature of the GDS, were positive in direction. Additional findings show a greater amount of neglect predicted more advanced clinical staging, and that there was no change to the relative order of effects by predictor compared to the MoCA model. The regression model accounted for 72.5% of the variance (R 2 = 0.725) in MoCA. The results indicate that childhood neglect, especially emotional neglect, might be an important risk factor for cognitive vulnerability in adulthood and highlight the necessity to intervene early in childhood to promote cognitive health in women.

1 Introduction Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that primarily affects older adults. This leads to declines in memory, cognitive abilities, and everyday functioning. It is the most common cause of dementia which has affected an estimated 50 million people worldwide. This figure expected to rise substantially as global populations age ( Alzheimer’s Association, 2022 ; Scheidt, 2023 ). Epidemiological evidence has consistently demonstrated that women are more prone to developing AD and that almost two thirds of cases are female ( Moustafa, 2021 ; Zhu et al., 2021 ). This sex difference has prompted an increased interest in sex-specific risk factors that might help to explain this difference ( Chiow and Cicero, 2025 ). The cumulative effects of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) such as trauma and chronic stress on cognitive health across the life span is an emerging focus of research ( Anda et al., 2005 ; Heim and Nemeroff, 2001 ). Physical, emotional, sexual abuse, and multiple types of neglect and household dysfunction have been linked to a wide variety of health issues as an adult, including mental disorders, cardiovascular disease, and neurodegenerative diseases like AD ( Graves et al., 2021 ). Especially childhood trauma can have a significant impact on memory and cognitive capacity in later life ( De Marco et al., 2017 ; Prieto et al., 2023 ). Critically, women experience ACEs more than men and are thus potentially more vulnerable to the long-term cognitive effects of ACEs ( Madigan et al., 2023 ; Moustafa, 2021 ). In addition to childhood stressors, women are also at higher risk of experiencing chronic social stressors such as for example caregiving responsibilities, gendered social expectations, and gender based violence. These can add to early life trauma and can also further lower cognitive resilience ( Fliege et al., 2005 ; Haahr-Pedersen et al., 2020 ; Patel and Oremus, 2023 ). It is believed that these stressors act partially through the dys-regulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and related stress-response mechanisms that play a role in depression and neurodegeneration ( Heim and Nemeroff, 2001 ; Lei et al., 2025 ; Graves et al., 2021 ; Prieto et al., 2023 ). This combination of biological and social vulnerabilities could render women a population in which early adversity may have lasting effects on cognitive aging. This is a premise that has been increasingly supported by social and structural determinants of brain health studies ( Livingston et al., 2020 ; Safiri et al., 2024 ). Women’s elevated AD risk thus reflects the combined influence of biological, psychological, and sociocultural factors. Gendered caregiving responsibilities and associated sociocultural stressors in various cultural contexts have been linked to heightened chronic stress and depressive symptoms, both of which are independent risk factors for accelerated cognitive decline ( Moustafa, 2021 ; Safiri et al., 2024 ). In Asia, especially in the India and China, cultural gender roles and family systems also play a role in the increased rate of emotional and physical neglect in women that can only have life-long consequences on cognitive abilities ( Jain et al., 2022 ; Xiang et al., 2022 ). In the Middle East, domestic violence is another trauma that women are likely to experience, because gender inequality and violence are more common in this region. Besides, gender inequality, domestic violence, and emotional neglect documented across European, Asian, and Middle Eastern settings may each contribute to neurodegenerative risk through accumulated adversity ( Haahr-Pedersen et al., 2020 ; Umberson and Karas Montez, 2010 ). Situating ACEs within broader theoretical frameworks offers additional explanatory power for understanding their long-term cognitive consequences. Similarly, the social and structural determinants of brain health framework highlights systemic inequities. For example; how including poverty, housing instability, discrimination, and limited educational opportunity create conditions in which ACEs are not only more likely to occur but also more difficult to recover from Livingston et al. (2020) , Röhr et al. (2022) , Adkins-Jackson et al. (2023) , Shaaban et al. (2026) . Recognizing ACEs as modifiable risk factors embedded within these broader structural conditions is therefore essential for designing public health interventions that address not only individual trauma histories but also the social environments that generate and sustain them. 1.1 Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) and Alzheimer’s disease The empirical case for ACEs as drivers of AD risk has grown considerably in recent years. A meta-analysis of available studies estimated that individuals with a history of ACEs carry approximately 1.35 times the risk of developing AD compared to those without such experiences ( Abouelmagd et al., 2024 ). This is also supported with longitudinal and retrospective cohort studies across diverse populations ( Corney et al., 2022 ; He and Yang, 2024 ; Radford et al., 2017 ). Critically, this risk follows a dose-response pattern. The greater cumulative ACE burden is associated with steeper cognitive decline and earlier onset of dementia-related markers in later life ( Hayes-Larson et al., 2025 ; Xiang et al., 2022 ). Not all ACE types, however, carry equivalent weight. Emotional neglect and sexual abuse, in particular, have been linked to more pronounced impairments. In adults, these impairments are related to memory and executive functioning and could involve structural changes in stress-sensitive neural circuits as potential mediating factors ( De Marco et al., 2017 ; Fleck et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2023 ; Heim and Nemeroff, 2001 ). Early trauma also increases the likelihood of depression, anxiety and social withdrawal, which are risk factors on their own for cognitive decline and dementia. Thus it generates cumulative pathways of psychological processes that lead from adversity to neurodegeneration ( Brown et al., 2021 ; Dafsari and Jessen, 2020 ; Prieto et al., 2023 ). There is also some evidence that early life adversity can be a contributor to both the process of amyloid accumulation and also the overall process of neurodegeneration in susceptible individuals, indicating a biological pathway as well as a psychological pathway to AD risk ( Abo Hamza et al., 2023 ; Rose et al., 2025 ). Trauma experiences as measured by the five subscales of the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire represent individual level ACEs and are not fully understood as capturing broader structural or socioeconomic adversity, which is a limitation of the current measure of trauma. 1.2 Cognitive vulnerability in women What makes women particularly susceptible to ACE-related cognitive decline goes beyond differential exposure rates. Inconsistent and/or intrusive parental behavior and sexual abuse have been shown to lead to higher levels of memory and executive functioning deficits among women compared to men who have been exposed to similar behaviors. This indicates a differential sensitivity to early adverse events for the sexes, and this could be due to the biological and socially learned differences in how stress is processed ( Graves et al., 2021 ; Haahr-Pedersen et al., 2020 ; Lian et al., 2024 ). Psychosocially, less access to cognitively stimulating opportunities, chronic symptoms of depression associated with the persistent discrimination, and less access to health care in low-resourced environments. This is added to these early life risks, thus adding up vulnerabilities throughout the life course ( Graves et al., 2021 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Safiri et al., 2024 ; Umberson and Karas Montez, 2010 ). Psychosocially, reduced opportunities for cognitive stimulation, chronic depressive symptoms linked to ongoing discrimination, and limited access to healthcare in lower-resource settings further compound these biological risks, creating layered vulnerabilities that accumulate across the lifespan ( Graves et al., 2021 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Safiri et al., 2024 ; Umberson and Karas Montez, 2010 ). 1.3 Current study Despite growing interest in the role of early trauma in AD risk, relatively few studies have directly examined gender-specific patterns in the relationship between ACEs and cognitive outcomes in later life ( Huang et al., 2023 ; Patel and Oremus, 2023 ). Despite the potential for various forms of ACEs to have different impacts on cognitive health ( De Marco et al., 2017 ; Huang et al., 2023 ; Xiang et al., 2022 ), very few investigations have distinguished between these types of ACEs. In addition, previous studies have mostly concentrated either on subjective cognitive complaints or on general demential status rather than with clinical staging (GDS) and objective cognitive screening (MoCA). The present study aims to address these gaps by examining the association between specific domains of childhood trauma (as measured by the CTQ) and both cognitive performance (MoCA) and clinical disease staging (GDS) in a sample of middle-aged and older women. Cognitive vulnerability in later life is defined operationally in this study as measurable cognitive decline (operationalized as MoCA performance below normal) and progression of clinical staging (operationalized as higher GDS score). This represents a range of cognitive risk states from sub clinical impairment to early dementia. In the general literature, these types of trajectories have been linked to progression to Alzheimer’s disease ( Abouelmagd et al., 2024 ; Corney et al., 2022 ; Nasreddine et al., 2005 ; Reisberg et al., 1982 ). The present study is based on cognitive screening and clinical staging, therefore cannot directly determine the risk of AD with the help of AD-specific biomarkers and longitudinal follow-up. We focus particularly on the roles of emotional and physical neglect, given emerging evidence that neglect may be especially harmful for long-term neurocognitive development ( Madigan et al., 2023 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ). We hypothesized that higher levels of childhood trauma, especially emotional and physical neglect, would be associated with poorer MoCA scores and more advanced GDS stages, even after accounting for age. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study design This was a cross sectional study to explore the relationship between childhood trauma and cognitive functioning and cognitive vulnerability in women at a later point in life. The study was carried out on patients selected from two departments, Psychiatry and General Medicine at Tanta University Hospital, Egypt. A total of 55 women aged 58–79 years were included, ranging from no cognitive impairment to mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and early dementia (mild AD and other dementias). The exclusion criteria were: (a) severe psychiatric disorders (e.g., schizophrenia), (b) neurological disorders other than dementia (e.g., major stroke, traumatic brain injury), and (c) inability to give informed consent. A battery of standardized questionnaires and clinical assessments were performed on all participants. Each of the three assessment instruments used in this study had a different method of administration, appropriate to the specific instrument. All trained clinicians in Psychiatry and General Medicine Departments of Tanta University Hospital had previous experience in Psychiatric Hospitals in administering both GDS and MoCA. The CTQ is a self-report instrument, however, that has been validated and was independently completed by participants under standardized conditions. 2.2 Participants The mean age of participants was 64.96 years (SD = 3.97), consistent with an age group at elevated risk for cognitive decline and AD. Participants were selected to represent a range of cognitive statuses, including women with normal cognition, MCI, and mild dementia (primarily early-stage AD). Demographic information about the participants in this study is reported in Table 1 . In respect to their occupation, the sample mainly consisted of housewives. The notable percentage of housewives is interesting because socioeconomic pressures such as financial dependency and social isolation are likely to affect mental health and cognitive resilience in this group. In terms of marital status, 45.5% of the women were married. Marital status can also proxy other aspects of social support, such as emotional or practical support, which may be protective for brain health, and loneliness or stress in the event of widowhood or divorce ( Umberson and Karas Montez, 2010 ). The participants higher education is also an important demographic parameter. This is correlated with increased cognitive reserve and can delay the onset of AD clinical manifestations ( Lian et al., 2024 ; Patel and Oremus, 2023 ). Participants age is also very important. In some cultures, the number of children may relate to higher caregiving burden and/or psychosocial stress, which might affect cognitive health ( Graves et al., 2021 ; Haahr-Pedersen et al., 2020 ). The demographic attributes of the sample are summarized in Table 1 . 2.3 Measures 2.3.1

title: Microglia sculpt dopamine receptor-mediated adolescent behaviors in a social experience dependent manner
abstract: Abstract Adverse childhood experiences like social isolation (SI) contribute to long term negative health outcomes and the development of severe psychiatric disorder. Adolescence is a unique period of coordinated social and motivational system development driven by dopamine (DA) signaling. Microglia, immune cells of the brain, may play a unique role in regulating SI-induced DA system changes and associated behavioral dysfunction. Male microglia refine dopamine D1 receptors (D1rs) in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) of adolescent male rats shaping play behavior. Here we characterized the molecular developmental impacts of postweaning SI from P21-P38, with a resocialization period to P54. We tested the role of microglial engulfment of D1rs in mediating behavioral consequences of SI using neutrophil inhibitory factor (NIF) to block complement-mediated engulfment required for D1r pruning. We found sex specific impacts of SI on brain development and the DA system. In SI males, microglia engulf more NAc D1rs than group housed (GH) controls. Within GH animals, NAc D1r density is positively correlated to play and allogrooming. In SI animals, NAc D1r density is negatively correlated to biting behavior, and is not correlated to play or allogrooming. Pharmacologically inhibiting microglial engulfment of D1r via bilateral NAc NIF injection prevents observed D1r:behavior correlations in GH and SI animals. NIF treatment interacts with SI, exaggerating aggressive-like behavior, showing a role for microglia in regulating aggressive-like behavior via complement pruning in adolescence. Microglia may play a unique role in regulating behavior that drive negative health outcomes in the face of developmental stress, including SI.

title: Risk and Resilience Factors of Participants in Urban Community Gun Violence Intervention & Prevention: Insights from the Advance Peace Program
abstract: Urban community-based gun violence prevention programs engage those with the greatest risk of perpetrating violence and provide them with services and supports to help them change their behaviors. Empirical studies of this public-health-oriented strategy, called community violence intervention (CVI), have been mixed, and few have reported which risk factors are most prevalent among participants. We offer detailed descriptive data about the risks and protective factors that participants in one CVI program, called Advance Peace, displayed at the onset of the intervention. Advance Peace operates in 13 cities and had over 1000 participants, or "fellows," between January 2021 and December 2024. We found that almost 34% of fellows were under 18 years old, 70.6% were African American, and over 90% were male. More than half (52.4%) reported poor mental health, 76.7% entered with four or more Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs), and over 30% had over 7 ACEs; more than 56% had been shot at, and almost half had a prior firearm-related arrest and a family member killed by a gun. We found that 49.2% had both four or more ACEs and at least two-gun violence exposures. Among program participants, only 17% were receiving any social services at enrollment. We also found that more than 62% wanted to change their lifestyle, and more than half had assets and strengths that could be protective or buffering factors that might prevent future gun use. We conclude that CVI programs should capture both the risks and strengths of program participants to ensure violence prevention interventions are trauma informed and healing centered.

title: A half-center oscillator regulates sleep pressure
abstract: Changes in oscillatory neural dynamics reflect-but may not necessarily determine-transitions between sleep stages and variations in sleep pressure. Here we show that sleep-control neurons innervating the dorsal fan-shaped body of Drosophila (dFBNs) produce slow-wave activity (SWA) that is causally linked to sleep. The dFBN ensemble contains bistable cells whose membrane voltages oscillate between hyperpolarized DOWN and depolarized UP states. The oscillations rely on interhemispheric competition of two half-centers connected by inhibitory glutamatergic synapses. dFBN-restricted interference with glutamate release disrupts SWA and baseline as well as rebound sleep, whereas the optogenetic replay of SWA induces sleep. dFBNs generate SWA throughout the sleep-wake cycle (despite mutual antagonism with arousing dopaminergic neurons) and adjust its power to sleep need via sleep history-dependent increases in excitability and homeostatic synaptic depression. The oscillatory format permits a continuous encoding of sleep pressure but requires mechanisms that convert the amplitude-modulated signal into binary sleep-wake states.

title: Investigating molecular and hemodynamic effects of LSD in the human brain
abstract: Lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) is a potent psychedelic with increasing therapeutic interest, yet qualification of target engagement using in vivo neuroimaging has not yet been performed. Using simultaneous positron emission tomography-magnetic resonance imaging technology, we describe multiple brain actions of LSD in seven healthy volunteers blinded to LSD dose received. Here we show that LSD occupies 5-HT2AR with a high affinity and increases both global cerebral blood flow (CBF) and internal carotid artery flow. LSD also decreases global connectivity, which was negatively associated with changes in CBF. We observe an anticlockwise hysteresis loop between plasma drug levels and subjective effects, suggesting atypical pharmacodynamic mechanisms. We contrast our CBF and global connectivity findings and their relation in a separate cohort of 25 participants administered psilocybin, highlighting key consistencies and differences. By establishing the dose-occupancy relation of LSD in humans, our findings provide insights for the clinical development of psychedelic compounds and demonstrate unique neurophysiological effects that distinguish LSD from psilocybin.

title: Parvalbumin cell state dynamics regulate gamma oscillations and are disrupted in Alzheimer's disease
abstract: Gamma oscillations are fundamental for cognitive processing, but the cellular and circuit dynamics that generate them remain poorly defined. Establishing a method for simultaneous calcium imaging and electrocorticography recordings in awake mice, we found that spontaneous gamma oscillations are accompanied by dynamic transitions between parvalbumin (PV) interneuron states. Rather than acting as a uniformly synchronized population, PV interneurons showed sequential recruitment, transient inactivation, and frequent transitions between activity states, indicating the formation of dynamic functional networks. In J20 Alzheimer's disease mice, these state transitions became dysregulated, leading to abnormal PV recruitment, impaired coupling between PV activity and gamma oscillations, and network hyperexcitability. Increasing interneuron excitability through expression of the voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.1 restored PV cell dynamics, gamma oscillations, and network stability. These findings reveal dynamic PV cell states as an organizing feature of gamma oscillations and identify their disruption as a circuit mechanism of network dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease.

title: A cross-species AAV platform for precise microglial interrogation
abstract: Targeting microglia with adeno-associated viruses (AAVs) remains challenging because of inefficient transduction, off-target expression, and inconsistent payload performance. Here, we develop an integrated, Cre-independent AAV platform that combines a compact 446-bp microglia-specific regulatory element (MSRE), a high-yield AAV2/9.m capsid, microRNA-mediated neuronal de-targeting, and a microglia-tailored codon-optimization strategy. Following direct intracranial delivery, the optimized vector achieves robust, long-lasting transgene expression with greater than 90% microglial specificity across multiple mouse brain regions, including in an Alzheimer's disease model. With doxorubicin-assisted delivery, the platform also enables efficient and selective microglial targeting in rats, rhesus macaques, and human ex vivo brain slices. Codon optimization supports the expression of otherwise challenging functional payloads, enabling calcium imaging, chemogenetic manipulation, and CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome editing. This cross-species toolkit provides a versatile resource for investigating microglial biology and developing microglia-directed therapeutic strategies.

title: The genetic landscape of myotonic dystrophy type 1: insights from nearly one million genomes
abstract: Myotonic Dystrophy type 1 (DM1) is a multisystem disorder caused by CTG repeat expansions in the dystrophia myotonica protein kinase (DMPK) gene. Current prevalence estimates of 1 in 3,000-8,000 have traditionally relied on clinically ascertained and geographically restricted cohorts, underestimating population burden and failing to capture ancestry diversity. Using large-scale whole-genome sequencing (WGS) datasets, we aimed to identify DMPK repeat expansions across nearly one million participants, define their ancestry-specific distribution, and evaluate associated clinical phenotypes, with particular focus on cardiac manifestations and early-onset cataracts. We analysed WGS participants from three cohorts: Genomics England (n = 80,110), UK Biobank (n = 490,086), and the All of Us Research Program (n = 414,830). DMPK repeat lengths were estimated using ExpansionHunter. Alleles were classified as Normal (≤37 repeats), Intermediate (38-49 repeats), or Pathogenic (≥50 repeats). Genetic ancestry was assigned using cohort-specific methods. Linked health record data assessed cardiac phenotypes in UK Biobank and early-onset cataracts in Genomics England and UK Biobank. Across all cohorts (n = 985,026), pathogenic DMPK repeat expansions were identified in 645 individuals (0.07%; ∼1 in 1,527), a prevalence two-to-five times higher than previous estimates. Most expansions occurred in those of European ancestry, although expansions were detected across all groups, including up to 1 in 6,693 African and Asian ancestry. In UK Biobank, individuals with a pathogenic expansion had increased odds of any cardiac diagnosis (odds ratio [OR]: 2.06, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.58-2.67; p = 5.8×108) and greater cardiac diagnostic burden (risk ratio 2.46, CI: 1.92-3.15; p = 1.6×10-13). Conduction abnormalities-particularly atrioventricular and left bundle-branch block, atrial fibrillation, and flutter-showed the strongest association with expansion status (OR: 4.86, CI: 3.38-6.79; p = 2.7×10-18). No sex differences were observed among those with a DMPK expansion, although male sex was independently associated with conduction disease in the overall population. Approximately one-in-ten individuals with pathogenic expansions had a cataract diagnosis before age 55. Most individuals with an expansion had no prior DM1 diagnosis, highlighting the value of systematic genetic testing in these phenotypes to improve diagnosis, shorten the diagnostic interval, and mitigate harm. By integrating WGS data from nearly one million individuals, this study refines understanding of the population distribution and clinical consequences of DMPK repeat expansions, revealing a reservoir of undiagnosed and potentially untreated multisystemic disease. These findings support routine inclusion of DMPK analysis within specified cardiac and ophthalmic diagnostic pathways to enable earlier detection.

title: Biallelic variants in PIKFYVE cause a hypomyelinating leukodystrophy with endolysosomal dysfunction
abstract: The PIKfyve-FIG4-VAC14 lipid kinase complex generates phosphoinositide PI(3,5)P2. Pathogenic variants in VAC14 and FIG4 cause neurodevelopmental disorders and PIKFYVE has been linked to autosomal dominant fleck corneal dystrophy. We searched for the underlyging, genetic cause of a neurodevelopmental disorder in five affected individuals from three families using exome- or genome sequencing. Cranial MRI images and clinical phenotypes were analyzed. Size, number and acidity of cellular vacuoles were investigated in patient-derived fibroblasts from family 1 using LysoSensor acidophilic probes. Levels of PI(3,5)P2 were quantified in patient-derived fibroblasts from family 1 using high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Pikfyve-mutant zebrafish larvae were injected with wildtype-mRNA or mutant mRNA harboring the PIKFYVE missense variant identified in family 3. Pikfyve-mutant zebrafish larvae were treated with metformin, bafilomycin A1, or rapamycin. We identified biallelic PIKFYVE variants in five affected individuals with hypomyelinating leukodystrophy, brain hyperintensities of inferior olives, thalami, long tracts, and optic nerves. Clinically, they presented with intellectual disability, spasticity, muscular weakness, and nystagmus. Additional features included feeding difficulties, auditory dysfunction, insulin resistance, microcephaly, peripheral neuropathy, and mild creatine kinase elevations. We detected four distinct PIKFYVE variants: three loss-of-function variants (family 1 & 2), and one p.Arg1156Pro missense variant (family 3). The pathogenicity of the p.Arg1156Pro variant was confirmed by phenotypic rescue of pikfyve-mutant zebrafish larvae injected with wildtype-mRNA but not with p.Arg1156Pro mRNA. Consistent with the role of PIKfyve in maintaining endolysosomal homeostasis, patient-derived fibroblasts of family 1 accumulated enlarged, hyperacidic vacuoles and showed a reduced PI(3,5)P2 production upon hyperosmotic stimulation. Exposing pikfyve-mutant zebrafisch larvae to the mTORC1 inhibitor and TRPML1 activator rapamycin attenuated cellular vacuolization, highlighting potential therapeutic approaches. Our findings establish PIKFYVE deficiency as a novel cause of hypomyelinating leukodystrophy and endolysosomal dysfunction.

title: Microglial Presenilin-1 modulates neuronal function and memory-associated behaviors
abstract: Microglial cells, the macrophages of the brain parenchyma, are increasingly recognized to play a key role in synaptic plasticity and function. Presenilin 1 (PS1) is an essential protein involved in learning and memory; the loss of neuronal Presenilin function causes cognitive deficits and impaired synapse plasticity in mice. Here we show memory enhancement in male mice lacking PS1 in microglia (PS1 ΔMG ). Leveraging high-throughput RNA sequencing with single-cell deconvolution-analysis, we estimate that PS1 ΔMG  increases Cd52-lo microglial population, a proliferative group enriched in AP-1 responsive genes; and increases chemokines  Ccl7  and  Ccl8  In silico prediction of binding partners showed that microglial CCL7 may act via inhibition of neuronal CCR5, a receptor known to negatively regulate learning and memory. By profiling active neuronal populations via PhosphoTRAP the data showed a non-autonomous cell effect of microglial PS1 by modulating genes involved in neuronal excitability and synaptic plasticity . Ex vivo  electrophysiology and in vivo calcium imaging in freely behaving mice confirm these effects with functional changes in CA1 hippocampus as seen by increased NMDA/AMPA ratios and increased amplitude of neuronal Ca2+ transients in freely behaving animals, respectively. Remarkably, PS1 ΔMG  mice exhibited increased memory retention in contextual fear conditioning and novel object recognition. Together, these data suggest a novel mechanism where microglial PS1 negatively regulates neuronal activity through modulation of NMDAR and memory-associated behaviors. Significance Statement  Microglia are increasingly recognized as active regulators of neuronal function, yet the molecular mechanisms that constrain their influence on synaptic activity remain incompletely defined. This study identifies microglial Presenilin-1 (PS1) as a key regulator of neuron-microglia signaling that shapes synaptic transmission and learning. We show that loss of microglial PS1 shifts microglia toward a transcriptional and signaling state that enhances NMDA receptor-dependent synaptic activity and improves memory, demonstrating that microglial molecular programs can directly modulate neuronal excitability. These findings establish microglial PS1 as a physiological brake on circuit plasticity and reveal that altering microglial signaling alone is sufficient to influence cognition. Targeting microglial regulatory pathways may therefore provide new strategies to enhance synaptic resilience and cognitive function in brain disorders.

title: Symmetries and continuous attractors in disordered neural circuits
abstract: A core challenge in neuroscience is reconciling idealized models with experimental data. Classical continuous-attractor models describe neural representations of continuous variables such as head direction. Symmetry in the weights generates a manifold of stable states, with tuning curves identical up to shifts. Rodent head-direction cells, by contrast, are markedly heterogeneous. Such heterogeneity, we show, is nevertheless compatible with these models. Here we build, directly from head-direction cell data, recurrent networks that behave as quasicontinuous attractors. A generative process then reproduces the heterogeneous tuning of these cells while making connectivity and dynamics tractable at large N. Although the weights appear disordered, they carry a circular symmetry whose eigenvalue degeneracies could signify continuous-attractor organization in connectome data. Dynamical mean-field theory recovers the ingredients of classical ring attractors, namely, Mexican hat interactions and a spontaneously broken symmetry producing bump states. Continuous-attractor mechanisms may thus operate in complex mammalian circuits.

title: Raphe nuclei in cognition: A network-level framework for behavioral-state control
abstract: Adaptive behavior requires organisms to maintain, update, and switch between behavioral states as environmental conditions change. The raphe nuclei (RN), best known as a major source of forebrain serotonin, have long been linked to arousal, inhibition, patience, affect, and flexibility, but these functions have often been considered separately. Here, we argue that recent advances in circuit tracing, cell-type-specific manipulation, high-resolution neuroimaging and neurostimulation, and computational modeling support a more integrated view in which RN are embedded within distributed cortico-subcortical and neuromodulatory networks. Across species, RN activity tracks environmental statistics such as value, uncertainty, threat, and reward context and contributes to transitions between motivational and cognitive states. We propose a network-level framework in which RN regulate when behavioral states should persist, update, or switch.

title: Highly replicable multisite patterns of adolescent white matter maturation
abstract: Adolescent brain development is difficult to study at scale because diffusion MRI (dMRI) measures are sensitive to technical variability across scanning environments. The Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study is the largest US-based longitudinal neuroimaging study of adolescent brain maturation. We present ABCD-Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) Community Collection (ABCC) release 3.1.0, a curated resource of more than 24,000 fully processed human ABCD dMRI datasets from participants aged 8-17 years. ABCC provides processed images, nuanced image quality metrics, advanced microstructural measures, and person-specific white matter bundle tractography. Across 62 bundles, measures of diffusion restriction and non-Gaussianity-including intracellular volume fraction from neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI), mean kurtosis tensor from diffusion kurtosis imaging (DKI), and return-to-origin probability from mean apparent propagator (MAP)-MRI-were more sensitive to development and more robust to variation in image quality than tensor-derived measures. Longitudinal harmonization of microstructural features with ComBat-GAMM markedly improved the cross-vendor generalizability of developmental effects. Together, ABCC accelerates reproducible, rigorous research on adolescent white matter development.

title: Target engagement and efficacy in disease-modifying trials of synuclein-related disorders
abstract: Disease-modifying trials in Parkinson's disease (PD), multiple system atrophy (MSA), and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) increasingly incorporate fluid and imaging biomarkers to demonstrate target engagement, de-risk subsequent phases of drug development and provide mechanistic evidence of biological activity. Whether biomarker modulation predicts clinical benefit remains unclear. We conducted a PRISMA-compliant review of phase II and III disease-modifying trials (2020-2025) that included at least one biomarker intended to assess target engagement. Twenty-six trials met inclusion criteria (PD=19, MSA=4, DLB=3; n=2,195 participants). Target engagement was reported in 14 of 19 PD trials (12 phase II/2 phase III), 1 of 4 MSA trials, and 2 of 3 DLB trials (all phase II). Concordance between target engagement and clinical improvement was uncommon, as only 8/26 studies (7 phase II/1 phase III) demonstrated both target engagement and statistically significant clinical benefit, and just two of these (both phase II, one in PD and one in MSA) were rigorously controlled with low or moderate risk of bias. Nine trials showed target engagement without clinical benefit, whereas two reported clinical improvement without measurable target engagement. Baseline biomarker-guided patient selection was uncommon and rarely aligned with the compound's mechanism of action. Patient-reported outcomes were widely used but rarely improved. Across recent disease-modifying trials in PD, DLB, and MSA, target engagement was frequently demonstrated, yet clinical benefit rarely followed. These findings question the predictive value of currently used target-engagement biomarkers and highlight the need to biologically align trial populations with the mechanisms targeted by experimental molecular interventions.

title: Extracellular vesicle α-synuclein topology reveals disease-associated conformers in brain and blood
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), and multiple system atrophy (MSA) are unified by pathological α-synuclein (αSyn) aggregation, yet diverge in terms of the cellular distribution of pathology and clinical phenotype. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as potential mediators or biomarkers of αSyn pathology, but whether their molecular constituents in the brain reflect disease-specific processes or conformations remains unknown. Here, we combined EV isolation, electrochemiluminescence, quantitative mass spectrometry and nanoscale single-vesicle imaging by direct stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (dSTORM) to map the topology, epitope exposure and cellular origin of αSyn in EVs isolated from post-mortem PD, DLB, MSA, and healthy control (HC) brains and assessed the tractability of these molecular signatures in blood. Proteomics and immunoblotting of EV lysates isolated from human brains confirmed that they were highly purified and derived from neurons and glial cell subtypes. Across diseases, αSyn association with EVs exhibited distinct patterns: In PD and DLB, both total αSyn levels normalised to CD81 and the percentage of neuronal (L1CAM+) EVs with aggregated αSyn as detected by aggregate-preferring antibodies, were increased, whereas in MSA, aggregated αSyn was detected primarily in neuronal and to a lesser extent glial EV subpopulations without an increase in total EV-associated αSyn. Further epitope mapping by dSTORM identified a distinct αSyn conformational arrangement, as detected by antibodies against an epitope spanning αSyn residues 34-45, that was enriched on the surface of L1CAM+ EVs in MSA compared to PD. This N-terminal immunoreactive conformer was tractable in serum and enriched on the surface of L1CAM+ EVs from MSA compared to PD patients or controls. Collectively, our findings suggest that the epitope accessibility and topology of EV-associated αSyn proteoforms, rather than their abundance alone, discriminate synucleinopathy subtypes, offering a framework for a blood-based conformational stratification of these disorders.

title: Voluntary movement initiation is associated with cardiac input in Libet's task
abstract: ​​The relationship between motor intention and initiation of voluntary movement remains a fundamental topic in neuroscience, originating from the seminal framework of B. Libet, introduced in 1983. Libet's paradigm significantly influenced discussions on intentionality, motor control, and free will. However, methodological critiques continue to challenge its interpretations, specifically the accuracy and validity of the 'urge to move' phenomenon. One understudied factor in this debate is the potential influence of interoceptive signals-such as cardiac activity-in shaping the experience of motor intention and movement initiation. In our study, we addressed this gap by examining whether cardiac signals modulate participants' experience of the 'urge to move', using behavioural and electrophysiological measures in 39 healthy human participants (17 males and 22 females) performing Libet's task. Crucially, when participants were asked to follow the 'urge to move', their button press timings were predominantly aligned with the diastolic phase of the cardiac cycle, indicating cardiac modulation of movement initiation. However, analysing heart evoked potential (HEP) amplitudes as a measure of cardiac input perception, we observed no differences in HEP amplitudes associated with changes in introspective demands during the task in both source and sensor spaces. Our results suggest that implicit perception of cardiac signals biases voluntary action initiation in Libet's task, independently of cortical interoceptive markers. These findings have implications for models of motor preparation, intentionality, and the bodily basis of voluntary action, challenging conventional interpretations of motor intention and informing debates on volition and interoception. Significance Statement  Our study provides evidence that implicit perception of cardiac signals influences movement initiation in Libet's task. We demonstrate, for the first time, that when attending to the 'urge to move', participants tended to initiate voluntary movements during the diastolic phase of the cardiac cycle. These findings challenge traditional views on factors affecting motor initiation in Libet's task, suggesting the relevance of interoceptive processing. By highlighting the role of cardiac input in experiencing motor intention, our findings expand on existing debates on volition, agency, and free will, further underscoring the importance of integrating bodily signals into these theoretical frameworks.

title: 5-HT(2A) receptors in layer 5 pyramidal neurons mediate the neuroplastic but not the hallucinogenic effects of psilocybin
abstract: It is unclear how serotonin 2A receptors (5-HT 2A Rs) in cortical layer 5 pyramidal neurons differentially contribute to psilocybin-induced hallucinations versus neuroplasticity. Here we show that psilocybin promotes synapse formation and maturation while accelerating the elimination of pre-existing synapses. Cell type-specific manipulation further demonstrated that 5-HT 2A R signaling in cortical layer 5 pyramidal neurons is necessary and sufficient for psilocybin-induced synaptic remodeling but dispensable for the head-twitch response, a rodent proxy of hallucination.

title: Multi-omic profiling of 85 iPSC lines from familial dementia reveals cellular diversity and regulators of organoid development
abstract: Systematic molecular characterization of human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines carrying disease-associated mutations is needed to distinguish disease-related biology from variation in cell state, genomic integrity, and genome-editing history, yet such systematic characterization is uncommon. Here, we profiled 85 human iPSC lines carrying MAPT mutations and isogenic controls using whole-genome sequencing, long-read sequencing of the MAPT locus, bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing, and DNA methylation arrays. Single-cell analyses identified four reproducible iPSC states and candidate surface markers for their isolation. Whole-genome sequencing revealed unintended editing events and recurrent 20q11.21 duplications, which were associated with increased ID1 expression and impaired cortical organoid patterning. Transcriptomic analyses identified pathways associated with organoid quality and changes linked to clonal selection and editing, underscoring the need to use unconverted lines as isogenic controls. By providing an in-depth genomic characterization of MAPT iPSCs, this dataset serves as a proof of principle to enhance iPSC utility in biological research.

title: Striatal astrocyte μ-crystallin (Crym) loss contributes to early-stage Huntington's disease pathophysiology
abstract: A striatal astrocyte subpopulation expressing μ-crystallin (gene: Crym) regulates perseverative behaviors, but its role in disease is unclear. We found that astrocytic Crym and μ-crystallin protein expression levels are reduced in human Huntington's disease (HD) tissue, cerebrospinal fluid, and HD mouse models. Selective astrocytic μ-crystallin restoration in a HD mouse model improved astrocyte and neuronal morphology, electrophysiology, gene expression, and early-stage compulsive and repetitive behaviors. Late-stage motor deficits remained mostly unchanged. Approximately 32% of the μ-crystallin rescued astrocytic genes overlapped with those dysregulated in human HD, indicating conserved molecular corrections. These results identify μ-crystallin-expressing astrocytes as modulators of HD pathophysiology and suggest that restoring μ-crystallin or targeting Crym-positive astrocytes could be beneficial in early disease stages.

title: Neuronavigated dual-target transcranial magnetic stimulation for schizophrenia negative symptoms
abstract: Negative symptoms in schizophrenia severely impair function and quality of life, yet respond poorly to current therapies. This multicenter, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial aimed to investigate the efficacy of neuronavigated dual-target repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) over the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (rDLPFC) and cerebellum for improving negative symptoms in early-stage psychosis (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04853485). Participants with first-episode schizophrenia or clinical high-risk for psychosis were enrolled from Shanghai Mental Health Center and Suzhou Guangji Hospital. Participants were randomly assigned to either a real or sham group under MRI-guided neuronavigation, targeting rDLPFC with 1Hz at 100% motor threshold(MT), cerebellar with intermittent theta burst stimulation(iTBS) at 120% MT for 20 consecutive days. Clinical assessments were conducted at baseline(T0), 10-session(T1), 20-session(T2) and one month after the intervention(T3). Cognition and MRI were evaluated at T0 and T2. The primary outcome was change of negative subscale score of the Positive and Negative Symptoms Scale(PANSS), while secondary outcomes included alterations in other PANSS subscale scores and fronto-cerebellar circuit functional connectivity. In total, 75 participants were included in the intention-to-treat analysis (36 active, 39 sham). The pre-specified primary linear mixed-effects analysis revealed a non-significant group-by-time interaction for PANSS negative subscale scores (F(3,174.6)=1.45, p=0.230). At the 4-week endpoint (T2), the nominal unadjusted between-group p-value was 0.049; after Sidak correction for multiple comparisons, the adjusted mean difference was -2.48 points (95% CI -4.99 to 0.03, adjusted p=0.150, Cohen's d=-0.51). Descriptive uncorrected t-tests indicated greater negative-symptom reductions in the active group at T1 and T2, and the 4-week negative-symptom response rate (≥50% reduction) was higher under real rTMS (χ2=9.5, p=0.002). A significant group-by-time interaction was observed for PANSS positive subscale scores (F(3,172.0)=3.26, p=0.023). Both groups exhibited substantial within-group symptom improvement. Resting-state fMRI demonstrated group-by-time interactions within cerebello-temporal, parahippocampal, caudate, and parietal networks (FWE-corrected p<0.05), and negative-symptom change correlated with cerebello-caudate connectivity (r=0.33, p=0.026). These findings suggest neuronavigated dual-target rTMS over rDLPFC and cerebellum may be associated with numerical improvements in negative symptoms in early-stage psychosis.

title: Dismantling Psychological Interventions for Youth with Complex Trauma: A Systematic Review and Component Network Meta-Analysis
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Complex trauma-related posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and comorbidities pose a significant mental health burden in children. However, the comparative effectiveness of psychological interventions and shared therapeutic components remains unclear.

METHODS: We conducted a systematic review, network, and component network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials of psychological interventions for children and adolescents with complex trauma. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, PsycINFO, and Cochrane Library were searched up to September 2024. PTSD was the primary outcome; retention and comorbid symptoms (depression, anxiety, dissociation, externalizing problems) were secondary outcomes.

RESULTS: Forty-eight studies (6,017 participants) were included in this review. Multimodal group interventions (SMD -1.68, 95% confidence interval [CI] -3.04 to -0.32), phase-based trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (TF-CBT) with parental involvement (-1.12, -1.53 to -0.70), TF-CBT (-1.06, -1.59 to -0.52), non-TF-CBT with parental involvement (-0.93, -1.70 to -0.17), eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (-0.85, -1.60 to -0.10), and phase-based TF-CBT (-0.79, -1.20 to -0.39) significantly reduced PTSD. Exposure emerged as the only significantly effective component for PTSD (-0.85, 95% credible interval [CrI] -1.60 to -0.06). Efficient component combinations included affective modulation with a therapeutic foundation of psychoeducation and nonspecific elements for PTSD (-0.97, 95% CrI -1.92 to -0.01) and exposure plus parental involvement with the same foundation for depression (-2.11, 95% CrI -4.06 to -0.20).

CONCLUSION: Trauma-focused approaches were the most effective treatments for pediatric PTSD and emotional comorbidities related to complex trauma. A more cost-effective intervention approach may prioritize exposure techniques, incorporate affective modulation, and include parental involvement when feasible.

title: Effectiveness of psychosocial interventions addressing informal caregivers' mental health: an umbrella systematic review with 26,481 participants
abstract:
AIM: We aimed to provide a comprehensive overview of the effectiveness of psychosocial interventions on informal caregivers' mental health, organized by the clinical condition(s) of the care recipient.

METHODS: We conducted an umbrella systematic review and random-effects meta-analyses to pool the results of the included studies for each combination of clinical condition, intervention type, comparison and outcome.

RESULTS: We included 19 systematic reviews and 50 meta-analyses, with 26,481 participants. Several interventions improved mental health outcomes in caregivers, and across various clinical conditions of the care recipients. In dementia caregivers, multicomponent interventions significantly reduced depressive and anxiety symptoms, and caregiver burden (SMD from -0.65 to -0.19). For caregivers of people with lung cancer, psychoeducation and psychological support reduced depressive (SMD = -1.66, 95% CI -3.19 to -0.13) and anxiety symptoms (SMD = -1.37, 95% CI -2.54 to -0.21). Multicomponent interventions reduced depressive and anxiety symptoms in parents of children with cancer (SMD = -0.38, 95% CI -0.64 to -0.12; SMD = -0.89, 95% CI -1.33 to -0.45). Caregiver burden of caregivers of people with psychosis and schizophrenia decreased after psychoeducation and skills-training (SMD = -2.10, 95% CI -3.46 to -0.74; SMD = -0.94, 95% CI -1.72 to -0.17). Certainty of evidence was low to moderate, and the strength of association was overall weak.

CONCLUSIONS: We rigorously assessed the quality, certainty of evidence, and the strength of associations. Despite the appraisals highlighting the need for further high-quality research, our results can inform policy and practice on the use of psychosocial interventions for caregivers of people with different clinical conditions.

title: Lack of fear acquisition to film clip unconditional stimuli despite contingency awareness: Implications for electrodermal fear conditioning
abstract: Fear conditioning is most commonly assessed by measuring electrodermal activity to a conditioned stimulus (CS) in anticipation of an electric shock or another unconditioned stimulus (US). Replacing the electric shock with aversive film clips is an innovation that potentially has higher ecological validity for posttraumatic stress disorder. The present report examined boundary conditions of this paradigm across two between subjects experiments, with a particular focus on the effectiveness of film clip versus electric shock USs in promoting physiological fear conditioning. In Experiment 1, we tested whether fear acquisition was influenced by the inclusion of a shock US (n = 30), prior exposure to a longer trauma film (n = 29), or the use of face (n = 33) versus shape (n = 33) conditioned stimuli (CSs). Fear acquisition was enhanced by the inclusion of a shock US and to a lesser extent by prior trauma film exposure; however, conditioning in groups using film clip USs alone was characterised by lack of conditioned electrodermal responding. Experiment 2 investigated whether this absence of conditioned responding reflected reduced contingency awareness by measuring online US expectancy across film-based (four US film clip group with n = 55 and one US film clip group with n = 44) and shock-based (n = 30) US conditions, as well as salivary stress responses following acquisition. Despite equivalent US expectancy, CS pleasantness, and subjective US ratings across groups, conditioned electrodermal responses during acquisition were observed only in the shock US condition. Differences between groups may be explained by differences in salivary cortisol reactivity, with higher cortisol responses following acquisition in the shock group. Together, these findings indicate that shock USs increase physiological arousal, which appears to be essential for electrodermal reactivity, irrespective of conditioned learning processes. This finding has potentially important implications for the interpretation of electrodermal measurement in fear conditioning paradigms.

title: Mantra Meditation for Pain Conditions: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract:
Background Pain is biopsychosocial in nature, and international guidelines now emphasise interdisciplinary treatment. Psychotherapeutic interventions such as mantra meditation (MM) are being increasingly studied for their potential benefits in pain management. Objectives To conduct a systematic review and meta‐analysis of the evidence for MM in improving biopsychosocial outcomes in acute and chronic pain conditions. Methods A systematic search of MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, CENTRAL, EMBASE and Scopus identified controlled clinical trials of MM for acute and chronic pain, with no date limits. Data were synthesised using an inverse‐variance random‐effects meta‐analysis of continuous outcomes with precalculated effect sizes (Hedges’ g). Results Seven studies ( n = 374) met inclusion criteria, with low‐to‐moderate methodological quality. Meta‐analyses showed significant effects of MM versus controls for improving mental quality of life (QoL) and reducing negative mood states. No significant effects were found for pain, physical QoL, depression symptoms, anxiety, stress, psychological well‐being or sleep. However, subgroup analysis indicated significant improvement in depression symptoms for participants with chronic pain compared with acute pain. Conclusion Further high‐quality randomised controlled trials are required to determine the efficacy of MM in pain management. Current evidence suggests MM may improve selected psychological outcomes, including mental QoL, negative mood states and depression in chronic pain. These findings indicate that MM has potential as an adjuvant intervention within holistic, interdisciplinary approaches to pain management.

1.
