Introduction Pain is defined by the International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP) as ‘an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage, or described in terms of such damage’ [ 1 ]. Although criticised for oversimplification [ 2 ], pain is usefully categorised into nociceptive, inflammatory and pathological subtypes [ 3 ], and as acute or chronic by duration [ 4 ]. Chronic pain lasts at least 3 months (e.g., endometriosis, cancer‐related pain) [ 5 ], while acute pain involves rapid onset and short duration (e.g., burns, childbirth) [ 4 ]. Shared physiological and psychological mechanisms [ 6 ] support examining both forms together. The biopsychosocial model best captures pain’s complexity, integrating biological, psychological and social influences [ 7 , 8 ]. Individuals with pain frequently experience anxiety, depression, stress, sleep and mood disturbances, impaired function and disrupted relationships [ 9 ], driven by inflammation and psychosocial factors such as poor mental health or limited support [ 10 ]. These erode quality of life (QoL). Global prevalence is 28% across 52 countries ( n = 199,862) [ 11 ], generating an annual economic burden of $560–635 billion in medical costs, lost productivity and disability support [ 12 ]. Such personal, societal and financial costs demand effective interventions. Pharmacological treatment predominates, beginning with over‐the‐counter analgesics before diagnosis [ 13 , 14 ] and progressing to tailored regimens of opioids [ 13 , 15 ] and NSAIDs [ 15 , 16 ]. Long‐term NSAID use carries cardiovascular and gastrointestinal risks [ 17 ]. Opioids exacerbate dependence, fuel the current crisis [ 18 ] and nearly double all‐cause mortality in older adults compared with NSAIDs [ 19 – 21 ]. Recognising these limitations and pain’s psychosocial burden, the UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) advocates multidisciplinary management [ 22 ]. This emphasises psychotherapeutic interventions delivered by mental health professionals [ 23 – 25 ], sometimes prioritised over pharmacotherapy or surgery [ 26 , 27 ]. Established psychological therapies include cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) [ 28 ], acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) [ 28 ], hypnotherapy [ 29 ] and mindfulness meditation [ 30 ]. CBT has the strongest evidence, significantly reducing pain and disability [ 31 – 34 ], as shown in a review of 75 trials ( N = 9401) [ 34 ]. ACT improves distress and function, particularly in chronic pain [ 35 , 36 ]. Hypnotherapy benefits irritable bowel syndrome and emotional well‐being [ 37 – 40 ]. Mindfulness meditation stands out for its accessibility—no therapist required, fully self‐administered [ 41 ]—and consistent reductions in pain intensity and distress across populations [ 42 – 48 ], aligning with demand for nonpharmacological self‐management. Mantra meditation (MM), a concentrative practice centred on repeated mantras [ 49 , 50 ], is emerging as a promising alternative. While MM improves mental health [ 50 – 52 ] and spiritual well‐being [ 53 ], its role in pain management is still nascent. Rooted in Hinduism, Buddhism [ 54 ] and Zoroastrianism [ 55 ], ‘mantra’ derives from Sanskrit roots denoting mental repetition that ‘saves’ or protects from suffering [ 56 ]. Mantras—sounds, words or phrases—may be breath‐synchronised [ 57 ], chanted aloud or silently [ 58 ] or simply listened to [ 57 ]. Examples include Transcendental Meditation, Kirtan Kriya and Sahaj Samadhi [ 59 – 62 ]. MM uniquely engages linguistic pathways rather than somatic focus [ 63 ], a mechanism paralleled in speech‐language pathology by melodic intonation therapy, where repetitive, rhythmic vocal production recruits dedicated linguistic‐motor networks in speech rehabilitation [ 64 , 65 ], and by neuroscientific evidence that sustained verbal recitation is associated with structural changes in memory‐ and language‐related brain regions [ 66 ]. Traditional science holds that efficacy peaks when mantras are ‘chetan’—transmitted by a perfected teacher [ 57 , 67 – 69 ]. Neuroimaging reveals MM’s mechanisms. One study showed 40%–50% reductions in thalamic, prefrontal and global brain responses to pain, with modest anterior cingulate attenuation, dampening emotional and motivational processing [ 70 ]. Another study ( n = 16) identified a signature of heightened attention (elevated anterior cingulate and dorsolateral prefrontal flow) paired with reduced arousal (decreased pons and cerebellar activity), confirming low effort and high feasibility [ 71 ]. Global interest is rising [ 51 ]; 1.6% of US adults (3.6 million) practised MM over 12 months, only 0.3% below mindfulness [ 72 ]. Despite this, no systematic review has synthesised MM’s effects on pain. Given the field’s early stage, broad inclusion criteria are recommended to capture available data comprehensively [ 50 , 73 , 74 ]. This review therefore evaluates MM interventions for acute and chronic pain conditions, across adult and paediatric populations, and all controlled study designs. It addresses four research questions: Can MM improve self‐reported pain intensity in individuals with pain conditions? Can MM improve QoL in people with pain conditions? Can MM reduce symptoms of depression, anxiety and stress in people with pain conditions? Can MM enhance mood states, psychological well‐being and sleep quality in people with pain conditions? 2. Method The present review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines [ 75 ]. The review protocol was registered prospectively on the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) on the 10th of October 2024, with reference number CRD42024598688 [ 76 ]. This project, due to being a review, was exempted from ethics approval. 2.1. Study Selection 2.1.1. Eligibility Criteria Studies were eligible if they were English‐language, peer‐reviewed, controlled trials (randomised or non‐randomised) involving human participants of any age or sex experiencing acute [ 4 ] or chronic [ 5 ] pain. Interventions had to consist of MM as the primary component, delivered in any format or duration (face‐to‐face or online); adjunctive breathing exercises or brief visualisations were permitted, but MM could not be combined with any other active intervention. Comparators could be any non‐MM control (wait‐list, treatment‐as‐usual or active). Outcomes were self‐reported using validated instruments and included pain intensity (primary), QoL, depression, anxiety, stress, negative mood, psychological well‐being and sleep quality. Studies were excluded if they were grey literature, conference abstracts, uncontrolled or did not evaluate an MM intervention. 2.2. Search Strategy and Study Selection A comprehensive search was conducted across Medline Complete, APA PsycINFO, CINAHL, Cochrane CENTRAL, EMBASE and Scopus (see Appendix A for sample strategy (see Table A1 )). Reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews were hand‐searched. No date limits were applied; searches were restricted to English‐language publications and completed on 15 October 2024, and updated on 10 th October 2025. Records were imported into Covidence [ 77 ]. Titles and abstracts were screened independently by two reviewers (Yao Coitinho Biurra, Zoe Coitinho Biurra), with conflicts resolved by a third (Anthony Thompson). Full‐text articles were assessed independently by the same two reviewers, with discrepancies resolved by discussion. 2.3. Data Extraction Data were extracted independently by two reviewers ((Yao Coitinho Biurra, Zoe Coitinho Biurra) into a pre‐piloted Excel spreadsheet (Appendix B), with conflicts resolved by AT. Extracted items included study characteristics (authors, year, country, design, setting), participant details (sample size, age, pain condition), intervention features (MM type, duration, delivery mode, comparator), outcome measures and all means and standard deviations (or standard errors) at every time point. A data extraction checklist is provided in Appendix C (see Table A2 ). 2.4. Data Synthesis and Statistical Analysis Comparable outcomes were synthesised using inverse‐variance random‐effects meta‐analyses in IBM SPSS [ 78 ], following the intention‐to‐treat principle. Postintervention data (first follow‐up after intervention end) were converted to Hedges’ g to accommodate small samples and varying reporting formats, using the George Mason University online effect‐size calculator [ 79 ]. Effect sizes were interpreted as small (g = 0.15), medium (0.40) or large (0.75) [ 80 ]. Heterogeneity was assessed with I 2 (< 25% low, 50% moderate, 75% high) [ 81 ]. Acute and chronic pain studies were pooled because of the limited evidence base [ 50 , 73 , 74 ]. Subgroup analyses by pain type (acute vs chronic) were performed only when ≥ 2 studies were available per category. When multiple measures existed for one outcome, the most appropriate was selected. A narrative synthesis complemented the quantitative results. 2.5. Quality Assessment Risk of bias was assessed independently by two reviewers (Yao Coitinho Biurra, Zoe Coitinho Biurra) using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool Version 1 [ 82 ], with disagreements resolved by discussion. The tool evaluates seven domains (random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting and other bias), each rated as low, high or unclear risk. 3. Results 3.1. Study Selection From the Literature Search All stages of screening are presented in the PRISMA flow diagram below [ 75 ] (see Figure 1 ). A total of 2588 studies were selected for potential inclusion, and 369 duplicates were removed. A further 2194 records were excluded after screening titles and abstracts against the selection criteria. The remaining 25 full‐text records were further assessed for eligibility, and another 18 were excluded, mostly due to the wrong study design or population. Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through discussion. The remaining seven studies met the selection criteria and were included in the final meta‐analyses. 3.1.1. Study Characteristics Table 1 summarises the key characteristics of the studies included in this review. Seven RCTs were included, with sample sizes ranging from 22 [ 86 ] to 99 [ 85 ]. Four studies were conducted in the United States [ 60 , 83 , 84 , 86 ], one in Germany [ 85 ], one in India [ 59 ] and one in the Netherlands [ 87 ]. 3.1.2. Participant Characteristics There were a total of 374 participants across 7 studies, with 188 participants in the intervention conditions and 186 in the control conditions. Mean ages ranged from 13.39 (STDV = 2.61) [ 87 ] to 64.14 (STDV = 9.13) [ 83 ] years. Six studies included adult populations, while only one [ 87 ] included a paediatric population ( n = 78). While six studies included female‐dominant samples (74.38% females vs 25.62% males), only one was male‐dominant (53%) [ 59 ]. Further participant characteristics are presented in Table 1 . 3.1.3. Intervention Characteristics Two studies [ 83 , 87 ] implemented Transcendental Meditation, two [ 84 , 86 ] applied a general MM, one [ 84 ] used ‘spiritual’ mantras, one [ 60 ] employed Kirtan Kriya, one [ 59 ] utilised Yogic Sound Resonance, and one [ 85 ] investigated Jyoti Meditation. The intervention delivery methods varied: three studies [ 83 , 84 , 87 ] provided group‐based in‐person training, where the intervention itself was later self‐directed by participants at home, based on what they learned during training. Three studies [ 59 , 60 , 86 ] followed a similar delivery format, but included additional pre‐recorded audios for guided at‐home sessions. Lastly, one study [ 85 ] provided the intervention via in‐person group sessions, but also allowed for at‐home practice. Intervention durations ranged from 1.5 weeks [ 59 ] to 12 weeks [ 60 , 83 , 87 ], while follow‐up timeframes ranged from 3 weeks [ 59 ] to 9 months [ 87 ] (see Table 1 for further details). 3.1.4. Control Characteristics As presented in Table 1 , all the studies employed parallel controlled group designs, with all but one study [ 59 ] using an active control. Active control interventions differed across studies: Three studies [ 84 , 85 , 87 ] compared the intervention to progressive muscle relaxation (PMR), two [ 60 , 86 ] used music listening, and one [ 83 ] used health education, while the nonactive control study [ 59 ] employed nonguided supine rest. 3.1.5. Outcomes and Measures All included studies measured both physiological and psychological outcomes (see Table 1 for further details). The measures used for the meta‐analyses were as follows: The PSS was used for stress, the PMS for mood, PWBS for psychological well‐being, CES‐D and RCADS for symptoms of depression, STAI and RCADS for symptoms of anxiety, SF‐36 for physical and mental QoL and the PSQI for sleep quality; meanwhile, NRS, VAS and SF‐36 (bodily pain subscale) were used for pain intensity. 3.2. title: Amygdala neurofeedback as an adjunct to residential dialectical behavior therapy for borderline personality disorder: a pilot randomized controlled trial
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is characterized by affective instability and amygdala hyperreactivity. Although dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) reduces symptoms and amygdala-related abnormalities, many patients show only partial remission. Real-time functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) amygdala neurofeedback (amy-NF) directly targets hyperactive limbic responses and has shown promise in uncontrolled trials. We examined whether amy-NF adds benefit to inpatient DBT.

METHODS: Thirty-six mid-therapy people with BPD and clinically significant residual symptoms (BSL-23 > 1.5) were randomized to DBT plus amy-NF (n = 23) or DBT alone, termed treatment as usual (TAU = 13). Post-treatment assessments were completed by 15/9 (amy-NF/TAU), with 15/8 and 12/7 completing the 3- and 6-month follow-ups. Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) of daily-life affective instability served as the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes included self-reports, amygdala responses during two fMRI tasks, and resting-state fMRI. Assessments occurred at pre-, post-, 3-, and 6-month follow-up.

RESULTS: Participants successfully downregulated amygdala activity during neurofeedback. EMA showed improvements in negative affect, inner tension, and affective instability over time, without consistent superiority of amy-NF. Self-reports likewise showed no additional benefit of amy-NF, and BSL-23 scores increased after discharge in both groups. Amy-NF was associated with transient pre-post reductions in amygdala activity during both viewing and regulation in the emotion regulation task, and with more stable amygdala reactivity over time than TAU in the faces task. Resting-state analyses showed transient pre-post increases in amygdala connectivity with precuneus and dorsomedial frontal regions in amy-NF.

CONCLUSIONS: Amygdala neurofeedback is feasible and reduced amygdala activity in BPD, but did not yield additional clinical benefit when delivered alongside intensive residential DBT, although the small sample may have limited power to detect such effects.

TRIAL REGISTRATION: The study protocol was preregistered 2020/03/26 on ClinicalTrials.gov and received the ID NCT04333888.

title: [The Use of Dialectical-Behavior Therapy in the Treatment of Substance Use Disorders]
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The treatment of substance use disorders (SUD) remains a persistent challenge. Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) is a multimodal cognitive-behavioral treatment approach that integrates acceptance- and change-oriented strategies and was originally developed to address severe emotion dysregulation. In the context of SUD, DBT-based adaptations and skills-oriented formats are particularly used to target emotion regulation, distress tolerance, mindfulness and relapse prevention. Aim: The aim of this review was to synthesize the current state of research in order to explore and evaluate the use and effectiveness of DBT-based interventions for SUD.

METHODS: A systematic literature search in databases, Google Scholar and Semantic Scholar identified 13 relevant studies from the period 2010 to 2024, which were narratively synthesized.

RESULTS: Despite methodological limitations, the findings suggested that the DBT-based formats used, in particular DBT skills training (DBT-ST), might improve emotion regulation, distress tolerance and adaptive coping strategies. Additionally, there was evidence for beneficial effects on substance use, abstinence and craving. Furthermore, several findings suggested promising treatment acceptance and adherence, although these results depended on the context and study design.

CONCLUSIONS: Overall, it can be concluded that DBT-ST, in particular, may be a suitable intervention option for individuals with SUD. However, further robust studies with standardized diagnostic procedures, longer follow-up periods and active control groups are needed to more precisely determine its specific efficacy and indications.

Die Behandlung von Substanzgebrauchsstörungen (SUD) stellt eine anhaltende Herausforderung dar. Die Dialektische Verhaltenstherapie (DBT) ist ein kognitiv-verhaltenstherapeutisches, multimodales Verfahren, das Akzeptanz- und Veränderungsstrategien verbindet und ursprünglich zur Behandlung schwerer Emotionsdysregulation entwickelt wurde. Im Suchtkontext werden insbesondere DBT-basierte Adaptationen und Skills-orientierte Formate eingesetzt, die auf Emotionsregulation, Belastungstoleranz, Achtsamkeit und Rückfallprävention abzielen. Die vorliegende Übersichtsarbeit bündelt den gegenwärtigen Forschungsstand, um den Einsatz und die Effektivität von DBT-basierten Interventionen bei SUD zu explorieren und zu bewerten. Methode: Anhand einer systematischen Literaturrecherche in Datenbanken, in Google Scholar sowie in Semantic Scholar wurden 13 relevante Studien aus dem Zeitraum 2010 bis 2024 identifiziert und narrativ synthetisiert. Die Resultate deuten trotz methodischer Einschränkungen darauf hin, dass die angewandten DBT-basierten Formate, insbesondere das DBT Skills-Training (DBT-ST), Emotionsregulation, Belastungstoleranz sowie adaptive Bewältigungsstrategien verbessern. Zudem zeigten sich Hinweise auf günstige Effekte hinsichtlich Substanzkonsum, Abstinenz und Craving. Weiters sprechen mehrere Befunde für eine vielversprechende Behandlungsakzeptanz und Therapietreue, wobei diese Ergebnisse kontext- und studiendesignabhängig sind. In der Zusammenschau lässt sich ableiten, dass insbesondere das DBT-ST für suchtkranke Personen eine geeignete Interventionsoption darstellen kann. Jedoch sind weitere robuste Studien mit standardisierter Diagnostik, längeren Nachbeobachtungszeiten und aktiven Kontrollgruppen erforderlich, um die spezifische Wirksamkeit und Indikationsstellung präziser zu bestimmen.

title: Computerized Cognitive Training in People with Depression: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Cognitive impairment and depression frequently co-occur, exacerbating disability. Identifying accessible interventions to enhance cognition in people with depression is imperative. Computerized cognitive training (CCT) is a potential strategy, but its clinical efficacy across settings remain unclear. We investigated the efficacy of CCT and potential moderators of cognitive and functional outcomes in individuals with depressive symptoms.

METHODS: In this systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO: CRD42020204209), we searched MEDLINE, Embase, and PsycINFO from inception to June 22, 2026 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of CCT in adults (≥18 years) with clinically significant depressive symptoms. Primary outcome was change in overall cognition. Secondary outcomes included depressive symptoms, psychosocial and daily functioning.

RESULTS: Fifty-three 53 RCTs (3831 participants) were included. CCT was efficacious for overall cognition (49 RCTs, (g=0.23; 95% CI 0.14 to 0.32; τ2=0.095) and depressive symptoms (35 RCTs, g=0.22; 95% CI 0.08 to 0.37; τ2=0.066) with substantial heterogeneity across studies, and did not extend to psychiatric symptoms and daily function. Greater cognitive benefits were associated with multidomain training, higher doses, session durations >30 min, and ≤3 sessions per week. Efficacy was independent of baseline symptom severity, and comparable across delivery modes.

CONCLUSIONS: CCT can improve cognition, depression and subjective outcomes in people with major or comorbid depression, but efficacy varies across outcomes, settings and intervention design factors. Future work is needed to confirm these factors, and examine what approaches and dose is required to enhance cognitive and functional outcomes of CCT.

title: The role of positive linguistic sentiment in extinction learning through exposure therapy
abstract: Exposure therapy is derived from extinction learning principles. Evidence suggests that reward processes, including positive affect, may influence extinction learning. Few studies have explored the role of reward and positive affect in exposure. This study sought to address gaps by examining whether linguistic markers of positive affect expressed during exposure predicted learning and clinical outcomes. Adults (N = 47) with social anxiety or panic disorder completed nine sessions of exposure therapy. Participants rated expected likelihood of feared outcome occurrence before and after each exposure, and the difference (expectancy change) was calculated as a measure of learning. Natural language processing was used to analyze sentiment in written and spoken language during consolidation of extinction learning immediately after exposure, resulting in a score that reflected tendency towards positive over negative affect. Anxiety symptoms were assessed weekly at each exposure session and at end of treatment. Higher positive sentiment was associated with greater expectancy change at the between-person level for written and within-person level for spoken sentiment. Higher within-person positive sentiment predicted lower next-session anxiety for spoken sentiment only. Sentiment did not predict overall clinical outcomes. This is the first study to test the role of linguistic sentiment in exposure learning mechanisms and outcomes. More positive sentiment during exposure consolidation may support greater learning and reduced next-session symptoms, but may be insufficient in affecting overall clinical outcomes. It is possible that exposure learning may be maximized by directing attention towards more positive exposure elements; further study is needed to test this.

title: Fear of positive evaluation impairs disengagement from positive and ambiguous dynamic social cues during late-stage attentional processing
abstract: Fear of Positive Evaluation (FPE) is a key cognitive feature of social anxiety, yet its neurodynamic impact on social attention remains unclear. This study used a cue-target paradigm with emotional biological motion cues (happy, angry, fear, neutral) and event-related potentials (ERPs) to systematically compare attention processing between individuals with high and low levels of FPE across distinct temporal stages. Behavioral results showed that individuals with high levels of FPE showed delayed responses specifically to neutral cues under valid conditions (i.e., the target appeared at the same location as the preceding cue). Electrophysiological results revealed that all participants showed consistent performance in early spatial orienting (N1); during the conflict monitoring stage (N2), neutral cues and valid targets generally enhanced the N2 amplitude. Critically, in late motivational evaluation stage (P3), the two groups displayed dissociated patterns: individuals with low levels of FPE demonstrated adaptive threat monitoring, with the strongest P3 response to angry cues under valid conditions and enhanced P3 to fear cues under invalid conditions (i.e., the target appeared at the opposite location). In contrast, individuals with high levels of FPE displayed maladaptive attentional engagement, with enhanced P3 amplitudes and impaired disengagement from happy and neutral cues under invalid conditions. Furthermore, they exhibited a reversed threat-sensitivity, as reflected in larger P3 amplitudes to fear cues compared to angry cues under valid conditions. These results demonstrate that FPE is characterized by stage-specific dysregulation, primarily marked by late-stage hyper-engagement with positive and ambiguous social signals rather than generalized threat sensitivity. This work provides direct neural evidence for the Bivalent Fear of Evaluation model and offers novel insights for developing intervention strategies targeting cognitive biases in the evaluation stage.

title: Visual feedback increases expiratory muscle training effort in Parkinson's disease: a randomised crossover trial
abstract:
Background Disorders of airway protection, including impaired cough and swallowing, are clinically important complications of Parkinson’s disease. Expiratory muscle strength training (EMST) is an established non-pharmacological intervention targeting these deficits. The aim of this study was to evaluate the acute effect of visual feedback provided by the SpiroGym mHealth app on expiratory muscle activation during EMST in people with Parkinson’s disease. Methods We conducted a single-center, randomised, two-period crossover trial in people with Parkinson’s disease. Participants performed EMST under two conditions, in randomised order: conventional EMST without visual feedback and EMST with real-time visual feedback provided by the SpiroGym app. Expiratory muscle activation was measured using surface electromyography of the abdominal muscles. The primary outcome was the within-participant difference in mean peak normalised internal oblique activity between conditions. Secondary outcomes included external oblique and rectus abdominis activity, associations with neuropsychiatric symptoms, and participant-reported usability ratings. Results Twenty participants were randomised, and 19 completed the study and were included in the final analysis. No study-related adverse events occurred. Visual feedback significantly increased mean peak normalised internal oblique activity compared with no feedback (118.2 ± 36.4% vs. 90.5 ± 23.0% of reference voluntary contraction; p < 0.001; Cohen d = 0.95). Without feedback, internal oblique activation significantly declined from 100.1 ± 22.2% in the first set to 84.4 ± 25.5% in the fifth set, whereas it remained stable with feedback (120.3 ± 29.4% to 119.9 ± 40.6%). External oblique activation was also significantly higher with feedback (122.2 ± 38.1% vs. 100.9 ± 32.4%; p = 0.002; Cohen d = 0.66), while rectus abdominis activation did not differ significantly between conditions (105.2 ± 41.3% vs. 90.2 ± 36.1%; p = 0.06; Cohen d = 0.43). No significant associations between feedback responsiveness and depression, apathy, or anxiety were detected. Participants rated the visual feedback as easy to understand and helpful for EMST performance. Conclusions Real-time visual feedback delivered by the SpiroGym app acutely increased and stabilized expiratory muscle activation during EMST in people with Parkinson’s disease. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06942533, 1 May 2025. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s12984-026-02104-5 .

Background Parkinson’s disease (PD) is one of the fastest growing neurodegenerative disorders worldwide. This trend is partly driven by population ageing, as the incidence of PD rises with age [ 1 ]. However, age-adjusted prevalence is also increasing, suggesting additional contributors such as improved diagnostic accuracy and environmental factors [ 2 ]. Resistance training plays an important role in the non-pharmacological management of PD [ 3 ]. Such interventions may target several characteristic PD-related impairments, including bradykinesia, reduced muscle strength, impaired balance, gait difficulties and reduced functional mobility. In addition, resistance training may have beneficial effects on selected non-motor domains, including cognition and quality of life [ 4 , 5 ]. They have also been associated with slower disease progression [ 6 ] and improved quality of life [ 5 ]. One PD-specific application of resistance training aimed at supporting airway protection is expiratory muscle strength training (EMST) [ 7 ]. Airway protection is clinically relevant in PD, as both cough and swallowing are frequently impaired. These deficits are multifactorial and may involve impaired muscle control and peripheral muscle weakness [ 8 , 9 ]. This impairment increases the risk of aspiration and aspiration pneumonia is a leading cause of death in people with PD (PwP) [ 10 – 12 ]. EMST is performed using a calibrated device with a one-way, spring-loaded valve that provides resistance during forced expiration, thereby overloading the expiratory muscles involved in cough and the suprahyoid muscles involved in swallowing, and improving their force-generating capacity [ 9 , 13 ]. This provides a rationale for targeting the muscle weakness component that may contribute to cough and swallowing dysfunction. In addition, because the EMST maneuver mimics many of the movements required for cough production, it may also address the impaired coordination component [ 14 ]. Available detraining data indicate that EMST-related gains may be partly retained after intensive training [ 13 ]. Other research, by contrast, found that detraining was more pronounced in individuals with poorer baseline swallowing function, in whom a three-month detraining period returned swallowing function to baseline (pre-EMST) levels [ 15 ]. This suggests that, in PwP receiving EMST for clinically relevant cough or swallowing impairment, maintenance programmes are needed to sustain the functional gains [ 15 , 16 ]. However, the optimal duration, frequency, and intensity of long-term EMST in PwP remain insufficiently established in the current literature. In this context, SpiroGym, a mobile health (mHealth) application designed to support long term adherence to EMST by providing real-time visual feedback and longitudinal tracking of training progress, has been introduced [ 17 – 19 ]. In a previous randomised controlled trial, PwP were randomised to conventional EMST or the same EMST protocol enhanced with the SpiroGym app [ 20 ]. The study protocol consisted of 8 weeks of semisupervised intensive EMST followed by 16 weeks of unsupervised maintenance training. One key finding was that expiratory muscle strength, measured as maximal expiratory pressure (MEP), improved in both groups, but the gains were significantly larger in the SpiroGym group at the 8-week visit. Because the intensity of EMST was identical in both groups and adherence rates were comparable, the greater strength gains observed with SpiroGym may reflect more effective within-session training effort facilitated by real-time visual feedback [ 20 ]. This interpretation is consistent with evidence from resistance training research showing that visual feedback can enhance acute performance within a training session and promote greater long-term adaptations [ 21 ]. However, it remains unclear whether visual feedback increases acute expiratory effort during repeated EMST maneuvers in PwP. Therefore, the primary objective of this randomised crossover trial was to evaluate the acute effect of visual feedback provided by the SpiroGym app on expiratory muscle activation during EMST in PwP, as assessed by surface electromyography (sEMG). We hypothesized that visual feedback provided by the SpiroGym app would increase expiratory muscle effort during EMST compared with EMST performed without feedback. Methods Study design This was a two-period, two-sequence (AB/BA), single-center, randomised crossover trial, with each participant receiving both interventions: a control condition (EMST without visual feedback) and an experimental condition (EMST with visual feedback). The rationale for the crossover design was to enable each participant to serve as their own control, thereby reducing the impact of interparticipant variability on study outcomes, minimizing confounding factors, and enabling a more precise comparison of the effects of visual feedback. The trial was prospectively registered (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06942533; 1 May 2025) and reported in accordance with CONSORT guidelines for randomised crossover trials [ 22 ]. The intended primary outcome was internal oblique (IO) muscle activation during EMST, quantified by surface electromyography (sEMG), with external oblique (EO) and rectus abdominis (RA) activation as secondary outcomes. In the original registration, however, these outcomes were specified at the group level (“abdominal muscles”) rather than at the level of individual muscles. The registration was subsequently updated on 24 November 2025, before the statistical analysis, to name the IO as the primary outcome and the EO and RA as secondary outcomes. This refinement affected only the labelling of the outcomes in the public registry and did not change the hierarchy of outcomes or how they were recorded, analysed, or reported. The trial was conducted at the Department of Neurology, General University Hospital, First Faculty of Medicine, Charles University in Prague, Czech Republic, between May 2025 and November 2025. Participants Participants were recruited through convenience sampling from the Movement Disorders Centre at the study site between May 2025 and September 2025. Inclusion criteria were: (1) a diagnosis of PD confirmed by a movement disorder specialist according to the UK Brain Bank criteria [ 23 ], (2) modified Hoehn and Yahr stage of I–IV in the ON medication state, (3) age between 40 and 80 years, and (4) a stable dopaminergic medication dose for ≥ 1 month prior to enrollment and throughout the study period. Exclusion criteria were: (1) suspected parkinsonism due to causes other than idiopathic PD, (2) significant cognitive impairment (Montreal Cognitive Assessment score < 19) [ 24 ], (3) severe respiratory disease documented in the medical record, (4) uncontrolled hypertension, (5) severe visual impairment not correctable with lenses; and (6) previous experience with EMST and with the SpiroGym app. Randomisation and blinding A simple computer-generated random allocation sequence was created prior to study initiation using a web-based randomisation tool (randomizer.org) by the study team. Participants were randomised in a 1:1 ratio to one of two treatment sequences (Control-Experimental, or Experimental-Control). Allocation concealment was ensured by using sealed opaque envelopes containing the sequence order, which were opened only after the participant had been enrolled in the study. Assessor blinding was not feasible during data collection because the use of the SpiroGym app in the experimental condition was apparent. However, sEMG data were de-identified and condition-coded after acquisition, and the assessor extracting sEMG outcomes was blinded to condition. The study statistician was blinded to experimental condition and analyzed condition-coded data. Participants were informed that the study compared the acute effects of two EMST conditions and that they would complete both conditions in a randomised order. They were not provided with a specific study hypothesis. If participants asked which condition was expected to be more effective, they were told that both were considered beneficial and that the study aimed to evaluate their effects. Study outcome parameters The primary outcome was the within-participant difference in mean peak normalised sEMG activity of the IO muscle between EMST performed with and without visual feedback. The IO was selected as the primary outcome for three reasons. First, abdominal muscles as a group are key contributors to forced expiratory effort [ 25 , 26 ], with significantly greater contributions from the IO and transversus abdominis (TA) than from the EO and RA [ 26 , 27 ]. Second, the TA lies deep to the IO and EO abdominal muscles, and therefore cannot be selectively assessed using sEMG. Third, EMST in the present study was performed at 75% of MEP. At this intensity, the IO has been reported to be the only abdominal muscle reaching an activation level (> 40% of maximal voluntary contraction) considered sufficient to drive strength-related adaptations, whereas the EO and RA remain below this level [ 28 ]. Accordingly, IO sEMG during EMST was used as a physiological surrogate of within-session expiratory effort that may help explain the previously observed between-group differences in MEP [ 20 ]. Prespecified secondary outcomes included within-participant differences in mean peak normalised EO and RA sEMG activity to characterize the pattern of superficial abdominal muscle recruitment during EMST and participant-reported subjective ratings of SpiroGym usability, perceived visual feedback helpfulness, and sEMG electrode-related discomfort. Additional exploratory outcomes included correlations between the within-participant difference in normalised IO sEMG activation and self-reported neuropsychiatric symptoms assessed using questionnaires validated for use in Parkinson’s disease: the Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI) [ 29 ] for depression, the Starkstein Apathy Scale (SAS) [ 30 ] for apathy, the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory for anxiety state (STAI-state) and trait (STAI-trait) [ 31 ]. Assessment visits All assessments were conducted in the ON medication state (approximately 1 h after intake of antiparkinsonian medication) and at the same time of day. For the study flow diagram, see Fig. 1 . The two study visits were separated by a two-week interval without EMST training to minimize potential carryover effects. This interval was chosen because neural adaptations that can occur after a single session of resistance training, and could otherwise influence between-visit differences in sEMG, are expected to dissipate over a two-week rest period [ 32 ]. PwP were instructed to keep their physical activity as similar as possible during the two days preceding each study visit in order to minimize potential differences in fatigue. During both the control and experimental conditions, the study team did not encourage or motivate participants. Instead, instructions were delivered in a neutral tone, using only “pause” (to indicate that EMST should not be performed) and “now” (to cue the participant to perform the EMST maneuver). Before each study visit, PwP were assessed for fatigue using the visual analog fatigue scale (VAFS; 0 = no fatigue, 10 = worst possible fatigue). The VAFS has been shown to be a reliable measure of overall fatigue in individuals with PD [ 33 ]. In addition, to reduce potential learning effects, i.e. that PwP would perform EMST better after the first training condition, a practice (familiarisation) session was held two weeks before the main experiment. During this session, MEP was assessed using a flanged rubber mouthpiece connected to a pressure manometer (MicroRPM, Vyaire Medical), in accordance with current recommendations [ 34 ]. Participants were then introduced to EMST and practiced the maneuvers without visual feedback at 75% of their MEP — the same resistance subsequently used in both the control and experimental conditions. Practice continued until the study physiotherapist deemed the technique and maneuver quality satisfactory. MEP was measured during the familiarisation session only and was not re-measured at the first or second study visit. title: Effects of Mindfulness Therapy on Stress Biomarkers and Psychological Symptoms in Women With Recurrent Pregnancy Loss: A Randomized Clinical Trial
abstract:
ABSTRACT Women with recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL) exhibit high levels of depression, anxiety, and stress, which negatively impact their quality of life. This randomized clinical trial evaluated the effects of an eight‐week online Mindfulness‐Based Intervention (MBI), with weekly one‐hour sessions, on psychological and biological markers of stress in 35 women with RPL. Participants were randomly assigned to either the MBI or standard care (control group) and assessed before and after the intervention through salivary biomarkers (cortisol, alpha‐amylase, and Immunoglobulin A—IgA) and the validated questionnaires Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale‐21 (DASS‐21) and Psychological General Well‐Being Index (PGWB‐I). No significant time × group interactions were observed for salivary biomarkers, including cortisol ( p = 0.672), alpha‐amylase ( p = 0.342), and IgA ( p = 0.148). Participants in the MBI group showed significant reductions in total DASS‐21 ( p = 0.018), depression ( p = 0.026), and stress ( p = 0.015) scores, whereas anxiety did not differ significantly between groups ( p = 0.121). They also showed robust improvements in overall well‐being ( p < 0.001) and multiple PGWB‐I domains. These findings suggest that MBI may improve self‐reported psychological well‐being in women with RPL; however, as no significant effects were observed in the primary biomarker outcomes, these secondary psychological findings should be considered exploratory and hypothesis‐generating. Trial Registration https://ensaiosclinicos.gov.br/rg/RBR‐4xc76cr

1 Introduction Recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL) is traditionally defined as the occurrence of three or more consecutive pregnancy losses before 20 weeks of gestation (Rai and Regan 2006 ), although more recent guidelines consider two or more losses sufficient for diagnosis (Tulandi and Al‐Fozan 2024 ). It affects approximately 1% of couples trying to conceive when defined by a minimum of three losses, and about 3% when the definition includes two or more losses (Rai and Regan 2006 ). Miscarriage is associated with an increased risk of mental health disorders, including depression and anxiety. It is estimated that up to two‐thirds of women with RPL experience some form of psychiatric illness (Klock et al. 1997 ). Psychological distress may persist for extended periods and often intensifies with successive pregnancy losses (Bergner et al. 2008 ; Carp 2014 ). Studies have confirmed that women with RPL tend to exhibit high levels of depression, anxiety, and stress, with a marked negative impact on their quality of life (He et al. 2019 ; Hedegaard et al. 2021 ; Kolte et al. 2015 ). In this context, mindfulness‐based interventions (MBIs) have emerged as promising strategies to promote emotional well‐being and improve quality of life in women affected by RPL (Jensen et al. 2021 ; D. N. Wang et al. 2021 ). Mindfulness is defined as a meditative practice that involves maintaining a moment‐by‐moment awareness of thoughts, emotions, and bodily sensations with a non‐judgmental attitude (Kabat‐Zinn 2003 ). It typically includes exercises that help individuals become more aware of their internal experiences, promoting emotional regulation through slow, conscious breathing (Gasnier et al. 2017 ). Over the past decades, MBIs have been extensively explored as tools for enhancing well‐being in various populations, including women with RPL (Jensen et al. 2021 ; D. N. Wang et al. 2021 ). The assessment of salivary biomarkers, such as cortisol, alpha‐amylase, and immunoglobulin A (IgA), offers non‐invasive, reliable methods to monitor physiological changes associated with stress‐related psychological conditions (Blair et al. 2017 ; Chojnowska et al. 2021 ; Gröschl 2008 ). The relationship between mindfulness and stress‐related biomarkers has been the focus of growing research (Lynch et al. 2011 ). These biomarkers reflect activity in both the immune system and the autonomic nervous system, and are regulated by the hypothalamic‐pituitary‐adrenal (HPA) axis, which plays a central role in the biological stress response (Chojnowoska et al. 2021 ; Engeland et al. 2019 ). Cortisol is a glucocorticoid hormone secreted by the adrenal cortex in response to activation of the HPA axis. Under stress, the hypothalamus releases corticotropin‐releasing hormone (CRH), which stimulates the pituitary gland to secrete adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), leading to cortisol production (Blair et al. 2017 ; Kirschbaum and Hellhammer 1989 ). Free cortisol diffuses passively through the membranes of the salivary glands and is secreted into the saliva. Thus, salivary cortisol concentration directly reflects its free and biologically active fraction, providing a reliable measure of the hormone levels available in the body (Blair et al. 2017 ; Gröschl 2008 ; Inder et al. 2012 ). Elevated salivary cortisol levels are often observed in individuals with chronic and acute stress and are commonly linked to depressive symptoms and anxiety (Blair et al. 2017 ; Gröschl 2008 ; Saraiva et al. 2005 ). According to meta‐analyses, MBIs have induced changes in salivary cortisol levels but the findings are inconsistent (Sanada et al. 2016 ; O'Leary et al. 2016 ; Vargas‐Uricoechea et al. 2024 ). In turn, salivary alpha‐amylase is an enzyme regulated by the sympathetic nervous system. Its levels increase in response to acute stress due to heightened sympathetic activation. As a result, salivary alpha‐amylase has been recognized as a sensitive and rapid biomarker of autonomic nervous system arousal, complementing cortisol measurements in stress research, particularly in studies focused on anxiety and acute stress responses (Engeland et al. 2019 ; Chojnowska et al. 2021 ; Nater and Rohleder 2009 ). Research indicates that MBIs can effectively reduce salivary alpha‐amylase levels, suggesting reduced sympathetic nervous system activation (Aguilar‐Raab et al. 2021 ; Hassanvandi et al. 2025 ). Secretory IgA is a key component of mucosal immune defense, especially in the oral and respiratory tracts (Chojnowska et al. 2021 ). Stress can modulate salivary IgA levels: acute stress typically increases its secretion, whereas chronic stress may have variable effects depending on the intensity and duration of exposure (Segerstrom and Miller 2004 ). Therefore, the aim of this study was to evaluate salivary biomarkers of stress (cortisol, alpha‐amylase, and IgA), along with levels of depression, stress, anxiety, and general psychological well‐being in women with RPL before and after a MBI. 2 Methods 2.1 Study Approval and Registration This randomized controlled trial (RCT) was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais (Decision Number 5.895.786) and registered at the Brazilian Clinical Trials Registry, REBEC (Primary ID Number RBR‐4xc76cr) and Brazilian Ministry of Health Human Research Registry (Protocol ID 93675118.1.3001.5093). Participation was entirely voluntary, and all participants provided written informed consent prior to enrollment. 2.2 Participants Between July 2024 and March 2025, women aged 18 years or older with a history of at least two pregnancy losses before 20 weeks of gestation (excluding ectopic or molar pregnancies) under investigation for RPL at a tertiary academic hospital in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, were invited to participate in the research. These women were referred from various other hospitals and clinics in the region. Recruitment was conducted either in person, in a private setting, or via WhatsApp messaging. All participants underwent a standard RPL workup according to the clinic's protocol, which included karyotyping of the couple, screening for antiphospholipid syndrome, serum Thyroid‐Stimulating Hormone (TSH), serum prolactin (if clinically indicated), transvaginal ultrasound, and hysteroscopy. Eligible participants were required to have internet access via mobile phone, computer, or tablet. Exclusion criteria were diagnosis of chronic inflammatory or autoimmune disease, dementia, current smoking, inability to complete self‐administered questionnaires, being pregnant at the time of recruitment or prior experience with mindfulness practice or MBI programs. 2.3 Randomization, Allocation, and Concealment Eligible participants who agreed to participate and signed the informed consent form were randomly assigned to either the intervention or the control group. Randomization was conducted using a computer‐generated sequence prepared in advance. Each participant then drew a numbered slip from a sealed opaque envelope, which corresponded to their group assignment. Thirty‐five participants were randomized (Figure 1 ). The intervention was open‐label (unblinded to participants and facilitators); however, outcome analysis was blinded. Self‐reported questionnaires and biochemical assays were assessed by evaluators blinded to group allocation. 2.4 Intervention Women allocated to the intervention group participated in an 8‐week online MBI program delivered via Google Meet. The time interval between allocation and the first group meeting was 1 week. Sessions were held once weekly for 1 hour in synchronous format. The intervention followed a structured protocol based on the ‘Mind‐Body Therapy’ developed by Georgetown University (Saunders et al. 2007 ), which was previously validated in Brazil (Paiva et al. 2016 ). The sessions were conducted by an experienced therapist with over 15 years of mindfulness practice. Sessions included mindfulness meditation, relaxation, and visualization. Each group had up to five participants. The first session was introductory, with a brief meditation and explanation of the MBI approach. Subsequent sessions began with a short mindfulness meditation, followed by a ‘gratitude check‐in’ where participants shared something they were grateful for during the week. A mindfulness technique was then introduced and discussed. At the end of each session, participants received ‘homework,’ including mindful eating, healthy habits, journaling, and physical activity. A guided audio was also shared weekly to support individual practice. Participants in the control group received standard care only, consisting of consultations with specialists and the routine diagnostic workup for RPL. 2.5 Study Outcomes The primary outcome measures were changes in salivary concentrations of cortisol, alpha‐amylase, and IgA. Secondary outcomes were psychological symptoms of depression, stress and anxiety, and general well‐being, as measured by validated psychometric instruments. Saliva collection and questionnaire responses were performed 1 week before the start of the intervention and 1 week after its end. 2.6 Sample Collection and Processing Saliva samples were collected in the morning, between 8:00 and 9:00 a.m., in person with the assistance of the researcher for all participants, using Salivette tubes (Sarstedt, Germany) and sterile containers to ensure standardized conditions and minimize contamination risk. Awakening time was not individually recorded. Salivary samples were collected at a single time point, which precluded dynamic cortisol assessments such as the cortisol awakening response, diurnal decline, or total daily output (Sanada et al. 2016 ). For samples collected with Salivette devices, participants were instructed to keep the cotton swab in their mouth for approximately 3 minutes. For samples collected in sterile containers, participants were asked to slightly tilt their head forward, allowing saliva to accumulate naturally in the oral cavity, and to let it gently drip into the container without forceful spitting until a minimum volume of 2 mL was reached. Prior to collection, all participants were instructed to fast, refrain from drinking beverages (except water), and avoid brushing their teeth for at least 60 minutes, as well as to remain at rest for 1 hour before the procedure. After collection, the samples obtained with Salivette devices were centrifuged for 2 minutes at 2500 × g and immediately frozen in the same tube at −20°C, where they remained stored until shipment to the laboratory for analysis. The samples collected in sterile containers were also kept frozen at −20°C until laboratory assays were performed. Saliva collected in Salivette tubes was used for salivary cortisol determination, whereas samples collected in sterile containers were used for the analysis of salivary IgA and alpha‐amylase levels. 2.6.1 Salivary Cortisol Assay Salivary cortisol concentrations were determined by electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (ECLIA) using the Elecsys Cortisol II kit on a Cobas e analyzer (Roche Diagnostics, Mannheim, Germany). Frozen saliva samples were analyzed individually with ready‐to‐use liquid reagents, requiring no manual preparation. System calibration was performed using a two‐point adjustment linked to a lot‐specific master curve automatically recognized by the reagent barcode. The assay's measurement range was 1.5–1750 nmol/L, with values below 1.5 nmol/L reported as undetectable. The analytical limits were: LoB = 1.0 nmol/L, LoD = 1.5 nmol/L, and LoQ = 3.0 nmol/L. Quality control procedures were conducted according to the manufacturer's recommendations, using PreciControl Universal and/or PreciControl Cortisol Saliva materials. Reported intra‐assay and inter‐assay coefficients of variation are 2%–6% and 3%–12%, respectively. For interpretation, results were compared with the reference salivary values provided in the manufacturer's insert: morning (6–10 a.m.), < 20.3 nmol/L (95th percentile); afternoon (4–8 p.m.), < 6 nmol/L; and midnight (± 30 min), < 7.56 nmol/L. 2.6.2 Salivary Alpha‐Amylase Assay Salivary alpha‐amylase concentrations were determined by spectrophotometry using a commercial assay kit on the AU5800 analyzer (Beckman Coulter). Samples were previously diluted at a ratio of 1:200, and final results were obtained after correction for the dilution factor. Calibration was performed according to the manufacturer's instructions, with the enzymatic activity of the calibrator being lot‐dependent (144 U/L for the lot used). The lower limit of detection was 10 U/L, and the assay sensitivity was 0.77 U/L. Analyses were conducted in single‐test mode, without replicates, yielding intra‐assay and inter‐assay coefficients of variation of 1.4% and 1.6%, respectively. For interpretation, results were compared with the reference range reported in the literature (80,000–625,000 U/L). 2.6.3 Salivary Immunoglobulin A Assay Salivary IgA concentrations were determined by nephelometry using a commercial assay kit on the Atellica analyzer (Siemens), as confirmed in the Siemens BN reference system. No prior extraction or dilution of samples was required. Analyses were performed in single‐test mode without replicates. title: The economic burden of Borderline Personality Disorder: direct and indirect costs, and evidence from evaluations of interventions
abstract:
Background Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) is characterized by longstanding patterns of difficulty in functioning, and when left untreated, BPD can impose a substantial financial burden on individuals and society, in terms of higher healthcare costs as well as broader societal costs. Aims To conduct a critical review of the direct and indirect costs related to BPD. Additionally, to critically evaluate the economic evidence on interventions for BPD. Methods A comprehensive search strategy was conducted across PsycINFO, PubMed, and SCOPUS. Studies were screened in two phases: an initial title and abstract review, followed by full-text screening against a predefined eligibility criteria. Results Across 23 studies, high direct and indirect costs were consistently reported. Economic evaluations primarily examined established psychological interventions for BPD, such as Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), Cognitive Behavior Therapy (CBT), and Schema-Focused Therapy (SFT), comparing costs and quality-of-life outcomes, with most demonstrating cost savings through reduced inpatient and emergency service use. Conclusions This review highlights the substantial economic burden of BPD, driven by high service use, productivity losses, and unmet needs. While interventions such as DBT, CBT and SFT show potential cost-effectiveness, inconsistent cost definitions and the omission of key components, including informal care and long-term impairment, likely lead to an underestimation of true costs. More comprehensive and standardized economic evaluations are needed.

1 Introduction Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) is a serious mental illness characterized by persistent patterns of affective instability, an unstable self-image, fear of abandonment, impulsivity, and behavioral dysregulation ( 1 ). BPD is estimated to be present in 0.7–2.7% of adults over their lifetime, with higher rates of BPD observed in clinical settings, for example 22% among inpatient populations and 12% in outpatient services ( 2 , 3 ). Onset typically peaks during adolescence and young adulthood ( 4 ), where symptoms can fluctuate over time, with periods of improvement and recurrence even without treatment ( 5 ). Individuals with BPD often experience complex unmet needs that contribute to long-term adverse effects, such as high-level functional impairment and premature mortality ( 6 ). Although research indicates that BPD diagnosis should not be controversial, it continues to be perceived as such by some, partly due to stigma and prejudicial attitudes toward the diagnosis ( 7 ). Additionally, terminology varies internationally; historically, ICD-based systems including those used in the United Kingdom and Europe, traditionally use Emotionally Unstable Personality Disorder ( 8 ), while more recent diagnostic frameworks, ICD-11 and the DSM-5 Alternative Model for Personality Disorders, adopt dimensional models ( 1 , 9 ). Most economic studies rely on the categorical BPD construct, and this review uses the term BPD for consistency with the evidence base. BPD poses a significant economic burden to the healthcare sector and society, in terms of direct and indirect costs ( 10 ). BPD is associated with substantial societal costs of €31,130 per person annually ( 11 ), reflecting both intensive service use and substantial productivity losses ( 12 ). These costs are substantially higher than those observed for other mental disorders (e.g. depression and alcohol dependence are associated with estimated costs of €7,139 and €1,110 annually per person respectively ( 13 , 14 )). People with BPD are disproportionately high service users, in comparison to those without BPD, with elevated rates of emergency presentations, repeated inpatient admissions, crisis-team involvement that concentrate spending in acute services ( 15 ). A ten-year prospective follow-up of the McLean Study of Adult Development cohort for those with BPD found sustained outpatient treatment use with more intermittent inpatient reliance, and although many individuals with BPD discontinued psychotherapy or medication at least once, most later resumed treatment, underscoring the fluctuating pattern of service use ( 16 ). In relation to indirect costs, individuals with BPD experience markedly disrupted work trajectories, spending a smaller proportion of adulthood in employment and facing far higher rates of job loss than their non-BPD peers, thereby driving significant productivity losses ( 17 ). The considerable economic burden of BPD, together with its detrimental effects on quality of life ( 18 , 19 ), emphasizes the urgent need for interventions that are not only effective in terms of leading to clinical benefits, such as improving functioning, reducing symptom severity and lowering self-harm and crisis use ( 20 , 21 ), but also have good value for money, representing efficient use of limited healthcare resources. However, current economic evidence on BPD is limited. Meuldijk et al. ( 22 ) conducted a systematic review of cost-evaluations for BPD interventions and results suggest that effective treatment is likely to be cost-effective, with potential reductions in healthcare and community service use. However, the review highlighted substantial methodological limitations, including heterogeneity in cost definitions and measurement, variation in study design and quality, and limited generalizability across healthcare systems, all of which restrict comparability and warrant caution in interpretation. Meuldijk et al. ( 22 ) noted that the number of economic evaluations remains small relative to the wider clinical literature on personality disorders. As their review included studies published only up to 2015, a critical review is needed as more recent psychological interventions, updated economic analyses, and advances in methodological approaches were not captured. Although previous literature highlights the large societal burden associated with BPD, key gaps remain in understanding the main direct and indirect cost drivers, and important components, such as informal care and criminal justice involvement are consistently excluded in cost calculations. To our knowledge, no comprehensive critical review currently synthesizes these costs and as a result, important questions remain unresolved, including which factors account for the largest proportion of costs and whether key components are systematically captured. Overall, an up-to-date critical review is essential to critically synthesize literature on the main direct and indirect cost drivers for BPD and evaluate newer evidence on the cost-effectiveness of interventions for BPD. A critical review is particularly valuable in the context of BPD because the existing economic literature is fragmented, and methodologically heterogeneous in how costs and outcomes are measured and interpreted. Such an approach enables a deeper examination and critique of how economic evidence has been generated for BPD ( 23 ), it highlights gaps that have limited the field’s development, and clarifies where future research and resource allocation should be directed, functions that extend beyond the scope of a standard systematic review ( 24 ). Therefore, this critical review aims to critically evaluate: 1) the direct and indirect costs of BPD and 2) the economic evidence of interventions for BPD, including findings from full and partial economic evaluations. 2 Methods This critical review adopted a systematic approach to identifying and gathering extant literature, which followed three stages: planning and searching, selection and data extraction, and evaluation. In line with the aims of this critical review, we explicitly defined our scope by focusing on studies involving individuals with BPD, examining direct and indirect costs, and evaluating economic evidence on interventions. 2.1 Planning and searching Within the study team, specialists in health economics and mental health identified key themes to explore the aims of the research: to explore and critically evaluate 1) the costs of BPD, and 2) economic evaluation evidence of interventions for BPD. Guided by the study aims, key themes were translated into search strings, incorporating terms related to BPD and health economics. These were applied across relevant databases using predefined SIGN economic evaluation filters ( 25 ). The final search terms ( Table 1 ) and the databases, capturing health economic and mental health research, were agreed upon between the study team and the university librarian. These included PsycINFO, PubMed and SCOPUS. Search strings were adapted to align with the indexing structures of each database for the keywords targeted (see Supplementary Table 1 for full search strings). After entering the search strings into each database, the searches yielded a total of 439 papers. After removing 129 duplicates, 310 papers were identified for further screening. 2.2 Selection and data extraction In line with the eligibility criteria, studies were included in the critical review if they featured: individuals with BPD or features of BPD (including any age category), within any geographic location, indirect and direct costs of BPD and/or economic evaluations (partial and full) of interventions (including any mental health intervention for BPD and any comparison group), and if they were published in English or had an English translation. Due to the limited research available in this area, we did not apply an exclusion criterion based on the year of publication. Studies which examined several personality disorders, including BPD, were included, due to the lack of studies solely investigating BPD. Literature was excluded if: it did not relate to BPD and health economics, if it only mentioned one key concept (for example, only BPD without the association with health economics) and did not have any costs or rates of utilization (such as intervention costs, hospitalization or medication fees). Any articles which were not retrievable were excluded as the researchers were unable to screen the papers (see Supplementary Table 2 for a summary of literature included in the review). Literature identified from the initial search on the databases was uploaded and screened through Rayyan ( 46 ). Once duplicates were removed, articles were screened in two phases. First, the primary researcher (MG) manually screened titles, keywords and abstracts. This first phase focused on identifying the key themes in the articles, an aspect of costing or an economic evaluation of an intervention, and whether the eligibility criteria were met. For the second phase of screening after studies had satisfied the initial screening process, MG performed a full text screen to investigate the applicability of the articles to the critical review’s aims. Queries regarding inclusion/exclusion were discussed and agreed upon with the other authors. 2.3 Evaluation Through searching the strings across three different databases, 439 articles were highlighted for screening. Papers were excluded if they did not meet the study’s inclusion criteria and if there were duplicates. After the first screening phase (abstract, title, and keyword screening against the inclusion criteria), 58 papers remained. Following the second phase of screening (full-text screening with the inclusion criteria applied) 23 papers remained ( Figure 1 ). A data extraction table was employed to record detailed notes on the remaining 23 papers. This included the study design, aims, key themes, the indirect and direct costs of BPD, the costs of interventions, cost savings, and strengths and limitations of the study. 2.4 Patient and public engagement Patients and members of the public were not involved in the design, analysis, or dissemination of this research and therefore consent was not obtained. 3 Results Based on the 23 studies that remained after screening had taken place, 10 studies discussed the direct and/or indirect costs of BPD from a societal perspective, while 10 studies explored economic evaluations of different BPD treatments in comparison to treatment as usual (TAU) or costs pre-treatment, and three studies discussed both aims. Characteristics of the studies can be found in the Supplementary Table 3 , which details additional information about the studies included in this review, including the design, geographic location of the studies and a summary of the key findings from all studies included in this critical review. 3.1 Costs associated with Borderline Personality Disorder To answer the first research question, costs were considered specifically through: 1) direct costs associated with BPD within the healthcare system, and 2) indirect costs not directly associated with treatment for BPD. Hastrup et al. ( 20 ) highlighted high total costs for individuals after a diagnosis of BPD in Denmark (€40,411), amounting to 16 times higher than individuals without a diagnosis (€2,440). Indirect costs amounted to 60% of the total for individuals with BPD (€23,184), specifically for public transfer costs, such as sick pay and unemployment benefits. For individuals with BPD, annual healthcare costs were €16,728, with approximately half attributable to mental health care; this was higher compared to those without BPD (€2,288). Compared to individuals without BPD, health care costs increased at the time of a diagnosis, compared to three years prior to a diagnosis and gradually declined over five years after a diagnosis. This surge in expenses was primarily due to psychiatric in-patient admissions and somatic care costs. Notably, psychiatric in-patient care accounted for half of all health care costs prior to a diagnosis of BPD, making it the most significant single cost category among individuals before a diagnosis of BPD. High combined direct and indirect costs were also highlighted by other literature ( 21 , 34 ); for example, a German cost-of-illness study reported mean annual costs of €31,130 per person with BPD ( 11 ), with 49.2% attributable to medical costs, 5.5% to direct non-medical costs, and 45.3% (€14,086) to indirect costs. Costs for BPD exceeded those for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD). A German study reported mean annual costs of €4,636 vs €2,020 one year before diagnosis, €7,478 vs €3,638 one year after, and €11,817 vs €6,058 two years after diagnosis, respectively ( 28 ). title: Long-term effectiveness of transdiagnostic cognitive-behavioural therapy for anxiety and depression in primary care: the PsicAP-CV trial
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Anxiety disorders and depression represent a global public health challenge due to their high prevalence, severely impacting quality of life (QoL) and functioning, and imposing a massive economic burden on public systems. This study evaluates the effectiveness of a group transdiagnostic cognitive behavioural therapy (TD-CBT) protocol through a stepped wedge cluster randomised controlled trial (SW-CRT) in Spanish primary care (PC).

METHODS: The sample consisted of 316 PC patients (73.4% female; mean age=44 years) with mild-to-moderate symptoms of anxiety and depression. An immediate intervention group was compared with a delayed intervention group (three months on a waiting list). Patients were assessed at pre-treatment, post-treatment, and 3- and 9-month follow-ups using mixed linear models.

RESULTS: Results revealed significant reductions in anxiety and depression symptoms with large effect sizes (d > 1.2) that remained stable up to 9 months. Improvements in QoL and functioning were heterogeneous, showing sustained long-term gains in work and family domains, but not in broader QoL or social functioning. No significant differences were found in clinical efficacy between groups, with solid reliable recovery rates (∼50%) and minimal deterioration. However, delayed access to treatment significantly increased long-term dropout rates (64.2% in the delayed group vs. 44.0% in the immediate group at 9 months).

CONCLUSIONS: In conclusion, group TD-CBT is an effective and safe intervention offering robust functional and symptomatic recovery. Crucially, while delayed treatment does not reduce clinical efficacy for completers, immediate access is essential to maximize patient retention and optimize resources in the public system.

title: Dynamic change patterns in suicidal ideation differ in Brief Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (BCBT) and Present-Centered Therapy (PCT)
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Although Brief Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (BCBT) is more effective than Present-Centered Therapy (PCT) for preventing suicide attempts, the two treatments have similar efficacy for reducing suicidal ideation severity. Traditional severity scores may obscure meaningful differences in how specific dimensions of suicidal ideation actually change during treatment. This study examined how quickly and consistently different dimensions of suicidal ideation changed during BCBT and PCT.

METHOD: The first five items of the Scale for Suicidal Ideation (wish to live, wish to die, reasons for living versus dying, suicidal desire, and passive desire for death) were administered at every scheduled therapy session during a randomized clinical trial comparing BCBT to PCT among high-risk U.S. military personnel and veterans. We estimated separate continuous-time multivariate change models for each item and applied eigen-decomposition to the matrix of regression coefficients to characterize dominant change patterns.

RESULTS: In both treatments, some dimensions of suicidal ideation changed quickly while others changed slowly, and change was not evenly distributed across all five dimensions. Dimensions of suicidal ideation changed faster and in greater synchrony during BCBT than PCT.

CONCLUSIONS: Suicidal ideation reductions may arise through qualitatively different change processes across treatments even when the overall magnitude of change is similar. BCBT appeared to produce faster, more coordinated change across dimensions of suicidal ideation whereas PCT produced slower change that was less consistent across dimensions. These findings highlight the value of dynamical systems approaches for understanding mechanisms of therapeutic change that go beyond mean-level severity scores.

title: The effects of induced yearning on attentional breadth of bereaved individuals: A cross-cultural study between China and Switzerland
abstract: Bereaved individuals may experience persistent yearning for the deceased, marked by intense desire, mixed feelings, and recurring mental images of their loved one. Although the Attentional Scope Model links repetitive thinking to attentional breadth (i.e., the range of contextual information attended to at a given moment), how yearning influences attentional breadth across cultures remains unclear. We examined whether induced yearning would alter attentional breadth, whether this pattern differed for self- and other-related information, and whether these effects varied across cultural contexts and levels of grief-related vulnerability. In an online experiment, 398 bereaved adults from China (n = 236) and Switzerland (n = 162) completed baseline questionnaires and were randomly assigned to a loss-focused yearning condition or a separation-focused control condition in a yearning induction task. They then completed an attentional breadth task requiring them to detect targets presented either close to or far from a central self- or other-related word. More accurate detection of distant targets indicated broader attention. Results showed that attentional breadth differed by the interaction among cultural context, induction condition, word type, and target distance. Among Chinese participants in the yearning condition, higher trait yearning was associated with relatively broader attention around self-related than other-related information. In contrast, greater PGD symptom severity was associated with stronger attentional narrowing across cultures, but only in the control condition. These findings suggest that the effects of induced yearning on attentional breadth are context dependent. They offer insights into the underlying attentional processes involved and may inform culturally responsive interventions.

title: Infant hippocampal and amygdala volume in an observational follow-up from a randomized clinical trial for maternal prenatal depression
abstract: Prenatal maternal depression may have intergenerational effects on offspring brain development, with potential socioemotional consequences. This observational follow-up study examines brain development and subsequent negative emotionality among 109 infants born to mothers participating in a randomized clinical trial (NCT03011801). In the prior trial, brief interpersonal psychotherapy significantly reduced prenatal depression symptoms and disorder as the published primary and secondary endpoints. Exploratory infant outcomes include hippocampal and amygdala volumes at 6 weeks and negative emotionality at 6 months. Here we show that infants of mothers randomized to interpersonal psychotherapy during pregnancy have lower right hippocampal volume than infants of mothers in the enhanced usual care group (p = .002, d = 0.62). No statistically significant group differences are observed in left hippocampal or amygdala volume. Smaller hippocampal volume predicts subsequent lower negative emotionality (r = 0.19, p = 0.045). In this study, a maternal prenatal depression intervention is associated with differences in infant brain development with implications for their subsequent emotional health.

title: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy as a Psychological Intervention for Primary Caregivers of Patients With Decompensated Cirrhosis: A Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract:
AIM: This study aimed to evaluate the effects of Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, relative to usual care, on psychological flexibility, resilience, caregiving burden, anxiety and depression in primary caregivers of patients with decompensated cirrhosis.

BACKGROUND: Primary caregivers of decompensated cirrhosis patients face high rates of anxiety and depression due to long-term caregiving stress, financial burdens and disease uncertainty. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy improves mental health in other chronic disease caregivers, but its effects on cirrhosis caregivers in China remain unstudied.

DESIGN: This was a randomized, assessor-blinded, parallel-group trial comparing Acceptance and Commitment Therapy-enhanced care with routine care alone in primary caregivers during hospitalization.

METHOD: A total of 120 caregivers were recruited at a Chinese hospital (January-April 2023) and randomly allocated to control (routine care) or intervention (routine care plus six-session Acceptance and Commitment Therapy) groups. Validated scales assessed psychological flexibility, resilience, burden, anxiety and depression at admission, discharge and 1 month postdischarge. Data were analysed using chi-square tests, independent t-tests for baseline comparisons and repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests for pairwise comparisons.

RESULTS: Compared to controls, the intervention group showed significantly lower scores in caregiving burden, anxiety, depression and psychological rigidity, alongside higher psychological resilience at discharge and 1-month follow-up. No adverse events were recorded in either group.

CONCLUSION: In this single-centre trial, Acceptance and Commitment Therapy reduced psychological rigidity and caregiving burden and improved psychological resilience. Its emphasis on accepting uncontrollable realities and acting on personal values may be well suited to the volatile context of cirrhosis caregiving, but multicentre trials with longer follow-up are needed before wider implementation.
