title: Artists Can Design Memory, and AI Can Predict It
abstract: Can artists deliberately design artworks to be remembered-or forgotten? Across three experiments, we tested whether visual-memory outcomes can be shaped through artistic design and how they are predicted by artists, laypeople, and artificial intelligence. We launched a nationwide art contest in which artists submitted works intended to be memorable or forgettable. Using recognition tasks with adults based in the United States (119 from Amazon Mechanical Turk, 892 from Prolific, and 62 visitors from a Chicago gallery), we found that artists achieved their intended memory outcomes. However, their success was asymmetric: Memorability was more readily increased than reduced. A neural network, ResMem, consistently outperformed human observers and artists in predicting which artworks would be remembered. Data-driven analyses identified psychologically interpretable features that explained nearly half the variance in memory and aligned with ResMem's predictions, but not with human judgments. Together, findings suggest that visual memorability can be engineered by humans, though asymmetrically, and is better captured by computational models.

title: Does Global Slowing Explain Age Effects in Inhibitory Control?
abstract: A long-standing debate in the study of cognitive aging centers around the issue of whether aging results in a selective deficit in inhibitory control beyond general slowing of cognitive processing. Previous studies have obtained mixed findings, in part because the typical free-response-time paradigm lacks the specificity required to disentangle component processes underlying inhibitory control. Here, we apply a forced-response paradigm and computational model to test whether aging results in overall speed differences or a selective deficit in inhibitory control. Across two experiments, over 200 older adults and younger adults completed a forced-response arrow-flanker task. We found strong evidence that older adults demonstrate a global slowing of processing without any selective deficit in inhibitory control in this task. Furthermore, we demonstrate that global slowing is sufficient to explain the mixed findings in previous free-response-time studies. Overall, these results argue against a selective inhibitory-control deficit in older adults.

title: Naturally disengaging control to reveal habits
abstract:
Habits are an essential part of everyday decision-making, yet the mechanisms underlying human habit formation and expression are difficult to study in laboratory settings, where participants typically engage strong goal-directed (GD) control that can mask habitual tendencies. Recent approaches have successfully elicited habits in long experiments by limiting the amount of GD control participants can exert (e.g., through forced response times). We extend this approach by designing a short behavioral paradigm that aims to induce and reveal habits without extrinsically limiting GD control, instead incorporating task features that we hypothesized would encourage participants to spontaneously relax GD control: a hierarchical multi-step trial structure, opportunities for self-correction, and frequent switches between extensively and minimally practiced behaviors. Across seven experiments, we demonstrate that this approach induces habitual control in a relatively brief paradigm. Specifically, overtraining increases slips of action toward the extensively-practiced context and reduces slips toward the minimally-practiced one, indicating behavioral inflexibility at early response times, while slower responses remain dominated by GD control. Systematic manipulation of task features across experiments revealed that allowing multiple response attempts was particularly important for reliably observing this overtraining effect; a hierarchical trial structure may further facilitate habit expression, though this remains inconclusive. More broadly, our paradigm provides a practical tool for investigating how habits form and interact with goal-directed control.

Introduction A habit is a stable pattern of behavior that has become routine and effortless, even automatic and difficult to change, through repetition ( Du et al., 2022 ). Habits are highly consequential: a considerable portion of our day-to-day behaviors are habitual ( Wood et al., 2002 ), and when adaptive, habitual control can be effective and efficient, limiting the need for costly cognitive control and freeing up cognitive resources. Conversely, because they are highly automatized, habits can also be associated with behavioral inflexibility and maladaptive decisions, and are thought to play a role in multiple psychiatric disorders, such as obsessive-compulsive disorder ( Gillan et al., 2011 ), addiction ( Everitt & Robbins, 2016 ), and anorexia nervosa ( Uniacke et al., 2018 ). Habits become evident in scenarios where they conflict with one’s current goals, yet are carried out nonetheless due to repetition-induced automaticity. As such, habits are typically characterized in contrast to goal-directed (GD) behavior, which is guided by explicit representations of action–outcome contingencies and current goals ( Balleine & Dickinson, 1998 ; Dickinson, 1985 ; Dickinson & Balleine, 1995 ). Studies using outcome devaluation and related paradigms in rodents have shown that a behavior that, early in learning, is directed toward achieving a particular outcome gradually comes to be performed automatically, even when the environment changes such that the behavior no longer reliably results in the desired outcome ( Adams, 1982 ; Dickinson, 1985 ; Dickinson & Balleine, 1995 ; Killcross & Coutureau, 2003 ). These paradigms have been combined with lesion studies to demonstrate that habitual and GD processes rely on partly dissociable neural networks: GD learning can be disrupted while leaving habit formation intact by damaging certain brain areas such as the dorsomedial striatum, and vice versa by damaging other brain areas such as the dorsolateral striatum( Balleine & Dickinson, 1998 ; Killcross & Coutureau, 2003 ; Lingawi et al., 2016 ; Yin et al., 2004 , 2005 ). The success of these classic approaches in explicating different forms of behavioral control in non-human animals has inspired efforts to translate them to humans. These efforts have met with mixed success ( de Wit et al., 2018 ; Gera et al., 2023 ; Pool et al., 2022 ; Tricomi et al., 2009 ), suggesting that existing experimental designs may be inadequate for reliably inducing and/or revealing habits in humans. In general, tasks developed to study habits in humans often fail to exhibit what is widely considered a key marker of habits: sensitivity to overtraining. That is, increased inflexibility with extended practice is considered critical for establishing that inflexible behavior reflects gradually-formed habits rather than weak GD control ( de Wit et al., 2018 ; Gera et al., 2023 ; Pool et al., 2022 ; Watson et al., 2022 ). Furthermore, putative markers of habitual behavior on these tasks tend to correlate with individual measures related to GD control, rather than with other measures purported to assess habitual tendencies. For example, devaluation sensitivity on habit tasks correlates with indices of model-based (but not model-free) control derived from sequential decision-making tasks ( Friedel et al., 2014 ; Gillan et al., 2015 ; Sjoerds et al., 2016 ), and performance in a lab-based slips-of-action task correlates with self-reported attentional control but not with self-reported slips of action (errors where a well-practiced action is executed despite being inappropriate) in a real-world slips-of-action task ( Linnebank et al., 2018 ). Finally, a recent comprehensive validation study found poor convergent validity across commonly used habit tasks, and no significant correlations between task-derived measures and self-reported real-life habits ( Nebe et al., 2024 ). Together, these findings suggest that many existing task paradigms are more sensitive to individual differences in GD control processes than to processes supporting habit formation or habitual control. Thus, the challenge in demonstrating habit formation in human laboratory tasks may lie partly in finding ways to reduce GD control so as to allow habits to emerge ( Buabang et al., 2024 ). Consistent with this view, one study found that over the course of training over multiple days, participants’ overt responses become no more devaluation-insensitive, but that their responses to devalued stimuli become slower, suggesting that habitual impulses are present in overtrained participants but can be suppressed with deliberate GD control ( Luque et al., 2020 ). Other work has shown that acute stress amplifies devaluation-insensitive responding in humans ( Schwabe & Wolf, 2009 , 2010 ), and another study successfully demonstrated overtraining-induced habits in humans using a forced response time paradigm ( Hardwick et al., 2019 ). Revealing habits by extrinsically limiting the amount of GD control participants can exert has ecological relevance: people are especially prone to performing unwanted habits when they are distracted, fatigued, or pressed for time. However, in naturalistic settings, habits also often emerge without such constraints, when GD control momentarily lapses, allowing habits to slip through. For instance, one might habitually turn left at a familiar intersection as when driving to work, despite intending to turn right toward the doctor’s office; the familiarity of the route reduces vigilance, allowing attention to wander at the critical moment. Such lapses reflect a momentary failure to engage control, not an inability to do so due to a time limit or acute stress. To investigate how habits influence behavior under these conditions, we developed a new, shorter paradigm that extends Hardwick et al. (2019) , incorporating features we hypothesized would create opportunities for GD control to spontaneously lapse without preventing participants from engaging it when they choose to. First, we embedded choices into a hierarchical multi-step trial structure, spreading out each trial over three dependent decision-making steps. We drew inspiration from research on chunked action sequences, which share both behavioral features—such as increased speed, consistency, and inflexibility with training ( Dezfouli et al., 2014 ; Dickinson & Balleine, 1995 ; Ostlund et al., 2009 )—and neural substrates ( Jin & Costa, 2010 ; Smith & Graybiel, 2013 ; Thorn et al., 2010 ) with habits. This design also draws on theoretical frameworks from hierarchical reinforcement learning, which propose that complex behaviors can be organized as temporally extended sub-policies or “options” that, once initiated, may be executed with reduced step-by-step deliberation ( Botvinick et al., 2009 ). In our task, context information is only visible in the first stage of each trial and must be held in mind to guide the correct response in the final stage. We hypothesized that this structure would 1) tax GD control by requiring participants to maintain context in working memory across intermediate steps, and 2) facilitate the emergence of habitual behavior by creating temporal distance between context encoding and the critical response, increasing opportunities for habitual impulses to intrude. We reasoned that this added complexity would make it less trivial for human participants to override habitual impulses with GD control. Second, we included both extensively practiced and minimally practiced contexts when testing for habits, forcing participants to switch between a putatively habitized behavior and a behavior requiring GD control. Previous research has shown evidence that this may help in revealing habits ( Luque et al., 2020 ). We hypothesized that requiring participants to flexibly switch between overtrained and moderately-trained contexts would 1) challenge the GD system, allowing habitual control to emerge more readily, and 2) provide a more sensitive measure of habit strength by combining evidence of inflexibility in novel contexts with evidence of entrenchment in familiar contexts. Third, we allowed participants to self-correct their responses, motivated by evidence that habitual and GD control are partly separate processes that follow distinct temporal dynamics, as demonstrated by Hardwick et al. (2019) . In their study, Hardwick et al. (2019) first trained participants on stimulus-response associations, then altered a subset of these mappings (contingency reversal), and finally assessed responding under the modified contingencies in the absence of feedback (extinction test) at controlled time delays. They showed that overtrained participants exhibited more slips of action (responses consistent with the original, no-longer-valid S-R mapping). Specifically, they observed a higher rate of slips of action in the 4-day relative to the minimal practice condition, with the effect being strongest at short time delays, just after minimum stimulus processing time. We reasoned that allowing multiple opportunities to respond would 1) lower the stakes of responding and thus reduce participants’ response inhibition ( Leng et al., 2025 ), allowing us to observe slips of action in their early responses without artificially constraining their response times, and 2) enable us to assess habit strength separately from the strength of GD control which would dominate choices at later response times. Together, these design features aim to encourage the natural relaxation of GD control. In other words, they create conditions in which GD control may spontaneously lapse—through working memory demands, competition between differentially practiced behaviors, and reduced response inhibition—without explicitly limiting deliberation through time pressure, concurrent cognitive load, or acute stress. Building on Hardwick et al. (2019) , we operationalized habits based on a contingency reversal (where the correct actions for a subset of stimuli are changed following initial learning), characterizing behavioral inflexibility in terms of slips of action arising from previously learned S-R associations. We extended the protocol by using a hierarchical trial structure, including both pre-reversal (original contingencies) and post-reversal (modified contingencies) contexts in the test phase, and allowing for multiple responses to test phase trials. Using our novel paradigm, we successfully detected an effect of overtraining such that extended practice amplified habitual control, as evidenced by decreases in slips of action in the pre-reversal context and increases in slips of action in the post-reversal context; further, we verified that the task features we added contributed to this effect. Importantly, we revealed in-lab habit formation within a few hundred iterations with a task duration of less than one hour, making this paradigm both practical and in line with the dynamics of real-life habit formation ( Buyalskaya et al., 2023 ; Lally et al., 2010 ). Our experiment reveals habits after a relatively short training procedure, providing a valuable tool for advancing our understanding of the mechanisms underlying habit formation and expression in the wild. We present a series of seven experiments testing this paradigm. Experiments 1a and 1b establish and replicate the core finding that overtraining increases habitual responding at early response times. Experiments 2a – 2d systematically manipulate task features to identify which elements are critical for revealing habits. Experiment 3 tests whether the overtraining effect can be observed within participants across different training durations. General Method We administered seven versions of a behavioral task designed to induce and reveal habit formation, with total task duration ranging from approximately 30 to 60 minutes depending on task version and training group (see Table A1 for a detailed breakdown of durations by experiment). All experiments shared the same core task structure (described below); Experiments 1a – 1b established and replicated the basic paradigm, Experiments 2a – 2d tested variants with specific task features removed or modified, and Experiment 3 used a within-participant design ( Table 1 ). A short (approximately 5 minutes long) demonstration of Experiment 1b is available at https://sarahoh.github.io/habitTask_demo/exp.html . (2019) ; we introduced additional novel features in an attempt to encourage natural disengagement of GD control (see Introduction ). Some experiments included variations on the core task design; these are detailed in each experiment’s Method section. Stimulus-Response Mappings (Contexts). Each context defined a complete set of associations between six avatar positions on a simple cross-shaped maze (S1–S6, corresponding to outside the maze, the center, and the top, right, bottom, and left arms) and six key press actions (A1–A6). title: From stigma to trust: A paradigm shift for understanding perceptions of individuals with bipolar disorder
abstract: Individuals with bipolar disorder (BD) face professional and personal challenges such as underemployment. Navigating these challenges involves the dilemma of whether to disclose their illness or conceal it and risk presenting symptoms. Examinations of these challenges are often anchored in stigma, which has attributed negative employment outcomes for individuals with BD to adverse reactions from managers following disclosure. Across three experiments, including a managerial sample and a novel chatbot interaction, and eight supplemental studies (N = 8,112), the present research proposes and tests a trust-based attributional model. Mania, the hallmark symptom of BD, signals activation-based unpredictability, which serially erodes the perceived trustworthiness of an employee, ultimately compromising a manager's trust and willingness to retain the employee. The current findings demonstrate that disclosure is not uniformly harmful and that stigma operates as a distal moderator. An employee disclosing in the absence of mania can appear less predictable, and managers high in preexisting stigma toward BD generally view employees as less predictable. However, when manic symptoms are visible, disclosure buffers against their negative impact by providing an explanation for the erratic behavior. Together, this research reveals that moving beyond stigma-centric accounts clarifies managerial perceptions of employees with BD, with disclosure and stigma shaping this trust-based process. title: "A girl is the champion!": Well-intentioned gendered messages can backfire
abstract: Initiatives aimed at promoting gender equity in majority-male domains often emphasize gender to highlight women's achievements (e.g., "Space4Women," "all-women spacewalk"). Does such gendered messaging help achieve equity goals? Two theoretical accounts offer competing predictions. An informational account suggests that referencing a gender alongside a domain should strengthen beliefs that the referenced gender participates and succeeds. A pragmatic account, however, predicts that explicitly marking gender may backfire by signaling that the referenced gender is atypical in the domain-otherwise, why mention it? We tested these two possibilities with U.S. children (ages 4-10; N = 326) and adults (N = 788). Participants learned about fictional activities described with either gendered messaging (e.g., "A girl/boy is the Gazzer champion") or control messaging (e.g., "Joan/Rob is the Gazzer champion"). Gendered messaging backfired compared to control messaging on average, causing participants to infer lower participation by the referenced gender and, among adults, lower ability. Gendered messaging also undermined participants' interest in the activities. A meta-analysis across experiments revealed small-to-moderate effects that were larger for adults than children, consistent with developmental changes in pragmatic reasoning. Finally, backfire effects disappeared for messaging about fictional groups, suggesting that background knowledge about the referenced group may be needed to trigger pragmatic inferences. Together, these findings advance theoretical accounts of pragmatic reasoning while indicating that well-intentioned gendered messaging may paradoxically undermine equity goals. A more effective alternative may be to clearly feature women in a domain without explicitly framing it as being "for them."

title: Individual differences in motor and auditory activation in second language speech learning: Roles of domain-general auditory processing
abstract: While existing models emphasize the critical roles of auditory and motor systems in speech perception, it remains unclear how individual learners differentially rely on these systems and how their relative weighting relates to language learning. This study investigates the neural mechanisms through which individual differences in domain-general auditory processing influence reliance on these networks during second language (L2) phonetic learning. Focusing on the acquisition of English [æ] and [ʌ] by 207 Japanese learners, we examined participants with varying auditory precision profiles using both behavioral and functional magnetic resonance imaging analyses as they performed discrimination tasks for speech and nonverbal sounds. The findings revealed a pattern consistent with a triangular relationship among learners' auditory precision, brain activation in motor-related regions, and L2 speech development. Learners with lower auditory precision tended to show less advanced L2 vowel proficiency and exhibited higher levels of sensorimotor activation during discrimination of English [æ] and [ʌ], but not during discrimination of nonspeech counterparts with comparable second formant variation. In light of theoretical accounts of adult L2 speech learning (Best & Tyler, 2007), one possible interpretation is that greater reliance on articulatory processing among less auditory-precise and less experienced or proficient L2 learners reflects the processing of L2 sounds through first language articulatory routines. In contrast, learners with higher auditory precision attained not only more advanced L2 vowel proficiency but also lower levels of sensorimotor activity, comparable to that observed during nonverbal processing, suggesting more balanced spectrotemporal and articulatory analyses of sounds, which optimize both the process and outcomes of L2 speech learning. title: Idea generation during emotion regulation: A proposed framework
abstract: The field of emotion regulation (ER) is increasingly recognizing the influence of context on an individual's regulatory processes, prompting researchers to examine how specific circumstances dynamically shape ER. Well-accepted theoretical models and supporting empirical studies frame such situation-specific ER as a sequence of stages involving decision points: choosing to regulate, selecting a strategy, deciding whether to maintain current regulatory efforts, and so forth. These frameworks, however, omit an underappreciated process that we argue underscores ER at its highest specificity: idea generation. In other words, individuals do not just select properties of their regulatory attempt, but must actually generate an attempt-a distinction that leverages an underexplored level of analysis in ER known as techniques. In this article, we integrate multiple theoretical perspectives across domains to demonstrate the feasibility in (and insight afforded by) measuring idea generation in ER. Next, we review how existing empirical paradigms already utilize generation-related principles in largely unacknowledged manners, with some studies that have specifically targeted these generative operations during ER. We combine these observations into a novel framework called Emotion Regulation Generation of Techniques, which serves to deepen the study of ER by delineating a generation stage that follows and informs selection mechanisms. To help study idea generation in practice, this framework is equipped with methodological protocols that draw from neighboring domains (e.g., divergent thinking), paired with future directions and testable hypotheses that can inform the role of idea generation in healthy regulation and in dysregulated affective disorders. title: Near-random behavior in strategic games
abstract: Humans struggle to produce random behavior when asked to do so, leading some to suggest that our ability to randomize is attenuated (or even absent). Here, we demonstrate that the capacity for random behavior is much greater than previously acknowledged: Humans can behave in (near) optimally random ways when the context demands it. We created a custom, online version of the game Battleship in which participants competed against one another. On each turn, one player chose a tile on a 3 × 3 grid to place a ship, while the other player tried to guess the ship's location. Across six preregistered studies, this strategic context led to dramatic increases in random behavior relative to closely matched non-strategic tasks. Such random behavior was also remarkably flexible and optimal depending on context; both players readily incorporated varying information about the game (e.g., that tiles can differ in value) while simultaneously accounting for their opponents' knowledge of that information. A computational model validated these findings and revealed nuanced differences across contexts. Contrary to decades of work finding that humans fail to randomize, we find that strategic games promote highly flexible, near-random behavior.

title: Dissociating accuracy and metacognition in nutritional judgements
abstract: The gap between nutritional knowledge and dietary behaviour remains poorly understood, yet may partly reflect systematic biases in how individuals evaluate food and assess their own nutritional judgements. Here, we introduce the MetaBites task, a novel two-alternative forced-choice paradigm assessing nutritional judgements under adaptive difficulty control. Thirty-two healthy volunteers compared foods on either caloric density or nutritional quality, the latter quantified using the Nutrient-Rich Foods (NRF) 9.3 index. Participants provided trial-level, block-level, and task-level confidence ratings, enabling assessment of metacognitive monitoring across multiple levels. The task showed adequate validity, supported by staircase convergence, a clear speed-accuracy trade-off, and higher confidence on correct relative to incorrect trials. Results revealed a dissociation across conditions: participants showed higher objective performance when judging nutritional quality, yet reported significantly higher confidence for calorie judgements, and task-level global confidence decreased significantly in the NRF condition but remained stable for calorie judgements. Metacognitive efficiency did not differ between conditions. Familiarity with food items was associated with choice behaviour in opposing directions across conditions, consistent with a tendency to perceive familiar foods as more nutritious and less calorie-dense. Liking rather than familiarity was associated with higher trial-level confidence. Together, these findings show that objective performance and subjective confidence can dissociate in nutritional judgements, with distinct heuristic cues shaping choice and confidence. The MetaBites task offers a promising tool for investigating metacognitive contributions to nutritional decision-making in both healthy and clinical populations.

title: Diversity in how people use racial categories to generalize
abstract: Generic statements, such as "Black people are strong", can imply that there are racial essences. But what about generic statements like "Black people face barriers to career advancement"? Statements like these may instead imply the existence of systemic racism. In three empirical studies, we examined the beliefs and attitudes held by Black (N = 387) and White (N = 400) American participants who endorse generic statements, controlling for endorsement of non-generic statements about the same events. For both Black and White Americans, generic statements about ability and character predicted a belief in racial essences (and endorsing the racial hierarchy), whereas generic statements about experiences and outcomes in social institutions predicted a belief in systemic racism (and rejecting the racial hierarchy). Thus, there is diversity in how and why people use race to generalize, and generic language flexibly accommodates that diversity.

title: The effect of social robot authority on epistemic vigilance in early childhood
abstract: Social robots are increasingly deployed as tutors and learning partners, yet their authority cues may discourage children from questioning or verifying information. We investigated whether robot authority influences Chinese children's epistemic vigilance and which source of authority drives this effect. In Study 1 (N = 128, ages 4 and 6, M age  = 5.39 years, SD = 0.92, 66 girls and 62 boys), robots with high and low overall authority asserted that all aliens in a task had three eyes. Children's verification behaviors were assessed in terms of the number of times they checked the information, the length of time they spent checking, and how much time passed between checks. Results showed that children engaged in significantly less verification in the high-authority condition, and 6-year-olds checked more often than 4-year-olds. Study 2 (N = 200, ages 4 and 6, M age  = 5.19 years, SD = 0.92, 97 girls and 103 boys) built on Study 1 by manipulating two sources of authority: role authority (teacher-like vs. peer-like) and cognitive authority (knowledgeable vs. unknowledgeable). The same task and outcome measures were used as in Study 1. The results showed that cognitive authority significantly decreased children's verification behavior, but there was no significant effect of role authority or child age. Together, these findings suggest that authority cues can shape how much evidence children seek before accepting robot testimony, particularly when the robot is presented as knowledgeable.

title: Children successfully use external cues as a cognitive strategy in an unsolvable memory task but demonstrate limitation
abstract: Cognitive offloading refers to the process of using aids to reduce the cognitive demands of a task. A simple type of offloading-like behavior involves using cues in the environment to later aid in making a correct choice or response when this would otherwise be difficult or even impossible. This project assessed children's ability for spontaneous creation of this type of cognitive strategy use. Children three to nine years old first participated in a task that produced uncertainty surrounding the future location of a preferred toy. Children assigned different toys to four opaque cups, one of which was uniquely colored, before the cups were mixed and re-presented. To guarantee success, children had to place their preferred toy in the uniquely colored cup. Otherwise, they would have to select among three identical cups with no information about where the preferred item was hidden. No instructions were provided initially about where to place items, allowing children to formulate their own approach. Children demonstrated high levels of proficiency. Although age was not a strong indicator of overall performance, older children reached the criterion for proficiency more quickly than younger children. Children also decreased their likelihood of making errors with increased experience. However, subsequent variations of the task showed that preschool age children struggled to set up the game in such a way that an optimal strategy could be implemented. This suggests the possible lack of awareness of why a strategy works to make a task solvable and ensure success at this age.

title: Further predictors of iconicity
abstract: Iconicity refers to a perceived resemblance between the form of a signal and its meaning (e.g., "meow" resembling the sound of a cat). Iconicity has been operationalized by having participants rate words in terms of their iconicity. This has enabled researchers to examine the lexical and semantic properties of words high and low in iconicity, for example finding that iconic words tend to be rich in sensory experience and semantically unique. In the present study I examined a suite of novel predictors that have not been examined in English iconicity. I discovered that while iconic words are low in frequency they are generally well known. They also tend to have more specific meanings, though this was moderated by concreteness and part of speech. Iconic words are also more polysemous and emotional. With one exception, there was no evidence that iconic words were more systematic. Together these results extend previous work, and reinforce the finding that iconicity must be understood through a lens of word use and of words as depictions.

title: Apathy is associated with lower perceptual curiosity
abstract: The hallmark of apathy is diminished goal-directed behaviour, yet its relationship to curiosity - the intrinsic drive to explore novel information - remains untested. Here, we examined whether trait apathy is associated with diminished perceptual curiosity. We presented online observers (N = 381) with images of either familiar, everyday objects; or novel, AI-generated objects, which appeared entirely realistic, but do not in fact exist. Observers used their mouse to interact with each stimulus before rating its familiarity, interest, and appeal, and then completed validated measures of trait apathy and perceptual curiosity. Our data yielded three convergent findings. First, trait apathy was associated with differences in how novel and familiar objects were subjectively rated - specifically, as trait apathy increased, observers rated novel objects as more familiar, and familiar objects as more interesting. Second, trait apathy was associated with changes in objective behaviour, such that, as trait apathy increased, observers spent less time viewing novel objects. Finally, scores on trait measures of apathy and curiosity were negatively correlated, such that those who reported higher levels of trait apathy had lower levels of perceptual curiosity. Emotional apathy in particular had the most consistent relationship across both task-based and trait measures of perceptual curiosity. Together, these findings demonstrate that lower perceptual curiosity is a key feature of the apathetic trait, and propose the existence of a previously unrecognised mechanism that links apathy to reduced engagement with perceptual novelty. These results have broad implications for current frameworks of motivation and curiosity in both healthy individuals and clinical populations.

title: When textures meet: Relational evaluations explain overall pleasantness beyond component pleasantness
abstract: In everyday touch, the hand often contacts multiple surfaces simultaneously. Yet little is known about how pleasantness is formed when texture pairs are explored at the same time. Previous research has shown that tactile signals presented to adjacent fingers can be integrated through averaging or assimilation processes. These accounts primarily address the integration of stimulus attributes and do not consider whether relations between textures may also contribute to evaluative judgments. The present study examined this possibility by obtaining ratings on five relational dimensions (similarity, contrast, harmony, emergence, and modulation) and testing whether these ratings helped explain the overall pleasantness of texture pairs beyond the mean pleasantness of the component textures. Across three experiments, participants evaluated the pleasantness of texture pairs, judged relational qualities between textures, and rated the tactile attributes of individual textures. The results showed that overall pleasantness could not be fully explained by the average pleasantness of the component textures. Instead, ratings on these relational dimensions-particularly similarity and contrast-provided additional explanatory power for overall pleasantness. Together, these findings suggest that the texture combination itself contributes to pleasantness in paired touch beyond the pleasantness of the component textures alone.

title: How social status shapes U.S. children's beliefs about social mobility
abstract: Children grow up within social hierarchies that shape their everyday lives. Social mobility is a core mechanism through which societies either challenge or maintain existing inequalities. The present study examined how U.S. children's social status-both experimentally manipulated and measured at the neighborhood level-shapes their beliefs about social mobility for themselves and their high- and low-status peers. Children (N = 130; 3-8 years; 70 girls, 59 boys, 1 non-binary; 12.3% Asian, 6.9% Black, 11.6% Latine, 20.7% Multiracial, and 48.5% White) were randomly assigned to either experimentally advantaged or disadvantaged groups. They were then assessed on their (1) general expectations about social mobility, (2) effort-contingent expectations for mobility, and (3) post-hoc explanations for upward and downward mobility. We found that compared to experimentally-disadvantaged children, experimentally-advantaged children were more likely to have higher expectations for themselves and high-status peers, but lower expectations for low-status peers. With age, disadvantaged children (experimental and neighborhood) exhibited higher expectations for themselves and lower expectations for high-status peers, whereas advantaged children's expectations remained stable. Older children were more likely to believe working hard leads to upward mobility and attribute upward/downward mobility to individual effort. This tendency was especially pronounced for their own upward (vs. downward) mobility, but less so when evaluating the upward mobility of high-status peers (vs. themselves). These results suggest that children's beliefs about social mobility develop throughout childhood, differ by target, and are shaped by their own social status.

title: Revising expectations in real time: processing speed constrains lexical form prediction in German 8-12 year-olds
abstract: Do children predict the lexical form of upcoming linguistic input as readily as they predict semantic features? We investigated word form prediction using the prenominal mismatch paradigm, which tests whether children experience processing costs when encountering prediction-inconsistent gender-marked articles. We also examined individual differences and whether prenominal mismatch effects reflect revision of an anticipated noun. German-speaking 8-12-year-olds self-paced through sentences that either confirmed or disconfirmed expectations about a predictable noun. In half of the items, a prediction-consistent or -inconsistent gender-marked article served as an early cue signaling whether the upcoming noun would match expectations. At the group level, there was no evidence for a prenominal mismatch effect, suggesting that under time pressure, children do not reliably pre-activate word-form information based on gender. However, processing speed predicted the presence of mismatch effects: Faster child readers showed early predictability costs pre-nominally, whereas slower child readers did not. In addition, in faster children, mismatch effects were associated with reduced integration costs at the unpredictable noun, suggesting that prenominal mismatch effects reflect a revision process, whereby children dampen their expectations for the initially predictable noun. These findings suggest that lexical prediction in middle childhood is not consistently supported in time-compressed settings, and that prenominal mismatch effects reflect the revision of an initially predicted lexical representation.

title: Functional Listening Difficulties in Children With ADHD: Associations With Language Abilities
abstract:
ABSTRACT Objective Listening difficulties are commonly reported in children with attention‐deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and are often interpreted as manifestations of inattention. However, it remains unclear whether functional listening difficulties are related to broader language abilities or whether they differ across ADHD subtypes. The present study examined the association between functional listening difficulties and language abilities in children with ADHD and explored whether these relationships vary between predominantly inattentive and combined subtypes. Methods This cross‐sectional observational study included 125 children diagnosed with ADHD, categorized into predominantly inattentive ( n = 32) and combined ( n = 93) ADHD subtypes. Functional listening was assessed using the Children's Home Inventory for Listening Difficulties (C.H.I.L.D.), with higher scores indicating better functional listening, and language abilities were assessed using the Turkish version of the Test of Early Language Development (TELD‐3:T). Between‐group differences were examined using Mann–Whitney U tests. The primary analysis was a hierarchical linear regression examining the adjusted association between total C.H.I.L.D. score and language performance, controlling for age, gender, and ADHD subtype. A C.H.I.L.D.‐by‐ADHD‐subtype interaction was examined in a secondary analysis. Results There was no statistical evidence of a difference between ADHD subtypes in C.H.I.L.D. or language scores (all p > 0.05). In the adjusted regression, higher total C.H.I.L.D. scores were associated with better language performance ( B = 6.66, β = 0.594, p < 0.001, 95% CI [4.996, 8.315]). Exploratory correlations between total C.H.I.L.D. and language scores were positive in the predominantly inattentive type ( r = 0.72), combined type ( r = 0.56), and total sample ( r = 0.61; all p < 0.001). The C.H.I.L.D.‐by‐ADHD‐subtype interaction was not significant ( B = 0.63, β = 0.031, p = 0.72, 95% CI [−2.919, 4.177]). Conclusions Better functional listening was associated with stronger language performance in children with ADHD. There was no statistical evidence that this association differed between ADHD subtypes. These findings highlight the relevance of considering both functional listening and language performance in the clinical assessment of children with ADHD.

1 Introduction Listening plays a central role in children's everyday communication and learning. Effective listening requires the ability to attend to, process, and interpret spoken information in dynamic real‐world environments. In contrast to laboratory‐based listening comprehension tasks that primarily evaluate linguistic understanding, functional listening refers to how effectively individuals manage auditory information in everyday contexts. Functional listening reflects the interaction of multiple processes, including auditory perception, attentional regulation, executive control, and language processing. In clinical settings, caregiver‐reported listening difficulties are frequently used to capture children's listening performance across real‐world environments such as classrooms, social interactions, and noisy situations. Importantly, functional listening should not be considered equivalent to language ability. While language assessments evaluate linguistic knowledge and processing capacity, functional listening reflects how effectively individuals apply these abilities in everyday auditory environments that place demands on attention and executive control. Attention‐deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent patterns of inattention and/or hyperactivity–impulsivity that interfere with functioning across settings (American Psychiatric Association [APA] 2022 ). Contemporary frameworks conceptualize ADHD as involving alterations in distributed neural systems responsible for executive control and attentional regulation (Faraone and Larsson 2019 ). Neurodevelopmental studies indicate atypical maturation within frontostriatal and frontoparietal networks in individuals with ADHD, including differences in the prefrontal cortex involved in working memory, inhibitory control, and top‐down attentional regulation (Cortese et al. 2012 ; Shaw et al. 2007 ). Consistent with these findings, meta‐analytic research has demonstrated significant impairments in working memory and inhibitory control among children with ADHD (Martinussen et al. 2005 ; Willcutt et al. 2005 ). These executive vulnerabilities may affect a range of cognitively demanding activities, including listening and spoken language processing. Listening comprehension requires the rapid integration of phonological, lexical, and syntactic information while maintaining spoken input in working memory (Baddeley 2003 ; Just and Carpenter 1992 ). Successful listening also depends on attentional control mechanisms that allow individuals to sustain focus on relevant speech while suppressing competing auditory stimuli. Because spoken language unfolds rapidly and cannot be revisited in the same way as written text, efficient coordination between attention, working memory, and linguistic processing is essential for effective comprehension. Difficulties in attentional regulation or executive control may, therefore, interfere with real‐time language processing and lead to challenges in everyday listening situations. These mechanisms are particularly relevant for children with ADHD. Emerging evidence indicates that children with ADHD demonstrate reduced spoken‐word recognition accuracy and slower processing efficiency in challenging listening conditions, such as environments with competing speech (Lemel et al. 2023 ). Neuroimaging studies further suggest atypical connectivity between auditory cortices and frontoparietal executive networks during listening tasks, indicating potential difficulties in coordinating speech perception with top‐down attentional control. Together, these findings suggest that listening difficulties in ADHD may reflect broader interactions between attentional regulation and language processing systems. Despite increasing recognition of these interactions, empirical research examining listening abilities in ADHD remains limited. Many studies have investigated language abilities, academic outcomes, or attentional symptoms separately, making it difficult to determine how listening difficulties relate to broader language functioning in this population. Furthermore, listening outcomes are often measured using tasks that primarily assess linguistic comprehension rather than functional listening performance in real‐world environments. This distinction is important because listening in everyday contexts requires children to manage auditory information while simultaneously coping with attentional demands, environmental distractions, and competing stimuli. Another unresolved issue concerns whether listening difficulties differ across ADHD subtypes. ADHD is typically classified into predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive‐impulsive, and combined subtypes based on symptom patterns (APA 2022 ). However, neurocognitive evidence suggests that executive control and attentional regulation systems are affected across subtypes (Cortese et al. 2012 ; Faraone and Larsson 2019 ). Consequently, functional listening difficulties may not necessarily differ between ADHD subtypes but may instead reflect shared cognitive mechanisms influencing language processing and attentional control. Understanding how functional listening relates to language abilities within ADHD populations may have important implications for clinical assessment and intervention. Listening complaints in children with ADHD are often interpreted primarily as manifestations of behavioral inattention. However, such difficulties may also reflect vulnerabilities in language processing that interact with attentional regulation during everyday communication. Examining the relationship between listening and language abilities may, therefore, provide insight into how attentional and linguistic mechanisms jointly contribute to communication challenges in ADHD. Accordingly, the present study aimed to compare functional listening difficulties and language performance between children with predominantly inattentive and combined ADHD subtypes, and to examine associations between listening difficulties and language abilities within a clinical ADHD sample. Based on previous evidence indicating that executive dysfunction occurs across ADHD subtypes (Martinussen et al. 2005 ; Willcutt et al. 2005 ; Sarıyer et al. 2023 ), it was hypothesized that listening and language scores would not significantly differ between subtypes, but that functional listening difficulties would be associated with language performance. Clarifying these relationships may contribute to a better understanding of how attentional regulation and language processing interact in ADHD and may inform multidisciplinary approaches to the assessment and management of communication difficulties in affected children. 2 Material and Methods 2.1 Study Design This cross‐sectional observational study was conducted at the child and adolescent psychiatry outpatient clinic of Osmangazi University between June 2025 and December 2025. Participants were recruited using a convenience sampling method from children diagnosed with ADHD who attended the outpatient clinic during the study period. A total of 125 children with an established ADHD diagnosis met the eligibility criteria and were enrolled in the study. No participants were excluded after eligibility assessment, and no participants withdrew from the study. Therefore, all 125 enrolled participants were included in the final analyses. No missing data were identified for the variables included in the analyses. 2.2 Participants A total of 125 children diagnosed with ADHD participated in the study. Participants were categorized into predominantly inattentive (AD; n = 32) and combined (CT; n = 93) subtypes. The CT group included 18 females (19.4%) and 75 males (80.6%), whereas the AD group included 29 females (90.6%) and 3 males (9.4%). The median age was 6.20 years (range: 4.10–7.90) in the CT group and 6.35 years (range: 4.30–7.80) in the AD group, with no significant age difference between groups ( p = 0.29). ADHD diagnoses were established by a child and adolescent psychiatrist according to DSM‐5 criteria. Children with comorbid neurodevelopmental or psychiatric disorders, hearing impairment, neurological conditions, or IQ below 85 were excluded. Because of the marked difference in sex distribution between the ADHD subtypes, sex was included as a covariate in the primary regression analysis. Other potentially relevant clinical and sociodemographic variables, including ADHD symptom severity, medication status, caregiver sex and relationship to the child, caregiver educational level, and socioeconomic background, were not systematically collected and, therefore, could not be included in the statistical models. 2.3 Data Collection Process Participants were recruited from a child and adolescent psychiatry outpatient clinic. Functional listening difficulties were assessed using the Children's Home Inventory for Listening Difficulties (C.H.I.L.D.), and language abilities were evaluated with the Test of Early Language Development (TELD‐3:T). Caregivers completed the C.H.I.L.D. questionnaire, while language assessments were administered directly to children. Data collection was conducted by a multidisciplinary team including a speech‐language therapist, an audiologist, and a child psychiatrist, in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. This study was approved by the Anadolu University Health Sciences Scientific Research and Publication Ethics Committee (Protocol No: 889468; Approval Date: May 28, 2025). Written informed consent was obtained from the parents or legal guardians of all participating children prior to data collection. All procedures were conducted in accordance with the ethical standards of the institutional research committee and the Declaration of Helsinki. 2.4 Measurements 2.4.1 Children's Home Inventory for Listening Difficulties Questionnaire The C.H.I.L.D. questionnaire (Anderson and Smaldino 2000 ) assesses listening difficulties in everyday situations. The family member version (C.H.I.L.D.–FM), designed for children aged 3–12 years, was used in the present study. The Turkish version has demonstrated strong validity and reliability (Yıldırım Gökay et al. 2024 ). The scale includes subdomains assessing listening in quiet, noise, distance, social settings, and media contexts. 2.4.2 Test of Early Language Development The Turkish version of the TELD‐3:T was used to assess participants’ receptive and expressive language development. The original TELD‐3 was developed by Hresko et al. ( 1999 ). The normative sample for the Turkish validity and reliability study consisted of 1200 typically developing children aged between 18 months and 8 years (Topbaş&Güven 2011 ). The findings demonstrated that the TELD‐3:T has strong and statistically significant validity and reliability. Furthermore, the test was shown to accurately assess receptive and expressive language skills and to identify children with language delays and language disorders. The TELD‐3:T combines verbal instructions with visual stimuli, such as objects or pictures, to which the child is expected to respond. In the current study, TELD‐3:T results were presented as spoken language standard scores. The overall spoken language development score was calculated by combining the receptive and expressive language scores. 2.5 Statistical Analysis Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 23.0. The normality of continuous variables was assessed using histograms, probability plots, and the Kolmogorov–Smirnov and Shapiro–Wilk tests. Because the variables were not normally distributed, continuous variables were summarized using medians and minimum–maximum values, and categorical variables were summarized using frequencies and percentages. The primary analysis was defined as an adjusted linear regression examining the association between total C.H.I.L.D. score and TELD‐3 language score in the full sample. Age, gender, and ADHD subtype were entered as covariates in the first step, followed by the total C.H.I.L.D. score in the second step. To examine whether the association between total C.H.I.L.D. score and language performance differed according to ADHD subtype, a C.H.I.L.D.‐by‐ADHD‐subtype interaction term was entered in a third step. The total C.H.I.L.D. score was mean‐centered before the construction of the interaction term. Between‐group differences in C.H.I.L.D. and TELD‐3 scores were examined using the Mann–Whitney U test. title: How the Brain Interprets Pain in Autistic People: Does Sex Matter?
abstract:
ABSTRACT Background While psychophysical studies suggest heightened pain sensitivity in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), the relationship between subjective pain experience and cortical neurophysiological responses and whether this relationship is sex‐dependent, remains poorly understood. Methods This cross‐sectional two‐group comparison study included 50 adults with Level 1 ASD and 52 age‐, sex‐ and IQ‐matched typically developing controls (TDC). Pain ratings and cortical contact heat‐evoked potentials (CHEPs) were recorded in response to 52°C phasic heat stimuli. ANOVA and regression models assessed the effects of group, sex and pain ratings on CHEP amplitudes. Results Compared to TDC, autistic participants reported higher pain scores ( p = 0.004) and had lower N 2 amplitudes ( p = 0.02). A significant Group × Sex interaction ( p < 0.001) was associated with the lowest N 2 amplitudes in autistic females ( p < 0.05). Regardless of group, in females, higher N 2 amplitudes were associated with higher pain scores ( p = 0.042; model p = 0.032), whereas this association was not significant in males ( p > 0.05). Within‐group correlation analyses in females showed a significant pain–N 2 amplitude relationship in TDC ( r = 0.734; p = 0.004) but not in autistic participants ( r = 0.371; p = 0.192). Across groups and sexes, higher N 2 amplitude values were associated with greater attention‐to‐detail autistic traits ( p = 0.009). Conclusions Our findings suggest a dissociation between subjective pain experience and cortical responses to nociceptive stimulation in autism, particularly among females, consistent with different salience‐related or attentional pain processing. These results underscore the importance of considering sex and autism when interpreting pain‐evoked cortical responses and challenge the assumption that pain‐evoked potentials provide universally objective measures of pain. Significance This study identifies sex‐related differences in the relationship between subjective pain ratings and cortical responses to nociceptive stimulation in autistic and typically developing individuals. Autistic females showed particularly attenuated N 2 amplitudes and a weaker correspondence between pain ratings and cortical responses, suggesting different salience‐related or attentional processing of nociceptive stimuli. These findings highlight the importance of considering sex and autistic traits when interpreting pain‐evoked cortical responses in autism.

1 Introduction Autism represents a group of neurodevelopmental conditions associated with changes in cognitive, emotional, social and behavioural changes (Association 2013 ). Differences in activity of central neural circuits in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), including autistic people with low support needs, are reflected in differences in brain metabolism (Tebartz van Elst et al. 2014 ; Wood et al. 2021 ) and structural and functional cortical organisation (Conti et al. 2017 ; Rane et al. 2015 ). These differences might translate into an imbalance of the excitation‐inhibition equilibrium of cortical networks which, in turn, is related to autistic symptoms. The reports on pain sensitivity in autism are contradictory; while some studies did not reveal differences between ASD and typically‐developed controls (TDC) participants (Failla et al. 2018 ; Vaughan et al. 2020 ), others report enhanced pain sensitivity to experimental stimuli (Asmika et al. 2018 ; Dubois et al. 2020 ; Failla et al. 2020 ; Vaughan et al. 2020 ). Our recent findings confirmed the latter, pointing towards a pro‐nociceptive psychophysical profile in ASD Level 1 (Hoffman et al. 2023 ). However, whether the psychophysical profile correlates with neurophysiological pain‐evoked responses in ASD has not been systematically studied. The cortical pain‐evoked potentials (pain EPs) are considered objective measures of perceived experimental pain, providing information on endogenous processing of nociceptive signals in response to noxious stimuli, manifested in the amplitude and latency of the N 2 P 2 components. There is a positive relationship between perceived pain and the amplitudes of pain EPs in healthy individuals, with females showing higher amplitudes (Chao et al. 2007 ; Granovsky et al. 2016 ; Granovsky et al. 2008 ; Roberts et al. 2008 ; Valeriani et al. 2012 ). Moreover, decreased pain scores in response to psychological or pharmacological analgesic manipulations are linked to decreased pain EPs amplitudes (Lier et al. 2020 ; Moont et al. 2011 ; Paloyelis et al. 2016 ; Truini et al. 2010 ). The described relationship between pain perception and pain EP amplitude in healthy individuals may position this measure as a sensitive and reliable physiological parameter for evaluating individual sensory profiles in various clinical situations. The relationship between pain behavioural and neurophysiological responses in individuals with neurodevelopmental conditions is of high research and clinical interest. However, to the best of our knowledge, this has not been systematically studied in autistic people. Currently, there are only two published reports that address pain EPs in ASD (Chien et al. 2020 ; Chien et al. 2017 ), noting relationships between autistic behavioural characteristics and pain EPs (Chien et al. 2017 ). However, these studies did not aim to explore the association between pain‐evoked psychophysical and neurophysiological responses, nor did they examine the role of sex. In this project, we aimed to evaluate the relationship between psychophysical and cortical neurophysiological correlates of pain‐evoked responses in adults with ASD Level 1. We hypothesised that due to the structural differences and underlying functional and neurochemical changes in the brains of autistic individuals, the relationships between subjective and objective pain characteristics will differ from those presented in TDC. We also hypothesised that these differences may be sex‐related. 2 Methods The institutional review board of the Rambam Health Care Campus (# 0496‐17), Tel Aviv University (# 0001123‐1) and University of Haifa (# 064/18) approved the study protocol in accordance with the Helsinki Declaration. Each patient signed a written informed consent form prior to commencing the experiment in the presence of a physician. 2.1 Participants Participants diagnosed with ASD Level 1 (low support needs) aged 18–55 years, verified according to the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule—Second Edition (ADOS‐2) interview performed by ADOS‐2 certified assessors, as well as age‐ and sex‐matched typically developing control (TDC) subjects, were recruited by a convenience snowball sampling from several autistic centers in the country and the general population, respectively, between May 2018 and November 2021. Inclusion criteria for both groups required no language barriers. Exclusion criteria for both groups included reporting on chronic pain diagnoses, pregnancy, scores lower than 80 on the verbal, performance and full‐scale IQ as measured by the Wechsler Abbreviated Scale of Intelligence—Second Edition (WASI‐II). In addition, the exclusion criteria for the TDC group included any neurological or psychiatric disorders. All participants were asked to avoid the use of analgesics, medication for attention‐deficit hyperactivity disorder and any sedative drugs 24 h prior to the experimental testing. 2.2 Study Design This is a cross‐sectional two‐group comparison study, described in detail in our recently published papers (please see Hoffman et al. 2023 ; Kalingel Levi et al. 2025 ). In the present paper, we explore the relationships between psychophysical and neurophysiological correlates of contact heat pain EPs in autistic and neurotypical males and females and their correlations with the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ) sub‐scales of Attention Switching Difficulty and Attention to Details (Baron‐Cohen et al. 2001 ). 2.3 Contact Heat‐Evoked Potentials ( CHEPs ) Stimulation Parameters CHEPs were recorded in response to the phasic heat stimuli at 52°C. Twenty phasic stimuli per block, given at the inter‐stimulus interval of 10 s, onset‐to‐onset, were applied to the upper volar aspect of the forearm on the right side and were slightly repositioned after each stimulus to avoid spatial summation. The heat stimuli were delivered by a 27‐mm diameter thermode that covered an area of 572.5 mm 2 (PATHWAY, Sensory Analyser System; Medoc, Israel). The baseline temperature was set at 32°C, the temperature increase and decrease rates were 70°C/s and 40°C/s, respectively. After each stimulus, the participants were asked to verbally rate their pain on a 0–100 numeric pain scale (NPS). 2.4 CHEPS Recording The recording was performed with a 64 ActiCHamp Brain Vision system (Brain Products GmbH, Munich, Germany). The sampling rate was set to 500 Hz with a 0.15–100 Hz bandpass filter and a notch filter of 50 Hz to reduce electrical noise interference. Each electrode's impedance was lowered to 20 kΩ or less. The reference electrode was placed on the bridge of the participant's nose. The ground electrode was placed on the forehead. 2.5 CHEPS Analyses The Cz (vertex) recordings, where the pain‐evoked potentials were reported to consistently demonstrate the largest amplitudes (Bromm and Lorenz 1998 ), were processed and analysed. Each recording epoch of 1500 ms included a period of 500 ms for baseline correction of single trials. Stimulus onset was marked by a TTL pulse from the CHEPs to the EEG system at the onset of the temperature increase. Subject data were included in further statistical analyses if there were at least 10 well‐identified evoked potential waveforms, free from blinking and eye movement, or muscle artefacts, within the 250‐ to 800‐ms time window after stimulus onset. We determined the amplitude and latency of the N 2 and P 2 peaks and the N 2 P 2 amplitude, on the averaged waveform from all artefact‐free traces. To minimise measuring errors, we excluded recordings with N 2 P 2 amplitude less than 5 μV from the analysis, which would have been of similar amplitude as the background electroencephalographic activity (Granovsky et al. 2016 ) and therefore considered as undetectable. 2.6 Statistical Analysis JMP (SAS Institute, Cary, NC) was used for statistical analyses. Demographic parameters, pain scores and CHEPs characteristics were compared using t ‐tests or non‐parametric comparisons, as appropriate. To improve data normality and comply with ANOVA's residual error assumptions, the CHEPs parameters underwent log transformation; for the same reason, the pain score values underwent the arcsine square root transformation. Note that on back‐transformation to original units, for graphical presentation, the amplitude values in the ANOVA models are presented as geometric means with asymmetric 95% upper and lower confidence limits (95% CL). ANOVA models explored the influence of group (ASD or TCD), pain‐evoked reports, sex and their interactions, on N 2 , P 2 and N 2 P 2 CHEPs amplitudes. The parameter of sex was included in the ANOVA models given its widely‐reported effect on pain EPs amplitudes (Granovsky et al. 2016 ; Roberts et al. 2008 ) and on the amplitudes of event‐related potentials (ERPs), in general (Conroy and Polich 2007 ; Hoffman and Polich 1999 ). Since the factor of sex was included in the CHEPs analysis, it was also included in the ANOVA model that tested the Group, Sex and their interaction on the pain scores. Further, following Chien et al.'s ( 2017 ) approach who tested the relationships between the AQ questionnaire‐based autistic traits (Baron‐Cohen et al. 2001 ) for attention and the CHEPS components amplitude of significant group difference, 3 additional ANOVA models tested the effect of attention characteristics via the AQ, a 50‐item self‐report measuring five domains linked to ASD, sub‐scores (the Attention to Detail and the Attention Switching Difficulty) on the relevant amplitude and their interaction with the factors of Group and Sex. Mood's non‐parametric median test was applied for the group comparison of CHEPs characteristics and the pain scores. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. 3 Results 3.1 Demographic and Descriptive Characteristics of the Study Population One hundred eighty‐three participants ( N = 95 were diagnosed with ASD Level 1) signed the consent form. ASD diagnosis had not been confirmed according to the ADOS‐2 in 16 participants; in addition, 2 autistic individuals had discontinued their participation and 3 were excluded based on the WASI‐II score < 80, resulting in 74 autistic individuals entered into the study. Further, the pain EPs recordings were missing or discontinued in 10 autistic persons for technical reasons ( N = 1) or refusal to undergo or complete the testing due to sensory reactivity ( N = 9). Thus, the autistic group for this study consisted of 64 participants. The TDC group included 87 participants (among 88 consented persons, one discontinued). Further, 25 TDC were identified with sensory modulation dysfunction (SMD)—a difficulty in regulating responses to sensory stimuli manifested as over‐ or under‐responsiveness and documented with altered brain activity (Granovsky et al. 2019 ) and therefore excluded. Thus, in total, this study comprised 64 participants diagnosed with ASD Level 1 and 62 TDC participants whose pain EPs recordings were completed. A detectable free of artefacts N 2 P 2 waveform in response to contact heat stimulation at 52°C was demonstrated in 50 autistic participants (15 females) and 52 TDC (13 females). Among the study participants, 20 reported routine use of one or more psychiatric medications (ASD = 18). Eleven individuals used antidepressants, 15 used antipsychotic medications and 6 used both. The TDC sub‐group was slightly older than that of the autistic sub‐group (28 years, range 18–47 vs. 24 years, range 19–50, p = 0.049). No IQ (WASI) group differences were detected (111.6 ± 11.2, ASD vs. 112.7 ± 9.4, TDC, p = 0.518). The descriptive data for CHEPs and pain responses are presented in Table 1 . 3.2 The Effect of Group and Sex Factors on the Pain Scores In line with our previously published data (Hoffman et al. 2023 ), a significant Group effect ( p = 0.004, model p = 0.021) was found, confirming higher pain perception in autistic individuals.
