title: Electrodermal Activity as a Metric of Arousal in Autistic Children Prior to Dental Treatment
abstract: Several prominent theories have asserted atypical arousal as a biological feature of autism. However, there is mixed evidence regarding atypical arousal patterns, particularly resting-state arousal, in autistic children, with research increasingly using psychophysiological measures, such as electrodermal activity (EDA), to help elucidate arousal levels in individuals who might not otherwise be able to identify such states. This study analyzed extant EDA data from 135 autistic children (6-12 years) collected during a baseline rest period in a dental environment to determine the relationships between tonic (mean skin conductance level; SCL) and phasic (frequency of non-specific skin conductance responses; NS-SCRs) arousal and participant characteristics, including sensory over-responsiveness, autism traits, expressive language, and general anxiety. EDA data were collected using pre-gelled electrodes placed on the distal phalanges of the participant's non-dominant hand using the BIOPAC MP150 system. Data preprocessing and epoch analyses were conducted using BIOPAC AcqKnowledge software. Conditional linear and, for the outcome variable anxiety, quadratic growth models were used to assess the temporal (within-participant across observations) relationship between EDA and behavioral variables. The results revealed a significant time-by-autism trait interaction for SCL, as well as linear and quadratic relationships between anxiety and NS-SCRs. No significant relationships were found between EDA arousal parameters and sensory over-responsiveness or expressive language abilities. A significant covariance relationship between SCL and NS-SCR frequency was also observed. Collectively, these results support previous characterizations of unique, within-autism-population arousal profiles related to autism traits, anxiety, and tonic-to-phasic covariance patterns.

title: Phenotypic Complexity and Diagnostic Utility of Exome Sequencing in ASD: Real-World Insights from Colombia
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a genetically heterogeneous condition; however, genomic data from Latin American populations remain limited. We investigated the molecular and phenotypic landscape of ASD in 916 Colombian patients who underwent whole-exome sequencing (WES) between 2022 and 2025. Clinical and genomic data were retrospectively analyzed, and phenotypes were standardized using Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms. Variants were classified per ACMG/ClinGen guidelines, and we assessed phenotypic burden, predictors of molecular diagnosis, copy number variants (CNVs), and functional convergence of candidate genes. A molecular diagnosis was identified in 112 patients (12.2%), including 82 with variants in ASD-associated genes or regions and 30 with findings related to other clinical features. We identified 16 novel pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants, along with 10 CNVs. Among trio-based patients, 70.9% of molecular diagnoses were de novo. Higher phenotypic burden was associated with molecular diagnosis, and global developmental delay was the strongest predictor after correction for multiple testing. Functional enrichment analysis of candidate genes showed convergence on pathways related to neuronal development, synaptic function, and ion transport. These findings highlight the genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity of ASD and support the value of integrating standardized genomic and phenotypic characterization in Colombian populations.

title: Ophthalmologic manifestations in children with autism spectrum disorder
abstract:
PURPOSE: To determine the frequency and clinical characteristics of ophthalmologic manifestations in children aged ≤16 years with autism spectrum disorder who were evaluated at a private academic healthcare network and a public tertiary hospital.

METHODS: This retrospective descriptive study was conducted through a review of the medical records of children aged <16 years with autism spectrum disorder who were examined between 2023 and 2024. Demographic characteristics, visual function testability, refractive errors, strabismus, and prescribed treatments were analyzed. Dynamic retinoscopy was used to objectively assess the binocular accommodative response. Statistical analyses included 95% confidence intervals (Wilson score method) and exploratory multivariate logistic regression.

RESULTS: A total of 144 children were included; 79.2% were male, and the mean age was 6.3±2.7 years. Refractive errors were identified in 81.9% of children, of whom 63.2% had clinically significant errors requiring optical correction. Strabismus was diagnosed in 32.6% of cases, with exotropia being the most prevalent type. Stereopsis was successfully assessed in 72.2% of children. Notably, dynamic retinoscopy demonstrated perfect agreement (κ=1.000, p<0.001) with the presence of clinically significant refractive errors. Multivariate regression showed that increasing age was strongly associated with successful visual acuity testing, whereas neurological comorbidities and greater autism spectrum disorder severity significantly increased the odds of non-testability. Among children who continued follow-up, 63.9% experienced significant improvement in visual acuity. Although optical correction was generally well tolerated, adherence to occlusion therapy was notably low (6.8%), and 42.4% of the cohort was lost to follow-up.

CONCLUSIONS: Ophthalmologic abnormalities, particularly refractive errors and strabismus, are highly prevalent among children with autism spectrum disorder. Given the limited reliability of subjective visual assessment in this population, objective measures, particularly dynamic retinoscopy and cycloplegic refraction, are essential for accurate diagnosis. The substantial loss to follow-up further highlights the need for adapted clinical strategies to ensure continuity of ophthalmologic care in this population.

title: To Collapse or not to Collapse Multiple Measures of the Same Psychological Construct: A Demonstration Across 14 Independent Studies of Autistic and Non-Autistic Children
abstract:
Large data repositories provide a valuable opportunity to combine multiple independent studies, creating large samples that can address questions not achievable within a single study. However, independent studies often use different instruments to measure the same behavior or psychological construct, such as cognitive ability, social functioning, or psychopathology. Investigators often combine samples that include different instruments under the assumption that instruments assessing the same construct capture the same underlying phenomenon. Yet this assumption of instrument interchangeability may be wrong. Collapsing different instruments into a single variable could introduce bias. Here, we established a quantitative method to demonstrate compatibility among multiple instruments with moderation analyses. We illustrate this method in domains of cognitive ability, anxiety symptoms, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder symptoms as exemplars that might interact with outcomes of interest (autistic features instruments). A total of 1,352 participants were included from autistic and non-autistic samples across 14 independent studies. Our findings suggest that within this sample, some commonly used instruments within a domain can be acceptably combined, whereas others demonstrate discrepant relationships with outcomes of interest. More importantly, we offer a generalizable approach for scientists seeking to leverage existing datasets for secondary analyses. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s10802-026-01512-4 .

Introduction A primary challenge to mental health research is identifying the precise relationship between brain imaging data and clinical phenotypes. Most studies are limited by small samples (Button et al., 2013 ; Yarkoni, 2009 ). Complex brain and behavior relationships are likely small effects that require thousands of participants to identify reliable and meaningful results (Marek et al., 2022 ). One path to address the gap is completing coordinated, large-scale multi-site studies, such as the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study (Casey et al., 2018 ) or a very large single-site study like the Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort (Calkins et al., 2015 ; Satterthwaite et al., 2014 ; Satterthwaite et al., 2016 ) that collect cognitive and mental health phenotype data and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans at a scale that is not typically available for most studies. These approaches are effective for studying neurocognitive development but require a significant investment from a funder and study coordination by project leaders. An alternative and cost-effective approach to generating a large-scale dataset is aggregating data from multiple small-scale, single-site studies. Research in the field of autism has produced two well-known efforts of such data aggregation: The National Database for Autism Research (Hall et al., 2012 ) and the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (Di Martino et al., 2014 ). The biggest challenge in post-hoc data aggregation is harmonizing behavioral and cognitive data from multiple independent studies that were conducted without knowledge of the future aggregation. Data harmonization, as defined by Cheng et al., ( 2024 ), refers to “the practice of combining different datasets to maximize their comparability or compatibility” (pp. 1). While attention has been given to combining or harmonizing MRI data (Fortier et al., 2016 ; Fortin et al., 2017 , Shen et al., 2025 ), behavioral and cognitive phenotypic data are often assumed to be comparable across studies with little to no quantitative assessment demonstrating their comparability. A common strategy is to combine different instruments that are believed to assess the same construct. For example, investigators may choose to administer different measures to estimate intellectual ability within their studies, such as the Differential Abilities Scales, 2nd Edition, Wechsler Intelligence Scales for Children, 4th Edition (now 5th Edition), or Wechsler Abbreviated Scales of Intelligence, 2nd Edition (Elliott, 2007 ; Wechsler, 2003 , 2011 ). When merging data across studies with these various cognitive instruments, scientists may collapse the Full-Scale IQ scores, 2- and 4-subtest estimate Full-Scale IQ scores, and the General Conceptual Ability scores from these measures into a singular “Full-Scale IQ” variable. While this approach is common (Bertollo & Yerys, 2019 ; Cola et al., 2022 ; Granader et al., 2014 ; Pugliese et al., 2015 ; Ratto et al., 2018 ; Yerys et al., 2019 ), there is limited empirical data supporting it as an appropriate strategy other than psychometric testing showing correlations between cognitive assessments among children hovering around r = 0.8 (Sattler, 2018 ). One concern with this collapsing approach is that, even if the instruments are moderately correlated, they may relate differently to one’s outcome of interest. For example, if various intellectual ability instruments have demonstrably distinct relationships to measures of social function in autistic individuals, then employing this collapsing approach in control variables for brain–behavior analyses related to social function may distort the outcomes. If our goal with big data is to elucidate relationships between brain and behavior measures, then we would not want these relationships to be biased by our collapsing approach. This concern exists for collapsing both primary behavior outcome measures (e.g., social function measures), as well as commonly controlled variables that interact with outcome measures (i.e., cognitive ability). Prior studies addressed this harmonization issue through advanced statistical modeling with item-level data or meta-analytic tools (van den Heuvel et al., 2020 ; Penberthy et al., 2005 ). The item-level analyses are elegant in their use of item-response theory and factor analysis to derive harmonized latent traits of a construct (e.g., memory). However, item-level data are not always available in aggregated datasets such as the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (Di Martino et al., 2014 ). Meta-analytic tools are ideal when the same instrument or nearly identical instruments are used across studies. For example, combining multiple measures of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) can be easier with meta-analytic tools that take advantage of measures based on the 18 diagnostic symptoms of ADHD (e.g., ADHD Rating Scale (DuPaul et al., 1998 ), Vanderbilt ADHD Diagnostic Parent Rating Scale (Bard et al., 2013 )). Unfortunately, many tools do not sample all 18 diagnostic symptoms, such as the Child Behavior Checklist (Achenbach et al., 2001 ). Thus, there is a critical need to develop analytic tools that harmonize phenotypic measures for which only aggregate data and scores are available, or the scales are not easily aligned at the level of individual items. By developing robust harmonization methods for diverse phenotypic measures of a construct, scientists can have confidence that collapsing multiple measures will not bias the results. Consider a hypothetical study that will probe brain and behavioral relationships with aggregated data from N different sites to understand autistic features. All sites use the same measures, including the Social Responsiveness Scale (SRS-2), quantifying autistic traits; the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule, 2nd Edition (ADOS-2), assessing observed autistic behaviors; and Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales (VABS)-Socialization Scale, capturing social autistic features. In contrast, the sites had a wide variety of instruments measuring cognitive ability, anxiety, or attentional problems. To control for the impact of these cognitive and co-occurring mental health factors on brain and behavior relationships related to autistic features, researchers may want to collapse the cognitive instruments into a single variable, as well as collapse relevant clinical instruments (e.g., anxiety or ADHD measures) into respective single variables. However, if various measures of cognitive functioning, anxiety, or ADHD have systematically different relationships with the autistic features outcome measures, then this collapsing approach could lead to biased results when included in brain-behavior analyses as control variables. Then the question is, should the researchers in this hypothetical study collapse those various instruments or not? Here, we addressed this exact question. We evaluated potential bias in collapsing various instruments of IQ, anxiety symptoms, and ADHD symptoms as they relate to autistic features instruments in a large-scale study that aggregated data from many smaller-scale studies in a post-hoc manner. The aggregated data comes from the Connectomic Heterogeneity in Autism Research through Multi-site dMRI harmonization (CHARM) project (5R01MH117807-05) (Shen et al., 2025 ). Studies of autistic and non-autistic children were our test case for this method. However, this method is applicable for any analysis of large, post-hoc aggregated datasets. Methods Participants 1,352 participants between the ages of 4 and 42 were included in analyses (Table 1 ). sample predominantly consists of a pediatric age range ( N = 1,282), with some studies recruiting individuals 18 + years of age ( N = 70). 812 participants had a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder, and 540 were classified as non-autistic (Non-ASD). Data were obtained across 14 studies from 7 independent study sites ([1] Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP)); [2] Georgetown University; [3] University of Wisconsin-Madison. (UW-Madison); Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) sites: [4] New York University, [5] Barrow Neurological Institute (BNI), [6] San Diego State University, [7] Trinity College Dublin. BNI and CHOP contributed a study of individuals up to age 25, and another study from CHOP recruited autistic adults ages 25 to 42. 44 participants were included with Full Scale IQ < 70 (See Table S1 for breakdown by site). Measures Autistic Features Measures. [1] Social Responsiveness Scale: Second Edition (SRS-2, Constantino & Gruber, 2012 ) is a validated 65-item informant report, 4-point Likert scale rating of autistic traits. Higher scores indicate more social difficulties. SRS-2 Total T-scores were used for analysis (standardization sample mean (M) = 50; standard deviation (SD) = 10). [2] Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS): The ADOS (Lord et al., 2000 ) is a validated, semi-structured observational assessment designed to elicit autistic behaviors to inform diagnosis. We used the 10-point calibrated severity score rating (Range = 1–10) (Gotham et al., 2009 ; Hus & Lord, 2014 ). [3] The Socialization Domain from the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales-2nd, Edition (VABS; Sparrow et al., 2016 ) is an informant interview or report of adaptive social functioning on a 3-point scale (0 (never), 1 (sometimes), and 2 (usually or often)). This scale captures social functioning that occurs without prompting or assistance. For this analysis, the Socialization domain (VABS-Socialization) Standard Score was used (M = 100 and SD = 15). Cognitive Ability Measures . [1] The General Conceptual Ability score was taken from the Differential Ability Scale, Second Edition (DAS-II; Elliott, 2007 ). [2] The 4-test or 2-test Full Scale IQ score, whichever was reported by the study, was taken from the Wechsler Abbreviated Scale of Intelligence, Second Edition (WASI-II; Wechsler, 2011 ). [3] The Full-Scale IQ score was taken from the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, Fourth Edition (WISC-IV; Wechsler, 2003 ). Cognitive ability scores from other measures (KBIT-2, (Kaufman & Kaufman, 2004 ; WISC-5; Wechsler, 2014 ) are included in reported sample characteristics (Table 1 ); however, these instruments were not included in the cognitive ability harmonization due to insufficient sample size. All cognitive measures used standard scores where the standardization sample M = 100 and SD = 15. Anxiety and ADHD Measures. [1] Screen for Child Anxiety Related Disorders (SCARED; Birmaher et al., 1997 ) is a 41-item scale that captures total childhood anxiety symptoms. Total raw scores were included in analyses (Range = 0 to 82). [2] Behavior Assessment System for Children - Second Edition (BASC; Reynolds & Kamphaus, 2006 ) is a multidimensional measure of clinical and adaptive behavior and personality. For this study, the anxiety (BASC-ANX) and attention (BASC-ATTN) subscales were included in the analyses. T-scores were used for analysis (standardization sample mean (M = 50; SD = 10)). [3] The Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL; Achenbach, 1999 ) is an instrument measuring behavioral/emotional problems. For this analysis, the attention problems (CBCL-ATTN) and anxiety problems (CBCL-ANX) subscales are included in analyses. T-scores were used for analysis (M = 50; SD = 10). [4] ADHD Rating Scale for Children and Adolescents (ADHD-RS; DuPaul et al., 2016 ) measures the frequency and severity of all 18 ADHD behaviors in youth with a 0 (Never/Rarely) to 3 (Very Often) score. Total raw scores were included in analyses (Range = 0 to 54). Analysis We used linear ordinary least squares regressions to identify whether the relationship between score (IQ, attention, anxiety) and multiple reference measures of social behavior is significantly moderated by the instrument type. Each regression model included a ‘collapsed’ domain score (IQ, anxiety, or ADHD) as the dependent variable, a binary variable for coding the specific instrument type (e.g., 0 = DAS-II; 1 = WASI-II; see Table 2 ), a variable for the reference social measure (outcome of interest), and an interaction term for the instrument type and the reference social measure. For anxiety and ADHD domains, some summary variables were standardized scores, and others were raw scores. The SCARED and the ADHD Rating Scale provided raw score counts, and these scores were not adjusted in primary analyses. However, in supplemental analyses, we extracted residuals for age (Table S3 ). A significant interaction term in predicting the dependent variable indicated that the included instruments were non-equivalent in their relationship with the reference measure and should not be combined within a study using that reference measure as a variable of interest. For example, if a ‘collapsed’ IQ score was significantly predicted by the interaction of our reference social measure (e.g., Social Responsiveness Scale, 2nd Edition) and instrument type, we would not have combined scores from those IQ instruments into a single variable for analyses examining social skills with the Social Responsiveness Scale. Regression models also included common control variables of age, gender, and diagnosis. title: Syndromic Autism in Helsmoortel-Van der Aa Syndrome: From Clinical Suspicion to Genetic Diagnosis
abstract: Syndromic autism refers to autism spectrum disorder (ASD) occurring as part of an identifiable genetic syndrome. Helsmoortel-Van der Aa syndrome (HVDAS/ADNP syndrome) is a rare autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in the ADNP gene. We report a 10-year-old boy with ASD and intellectual disability who exhibited delayed motor and language development, characteristic facial dysmorphism, early tooth eruption, endocrine abnormalities, electroencephalography (EEG) abnormalities, and urogenital findings. Following unremarkable karyotyping and chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA), whole-exome sequencing identified a heterozygous pathogenic de novo frameshift variant, c.1239_1240del, p.(Gln414Valfs*25) in ADNP. This case emphasizes the importance of considering a syndromic etiology in children with ASD accompanied by developmental delay, dysmorphic features, neurological findings, or multisystem involvement, and supports comprehensive genetic evaluation when first-tier testing is unrevealing.

title: Gut Microbiota Composition in Helicobacter pylori-Positive Adolescents With Autism Spectrum Disorder: An Exploratory Compositional Analysis
abstract: Alterations in the gut microbiota have been implicated in autism spectrum disorder (ASD), but reported microbial profiles remain inconsistent, potentially because of heterogeneity in factors affecting gut microbial composition. Because Helicobacter pylori infection is associated with alterations in the gut microbiota, we investigated whether ASD was associated with gut microbial composition in a cohort of H. pylori-positive adolescents. This cross-sectional study included seven adolescents with ASD and 80 controls before H. pylori eradication therapy. Gut microbiota was analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, with alpha diversity, centered log-ratio-transformed genus-level abundance, and overall community composition based on Aitchison distance evaluated between groups. No significant differences were observed in alpha diversity or overall microbial community composition. At the genus level, 82 genera met the prevalence criterion for individual testing, and no association remained significant after false-discovery-rate correction. The effect estimate for Roseburia was not statistically significant in either unadjusted or adjusted analyses. These findings do not support marked differences in overall gut microbiota composition associated with ASD within this H. pylori-positive cohort; however, the small ASD sample and substantial age imbalance limit the precision and interpretation of the findings.

title: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder polygenic risk score and incidence of cognitive impairment in older adults: A prospective multicohort study
abstract:
Abstract INTRODUCTION Preliminary evidence suggests a link between attention‐deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and later‐life cognitive impairment. Whether genetic risk for ADHD, estimated using an ADHD polygenic risk score (ADHD‐PRS), is associated with incident cognitive impairment (mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's disease dementia) remains unknown. METHODS We analyzed 7761 cognitively unimpaired (CU) older adults with whole‐genome sequencing from eight cohorts participating in the Alzheimer's Disease Sequencing Project (ADSP). RESULTS During follow‐up, 1347 participants developed cognitive impairment. Ten‐year cumulative incidence was 33.8% in the highest ADHD‐PRS tertile versus 23.4% in the lowest. In Cox models, higher ADHD‐PRS remained associated with greater risk of cognitive impairment after adjustment for education, apolipoprotein E ( APOE) ε4 status, or vascular risk. PRSs for other major psychiatric disorders were not associated with cognitive impairment in the same analytic framework. In a subsample with biomarker data, the association was not modified by baseline amyloid‐β status. DISCUSSION These findings support ADHD‐PRS as a novel correlate of cognitive impairment and vulnerability in aging.

Highlights Genetic risk for ADHD was estimated using PRSs. Across eight cohorts comprising 7761 participants, higher ADHD‐PRS was associated with greater risk of incident cognitive impairment. This association remained after additional adjustment for education, APOE ε4 status, or vascular risk. PRSs for other major psychiatric disorders were not associated with cognitive impairment in the same analytic framework. Baseline Aβ status did not modify the association between ADHD‐PRS and cognitive impairment.

1 BACKGROUND Dementia affects more than 55 million people worldwide, yet the full landscape of factors contributing to late‐life cognitive decline remains incompletely understood. 1 Attention‐deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder that affects approximately 5% of school‐aged children and can persist throughout the lifespan, with prevalence estimates of ∼2.5% in young adults and ∼1% among adults older than 60 years. 2 Emerging evidence suggests that ADHD is associated with a higher risk of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and dementia. 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia, 1 and a large population‐based study reported elevated risk for AD among relatives of individuals with ADHD, suggesting a potential shared genetic risk. 11 However, studies examining ADHD and later‐life cognitive impairment remain susceptible to residual confounding, including socioeconomic factors, health behaviors, and comorbid psychiatric and medical conditions. 12 Furthermore, most studies rely solely on electronic health records to ascertain dementia and ADHD diagnosis, 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 10 which may introduce bias due to differences in healthcare access, clinician recognition, and documentation practices. Crucially, existing cohorts of individuals diagnosed with ADHD in childhood have not yet reached an age where the risk of MCI or dementia can be adequately assessed, 13 limiting the feasibility of rigorous longitudinal evaluation. These limitations have prevented firm conclusions from being drawn about whether ADHD represents a genuine risk factor for cognitive decline. To complement this literature, genetic analyses have been proposed as an alternative approach. ADHD is highly heritable, 14 with common genetic variants contributing significantly to risk. 15 The ADHD polygenic risk score (ADHD‐PRS), which aggregates the effects of common variants identified in genome‐wide association studies (GWASs), has been associated with ADHD diagnosis and related traits. 16 Therefore, ADHD‐PRS may provide a useful tool to investigate the relationship between ADHD genetic risk and late‐life cognitive outcomes. Recent studies have begun to explore whether higher ADHD‐PRS is associated with increased risk for cognitive decline in older age. 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 However, most are focused on cognitive test performance, 18 , 19 , 20 and limitations in sample size and follow‐up duration restricted their ability to examine progression to clinical MCI or dementia. To address these gaps, we aimed to evaluate whether genetic risk for ADHD, estimated with an ADHD‐PRS, is associated with the risk of progression from cognitively unimpaired (CU) status to MCI or AD dementia. We further performed sensitivity analyses to explore the role of potential confounders previously associated with both ADHD and dementia, including vascular risk factors, 1 , 2 assessed possible ADHD specificity by examining PRS for other psychiatric disorders, tested whether baseline amyloid beta (Aβ) status modifies this association, and evaluated the longitudinal relationship between ADHD‐PRS and cognitive performance. RESEARCH IN CONTEXT Systematic review : The authors reviewed the literature using traditional sources, including PubMed. A growing number of studies have examined ADHD in relation to later‐life cognitive impairment. Relevant works are appropriately cited. Interpretation : Our results indicate that ADHD‐PRS, an estimate of genetic risk for ADHD, is associated with vulnerability to later‐life cognitive impairment. The absence of association with other psychiatric PRSs in the same models suggests a degree of specificity to ADHD. Clinically, the results suggest that individuals with higher ADHD genetic risk and those with diagnosed ADHD represent subgroups that may benefit from earlier/more frequent cognitive monitoring and targeted risk‐factor mitigation. Future directions : Future studies should clarify mechanisms linking ADHD‐PRS to cognitive impairment through comprehensive biomarker phenotyping, follow childhood‐diagnosed ADHD cohorts into later life with repeated assessments, and determine whether individuals with clinically diagnosed ADHD or elevated ADHD‐PRS could benefit from earlier cognitive monitoring. 2 METHODS 2.1 Participants We analyzed data from the Alzheimer's Disease Sequencing Project (ADSP), a large, multicohort collaborative initiative that integrates extensive longitudinal clinical characterization with large‐scale sequencing to accelerate discovery of genetic and other determinants of risk and resilience for AD and related dementias. 21 We included individuals who were CU at baseline and had available age, sex, education, whole‐genome sequencing (WGS), APOE genotype, clinical assessments (including diagnoses and cognitive function), and vascular risk measures. Baseline was defined as the first visit at age ≥50 years with available clinical assessment. Included cohorts were Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), Estudio Familiar de Influencia Genética en Alzheimer (EFIGA), Rush Religious Orders Study (ROS) and Rush Memory and Aging Project (MAP), National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC), Texas Alzheimer's Research and Care Consortium (TARCC), Washington Heights/Inwood Columbia Aging Project (WHICAP), and Wisconsin Registry for Alzheimer's Prevention (WRAP). Further information on each cohort can be found in the Supplementary Material (Tables S1 and S2 ). Across all cohorts, written informed consent was provided by participants, and research was conducted in accordance with approved Institutional Review Board (IRB) protocols. Secondary analysis of these data was approved by the University of Pittsburgh IRB. Complete data were available for 7761 participants. 2.2 Polygenic risk scores WGS data were obtained from ADSP Release 4, 22 generated and processed by the Genome Center for Alzheimer's Disease (GCAD). Sequencing was performed at 10 centers using Illumina technology (more details can be found elsewhere 22 ). Genetic data underwent the same robust quality control and imputation pipelines, 22 , 23 and fully quality‐controlled data were downloaded from the National Institute on Aging Genetics of Alzheimer's Disease Data Storage Site (NIAGADS). PRSs were computed using PRSice‐2 (version 2.3.5) 24 based on GWAS summary statistics for ADHD 15 and (in sensitivity analyses) autism spectrum disorder (ASD), 25 bipolar disorder (BD), 26 major depressive disorder (MDD), 27 and schizophrenia (SCZ). 28 After clumping to retain approximately independent variants (250‐kb window; LD r 2 = 0.1), we computed PRSs across 11 GWAS p value thresholds (1, 0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.005, 0.0005, 5 × 10 − 6 , 5 × 10 − 8 ). To reduce multiple testing and summarize liability robustly, we derived the first principal component (PC) across thresholds for each disorder‐specific PRS and used this score as the primary genetic liability measure. 29 PRS values were standardized (z‐scores). To investigate populational structure, principal component analysis was conducted using PLINK 2.0. 30 2.3 Clinical and cognitive outcomes Clinical diagnoses and cognitive outcomes were obtained from the ADSP Phenotype Harmonization Consortium (ADSP‐PHC) Cognitive Dataset (NIAGADS accession number: NG00067.v18). The ADSP‐PHC was established to harmonize phenotype data across multiple cohorts. ADSP‐PHC diagnostic codes (CU, MCI, AD dementia) were downloaded from NIAGADS. All cohorts included in this study had their own protocols for clinical diagnosis determination, described in cohort publications (see Tables S1 and S2 ). These protocols typically involved multidisciplinary diagnostic review and applied standard criteria. For neuropsychological outcomes, ADSP‐PHC composite scores for memory, executive function, and language were downloaded from NIAGADS. The ADSP‐PHC developed robust methods to harmonize data from the different neuropsychological batteries across cohorts, with full details found elsewhere. 31 2.4 Aβ biomarkers A subset of participants had Aβ status from positron emission tomography (PET) and/or fluid biomarkers. Aβ PET data were obtained from ADSP‐PHC PET Dataset (NIAGADS accession number: NG00067.v18), processed by NIAGADS using magnetic resonance imaging‐free pipelines with tracer‐specific transformation of global Aβ standardized uptake value ratio to Centiloids. Further information on processing can be found in ADSP‐PHC‐FluidBiomarker_White‐Paper_2024.12.16.pdf, available via NIAGADS. PET‐derived Aβ positivity was defined using a single Centiloid threshold of 25 across tracers, using the harmonized variable (“PHC_AMYLOID_STATUS”) after quality control. Fluid‐derived Aβ status was obtained from the ADSP‐PHC Biomarker Dataset (NIAGADS accession number: NG00067.v18), which harmonized cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) Aβ42 data across cohorts. Further methodological information on the harmonization steps can be found in ADSP‐PHC‐FluidBiomarker_White‐Paper_2024.12.16.pdf, available via NIAGADS. In summary, fluid‐derived Aβ positivity was defined using Gaussian mixture models to determine cutoffs and represented by the harmonized variable “AT_class.” For analyses with individuals with Aβ data, we defined “Aβ‐baseline” as the first clinical assessment at age ≥50 years with an available Aβ measurement (PET and/or fluid). If both PET and fluid were available at the same qualifying visit, PET was prioritized. Time‐to‐event models in the biomarker subsample used this Aβ‐baseline as time zero. 2.5 APOE ε4 status Apolipoprotein E ( APOE ) ε2/ε3/ε4 haplotypes were determined using rs429358 and rs7412. APOE ε4 status was modeled as ε4 carrier (≥1 ε4) versus non‐carrier. 2.6 Vascular risk score Harmonized vascular risk scores were obtained from the ADSP‐PHC Cardiovascular Risk Factor Dataset (NIAGADS accession number: NG00067.v18). They were computed as the first PC summarizing cardiovascular risk indicators (binary history of hypertension, diabetes, heart disease, and stroke, as well as continuous body mass index) and represented by the harmonized variable “PHC_PC1_All.” Further methodological information can be found in ADSP‐PHC‐CardiovascularRisk_README_2024.12.16.docx, available via NIAGADS. 2.7 Statistical analyses Kaplan–Meier methods were used to estimate the 10‐year cumulative incidence of cognitive impairment under right‐censoring and to visualize unadjusted differences across PRS tertiles (high vs low). We modeled progression from CU status to incident cognitive impairment (MCI or AD dementia) using Cox proportional hazards models, with ADHD‐PRS as a continuous predictor. Time was measured from baseline to first incident diagnosis, censored at last follow‐up or 10 years. This analytic window was selected to limit the influence of less stable estimates from sparse later follow‐up. Primary models adjusted for baseline age, sex, ancestry (first three PCs), and cohort. We then fitted three additional sensitivity models, each adding one of the following variables: education, vascular risk, or APOE ε4 status. To evaluate specificity, we repeated these models using PRS for other psychiatric disorders (ASD, BD, MDD, and SCZ) as predictors, applying the same modeling framework. In the biomarker subsample, we fitted analogous Cox models anchored at Aβ‐baseline and tested effect modification by Aβ status via an ADHD‐PRS × Aβ interaction term, additionally reporting Aβ‐stratified estimates. For continuous neuropsychological outcomes, we fitted linear mixed‐effects models to harmonized domain composites with fixed effects for ADHD‐PRS, time from baseline, their interaction (PRS × time), and covariates (baseline age, sex, ancestry PCs, and cohort), with participant‐specific random intercepts and random slopes for time. The PRS main effect was interpreted as baseline differences and the PRS × time interaction as differential rate of change. To evaluate whether the primary findings were influenced by diagnostic reversion after incident MCI/AD dementia, we identified participants who developed MCI or AD dementia and subsequently returned to CU status during the 10‐year analytic follow‐up window. We classified these participants as sustained CU reverters or transient CU reverters. Sustained CU reverters were defined as participants who returned to CU after incident MCI/AD dementia and remained CU at all subsequent visits. Transient CU reverters were defined as participants who returned to CU status after incident MCI/AD dementia but later reconverted to MCI or AD dementia. We then performed a sensitivity analysis in which sustained CU reverters were treated as nonevents and censored at their last available visit, whereas transient CU reverters were retained as events.
